title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 142 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 678–692 (Night 142, continuing directly from nights-141), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. about: Night 142 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Qaḍā Fakān comes to Kān Mā Kān at midnight, chides him in verse for sleeping, and the cousins part at dawn; a slave-girl betrays her, King Sāsān draws his sword on his daughter, and Nuzhat al-Zamān holds him back, warning that the vizier Dandān has raised the provinces for Kān Mā Kān. Kān Mā Kān rides out with the Bedouin Ṣabbāḥ to raid, drives off a robber band's herds, kills the robber chief Kahrdāsh — who had taken him for the warrior-maiden Fātin he loved — and returns to Baghdad in triumph. Sāsān's courtiers swear to kill him; Sāsān sends the emir Jāmiʿ with twenty horsemen against him while he hunts, and they all fall; Sāsān himself is seized, and Kān Mā Kān, keeping a vow not to eat until he is avenged, finds him a prisoner, spares him and brings him home to a hero's welcome. Sāsān, still plotting, sets the old slave-woman Bākūn on Kān Mā Kān with a poisoned dagger, and she begins to beguile him with a story of a ruined lover in a bath-house. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَالْأَرْبَعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāniyatu wa-al-arbaʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the second-and-forty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and forty-second night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْعَجُوزَ لَمَّا أَتَتْ إِلَى كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَأَخْبَرَتْهُ أَنَّ بِنْتَ عَمِّكَ تُسَلِّمُ عَلَيْكَ وَهِيَ تَأْتِي إِلَيْكَ هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ فِي نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ʿajūza lammā atat ilā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-akhbarathu anna binta ʿammika tusallimu ʿalayka wa-hiya taʾtī ilayka hādhihi al-laylata fī niṣfi al-layli
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the old-woman, when she came to Kān Mā Kān and told him that “the daughter of your uncle greets you, and she is coming to you this night in the middle of the night” —
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the old woman came to Kān Mā Kān and told him, “Your cousin sends you her greeting, and she will come to you tonight at midnight,”
sentences.n: The print sets the hero's name as one word here, ماكان, as it often does; it is still Kān Mā Kān. akhbarathu anna binta ʿammika, “told him that the daughter of your uncle”: the report slides from indirect into direct speech with no “she said”, a common move in this prose. bint ʿamm, “paternal uncle's daughter”, is the ordinary word for a cousin and, in this story, the beloved. taʾtī, imperfect, here with future sense, “will come”. The sentence that lammā opens is completed in the next unit by fa-fariḥa.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَجَلَسَ يَنْتَظِرُ إِنْجَازَ وَعْدِ بِنْتِ عَمِّهِ قَضَى فَكَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa Kāna Mā Kāna wa-jalasa yantaẓiru injāza waʿdi binti ʿammihi Qaḍā Fakāna
sentences.l: — then Kān Mā Kān rejoiced, and sat waiting-for the fulfilment of the promise of the daughter of his uncle, Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān was overjoyed, and sat waiting for his cousin Qaḍā Fakān to keep her promise.
sentences.n: fa-, “then”, opens the main clause after lammā (“when … then”). jalasa yantaẓiru, “sat waiting”: a verb of beginning or remaining followed by a bare imperfect describing what he did. injāz al-waʿd, “the fulfilling of a promise”. Qaḍā Fakān stands in apposition to binti ʿammihi, “his cousin, Qaḍā Fakān”.

sentences.t: فَمَا كَانَ نِصْفُ اللَّيْلِ إِلَّا وَهِيَ أَتَتْهُ بِمُلَاءَةٍ سَوْدَاءَ مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ وَدَخَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَنَبَّهَتْهُ مِنْ نَوْمِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-mā kāna niṣfu al-layli illā wa-hiya atathu bi-mulāʾatin sawdāʾa mina al-ḥarīri wa-dakhalat ʿalayhi wa-nabbahathu min nawmihi
sentences.l: And the middle of the night was not but that she came to him with a black wrap of silk, and entered upon him, and woke him from his sleep.
sentences.i: Midnight had no sooner come than she was there, in a black silk wrap; she came in to him and woke him from his sleep.
sentences.n: mā kāna … illā wa-, “it was not (yet) … but that”, the stock way of saying that one thing happened the very moment another did. bi-mulāʾatin, “with a wrap”: bi- of accompaniment, here of what she wore; a mulāʾa is a large sheet or mantle worn over the clothes outdoors. sawdāʾ, “black”, feminine of aswad, agreeing with mulāʾa. dakhala ʿalā, “to enter in to (someone)”, to come into a person's presence.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ كَيْفَ تَدَّعِي أَنَّكَ تُحِبُّنِي وَأَنْتَ خَلِيُّ الْبَالِ نَائِمٌ عَلَى أَحْسَنِ الْحَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu kayfa taddaʿī annaka tuḥibbunī wa-anta khaliyyu al-bāli nāʾimun ʿalā aḥsani al-ḥāli
sentences.l: And she said to him: How do you claim that you love me, and you are empty-of-mind, sleeping in the best of state?
sentences.i: And she said to him, “How can you claim to love me, when here you lie with an easy mind, asleep in the best of comfort?”
sentences.n: khaliyy al-bāl, “empty of mind”, i.e. free of care, untroubled: the lover's proper state is sleeplessness. Note the rhyme of al-bāl with al-ḥāl, a touch of rhymed prose (sajʿ). wa-anta …, “while you …”: a circumstantial clause introduced by wa-.

sentences.t: فَانْتَبَهَ وَقَالَ وَاللَّهِ يَا مُنْيَةَ الْقَلْبِ إِنِّي مَا نِمْتُ إِلَّا طَمَعًا فِي خَيَالٍ مِنْكِ يَطْرُقُنِي
sentences.tr: fa-intabaha wa-qāla wa-Allāhi yā munyata al-qalbi innī mā nimtu illā ṭamaʿan fī khayālin minki yaṭruqunī
sentences.l: And he woke-up and said: By God, O desire of the heart, I did not sleep except in-hope of a phantom from you that-would-visit-me-by-night.
sentences.i: He started up and said, “By God, my heart's desire, I only slept in the hope that a vision of you might come to me in the night.”
sentences.n: munyat al-qalb, “the wish of the heart”, a common endearment. ṭamaʿan, accusative of purpose, “out of eagerness, in hope”. khayāl, the phantom or image of the beloved that visits the lover in dreams, a staple of Arabic love poetry; ṭaraqa, “to come knocking by night”, is the verb proper to such a visit.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ عَاتَبَتْهُ بِلَطِيفِ الْكَلِمَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ʿātabathu bi-laṭīfi al-kalimāti wa-anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And at that she reproached him with gentle words, and recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: At that she reproached him in gentle words and recited these verses:
sentences.n: ʿātaba, “to reproach (a friend or lover) affectionately”, the reproof of love rather than of anger. bi-laṭīfi al-kalimāt, “with the gentle of words”: adjective placed before the noun in a genitive construction, “gentle words”. anshadat taqūlu, “she recited, saying”, the stock formula introducing verse.

sentences.t:
لَوْ كُنْتَ تَصْدُقُ فِى الْمَحَبَّةِ * مَا جَنَحْتَ اِلَى الْمَنَام
يَا مُدَّعِي طُرُقِ الْمَحَبَّةِ * فِى الْمَوَدَّةِ وَالْغَرَام
وَاللّٰهِ يَا بْنَ الْعَمّ مَا * رَقَدَتْ عُيُونُ الْمُسْتَهَام
sentences.tr:
law kunta taṣduqu fī al-maḥabbati * mā janaḥta ilā al-manām
yā muddaʿī ṭuruqi al-maḥabbati * fī al-mawaddati wa-al-gharām
wa-Allāhi yā bna al-ʿammi mā * raqadat ʿuyūnu al-mustahām
sentences.l:
If you were truthful in love, * you would not have inclined to sleep.
O claimer of the ways of love, * in affection and passion,
by God, O son of the uncle, not * have slept the eyes of the love-crazed.
sentences.i:
Were you sincere in love, * you would not have given way to sleep.
You who lay claim to love's ways, * to tenderness and passion:
by God, cousin, the eyes * of one love-maddened never sleep.
sentences.n: The metre appears to be kāmil, rhyming in -ām. The print's pointing is kept as given, including فِى with undotted final yāʾ beside فِي elsewhere, and يَا بْنَ, where the alif of ibn is elided after yā (yā bna). Classical idiom would expect law … la-mā; the plain mā, “not”, is common in verse. ibn al-ʿamm, “son of the paternal uncle”, i.e. cousin. al-mustahām, “one driven out of his wits by love”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَاكَانَ ذَلِكَ مِنْ بِنْتِ عَمِّهِ اسْتَحَى مِنْهَا وَقَامَ وَاعْتَذَرَ إِلَيْهَا وَتَعَانَقَا وَتَشَاكَيَا أَلَمَ الْفِرَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Kāna Mā Kāna dhālika min binti ʿammihi istaḥā minhā wa-qāma wa-iʿtadhara ilayhā wa-taʿānaqā wa-tashākayā alama al-firāqi
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard that from the daughter of his uncle, he was ashamed before her, and rose and excused-himself to her, and the-two embraced-each-other and complained-to-each-other of the pain of the parting.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard this from his cousin, he was abashed before her; he rose and begged her pardon, and they embraced and poured out to each other the pain of their separation.
sentences.n: istaḥā, “he was ashamed”, written with a single yāʾ: a shortened form of istaḥyā, accepted by the grammarians and common in later Arabic. iʿtadhara ilā, “to apologise to”. taʿānaqā and tashākayā are dual verbs of Form VI, which expresses something done mutually: “embraced each other”, “complained to each other”.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَالَا كَذَلِكَ إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَ الْفَجْرُ وَانْتَشَرَ فِي الْآفَاقِ فَعَزَمَتْ قَضَى فَكَانَ عَلَى الذَّهَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazālā ka-dhālika ilā an ṭalaʿa al-fajru wa-intashara fī al-āfāqi fa-ʿazamat Qaḍā Fakāna ʿalā al-dhahābi
sentences.l: And the-two did not cease thus until the dawn rose and spread in the horizons, and Qaḍā Fakān resolved upon the going.
sentences.i: So they remained until the dawn broke and spread across the horizons, and Qaḍā Fakān made ready to go.
sentences.n: lam yazālā ka-dhālika, “the two did not cease (to be) thus”, i.e. they went on so. ʿazama ʿalā, “to resolve on, set out to”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ بَكَي كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَصَعَّدَ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika bakā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And at that Kān Mā Kān wept, and sent-up the sighs, and recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: At that Kān Mā Kān wept, heaved deep sighs, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: The print spells bakā, “he wept”, with a dotted final yāʾ (بكي) rather than the usual ى; the reading is not in doubt, and the spelling is kept. ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāt, “he sent up the sighs”, a stock phrase of grief: zafra is a long, deep sigh.

sentences.t:
فَيَا زَائِرِي مِنْ بَعْدِ فَرْطِ صُدُودِهِ * وَفِى الثَّغْرِ مِنْهُ الدُّرُّ فِي نَظْمِ عِقْدِهِ
فَقَبَّلْتُهُ اَلْفًا وَعَانَقْتُ قَدَّهُ * وَبِتُّ وَخَدِّي لَاصِقٌ تَحْتَ خَدِّهِ
اِلَى اَنْ اَتَى الصُّبْحُ الْمُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَنَا * كَحَدِّ حُسَامٍ لَاحَ مِنْ جَوْفِ غِمْدِهِ
sentences.tr:
fa-yā zāʾirī min baʿdi farṭi ṣudūdihi * wa-fī al-thaghri minhu al-durru fī naẓmi ʿiqdihi
fa-qabbaltuhu alfan wa-ʿānaqtu qaddahu * wa-bittu wa-khaddī lāṣiqun taḥta khaddihi
ilā an atā al-ṣubḥu al-mufarriqu baynanā * ka-ḥaddi ḥusāmin lāḥa min jawfi ghimdihi
sentences.l:
So O my visitor after the excess of his turning-away, * and in the mouth of him the pearls in the stringing of his necklace,
so I kissed him a thousand and embraced his stature, * and I passed-the-night and my cheek clinging beneath his cheek,
until came the morning, the separater between us, * like the edge of a sword that gleamed from the hollow of its scabbard.
sentences.i:
O you who visit me after so long a coldness, * whose mouth holds pearls strung like a necklace:
I kissed you a thousand times, embraced your slender form, * and all night lay with my cheek pressed close beneath your cheek,
until the morning came to part us, * like a sword's edge flashing from the hollow of its sheath.
sentences.n: The metre is ṭawīl, rhyming in -dihi. The print's pointing is kept as given, including فِى beside فِي. The beloved is spoken of in the masculine (“his turning-away”, “his cheek”), the ordinary convention of Arabic love poetry whatever the beloved's sex; the idiomatic layer turns the address into “you”. al-durr fī naẓm ʿiqdihi, “pearls in the stringing of his necklace”: the teeth, white and even. qadd, “stature”, the slender upright figure praised in the beloved. The dawn as a drawn sword is a familiar image: the white light breaks out of the dark as a blade from its sheath.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ وَدَّعَتْهُ قَضَى فَكَانَ وَرَجَعَتْ إِلَى خِدْرِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi waddaʿathu Qaḍā Fakāna wa-rajaʿat ilā khidrihā
sentences.l: And when he finished from his poem, Qaḍā Fakān bade-him-farewell and returned to her curtained-chamber.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses, Qaḍā Fakān bade him farewell and went back to her chamber.
sentences.n: khidr, the curtained private quarters of a woman of rank. The print marks the doubled dāl of waddaʿathu.

sentences.t: فَاطَّلَعَتْ عَلَى سِرِّهَا بَعْضُ الْجَوَارِي فَذَهَبَتْ جَارِيَةٌ مِنْهُنَّ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ فَأَعْلَمَتِ الْمَلِكَ سَاسَانَ فَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَيْهَا وَدَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا وَجَرَّدَ عَلَيْهَا الْحُسَامَ وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَقْتُلَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-iṭṭalaʿat ʿalā sirrihā baʿḍu al-jawārī fa-dhahabat jāriyatun minhunna ilā al-maliki fa-aʿlamati al-malika Sāsāna fa-tawajjaha ilayhā wa-dakhala ʿalayhā wa-jarrada ʿalayhā al-ḥusāma wa-arāda an yaqtulahā
sentences.l: And some of the slave-girls came-upon her secret, and a slave-girl of them went to the king and informed the king Sāsān; and he betook-himself to her, and went-in upon her, and bared against her the sword, and wanted to kill her.
sentences.i: But some of the slave-girls discovered her secret, and one of them went and told King Sāsān. He went straight to Qaḍā Fakān, came in upon her, drew his sword on her and meant to kill her.
sentences.n: iṭṭalaʿa ʿalā, “to get wind of, find out”. ḥusām, “the cutting one”, a poetic name for the sword. jarrada ʿalayhā, “bared (the sword) against her”.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ أُمُّهَا نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ بِاللَّهِ لَا تَفْعَلْ بِهَا ضَرَرًا فَإِنَّكَ إِنْ فَعَلْتَ بِهَا ضَرَرًا يَشِيعُ الْخَبَرُ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ وَتَبْقَى مُعَيَّرَةً عِنْدَ مُلُوكِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalat ʿalayhi ummuhā Nuzhatu al-Zamāni wa-qālat lahu bi-Allāhi lā tafʿal bihā ḍararan fa-innaka in faʿalta bihā ḍararan yashīʿu al-khabaru bayna al-nāsi wa-tabqā muʿayyaratan ʿinda mulūki al-zamāni
sentences.l: And there came-in upon him her mother Nuzhat al-Zamān, and said to him: By God, do not do to her harm; for if you do to her harm, the news will-spread among the people, and she will remain reproached before the kings of the age.
sentences.i: Then her mother, Nuzhat al-Zamān, came in to him and said: By God, do her no harm! For if you harm her the story will spread among the people, and she will be a byword of shame before the kings of the age.
sentences.n: yashīʿu after the conditional in faʿalta: Classical would put the answer in the jussive (yashiʿ); the text has the plain indicative, as spoken Arabic does, and it is pointed as written. muʿayyara, “reproached, put to shame”, taken here of the girl; the phrase could also be read of the king himself (“you will remain a reproach”), but the feminine form points to her. The two halves rhyme on al-zamān.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ كَانَ مَاكَانَ مَا هُوَ وَلَدُ زِنًا وَأَنَّهَا تَرَبَّتْ مَعَهُ وَأَنَّهُ صَاحِبُ عِرْضٍ وَمُرُوَّةٍ وَلَا يَفْعَلُ أَمْرًا يُعَابُ عَلَيْهِ فَاصْبِرْ وَلَا تَعْجَلْ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam anna Kāna Mā Kāna mā huwa waladu zinan wa-annahā tarabbat maʿahu wa-annahu ṣāḥibu ʿirḍin wa-muruwwatin wa-lā yafʿalu amran yuʿābu ʿalayhi fa-iṣbir wa-lā taʿjal
sentences.l: And know that Kān Mā Kān, not is he a son of fornication, and that she was-reared with him, and that he is a possessor of honour and manliness, and does not do a thing he would-be-faulted for; so be-patient and do not hasten.
sentences.i: And know that Kān Mā Kān is no base-born child: she was brought up with him, and he is a man of honour and manly virtue who would do nothing to bring blame on himself. So be patient, and do not act in haste.
sentences.n: mā huwa, “he is not”: negating a nominal sentence with mā and a pronoun is spoken usage (Classical laysa). walad zinan, “a child of fornication”: she means he is nobly born and would not behave like a low fellow. muruwwa is the hamza-less form of murūʾa, “manliness, chivalrous virtue”.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّ أَهْلَ الْقَصْرِ وَجَمِيعَ أَهْلِ بَغْدَادَ قَدْ شَاعَ عِنْدَهُمْ خَبَرُ الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ أَنَّهُ قَادَ الْعَسَاكِرَ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْبُلْدَانِ وَجَاءَ بِهِمْ لِيُمَلِّكُوا كَانَ مَاكَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-inna ahla al-qaṣri wa-jamīʿa ahli Baghdāda qad shāʿa ʿindahum khabaru al-wazīri Dandāna annahu qāda al-ʿasākira min jamīʿi al-buldāni wa-jāʾa bihim li-yumallikū Kāna Mā Kāna
sentences.l: For the people of the palace and all the people of Baghdad, there has spread among-them the report of the vizier Dandān, that he led the armies from all the lands and came with them so-that-they-might make-king Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: For the whole palace, and all Baghdad besides, has heard the tale of the vizier Dandān: how he led the armies of every land and brought them here to make Kān Mā Kān king.
sentences.n: The sentence sets ahl al-qaṣr, “the people of the palace”, at the head as its topic and picks it up again with ʿindahum, “among them”, a construction common in narrative Arabic. yumallikū, form II of malaka, “to make someone king”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا وَاللَّهِ لَا بُدَّأَنْ أَرْمِيَهُ فِي بَلِيَّةٍ بِحَيْثُ لَا أَرْضَ تُقِلُّهُ وَلَا سَمَاءَ تُظِلُّهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā wa-Allāhi lā budda an armiyahu fī baliyyatin bi-ḥaythu lā arḍa tuqilluhu wa-lā samāʾa tuẓilluhu
sentences.l: And he said to her: By God, there is no escape that I throw-him into a calamity such that no earth bears-him and no sky shades-him;
sentences.i: He said to her: By God, I will cast him into such a calamity that no earth will bear him up and no sky give him shade.
sentences.n: lā budda an, “there is no escaping that, it must be that”; the print runs an onto budda (lā budān), kept as printed. lā arḍa tuqilluhu wa-lā samāʾa tuẓilluhu, “no earth to carry him and no sky to shade him”, a rhymed phrase for utter ruin; the print marks the doubled lām of both verbs.

sentences.t: وَإِنِّي مَا أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْهِ وَطَيَّبْتُ خَاطِرَهُ إِلَّا لِأَجْلِ أَهْلِ مَمْلَكَتِي وَدَوْلَتِي لِئَلَّا يَمِيلُوا إِلَيْهِ وَسَوْفَ تَرَيْنَ مَا يَكُونُ
sentences.tr: wa-innī mā anʿamtu ʿalayhi wa-ṭayyabtu khāṭirahu illā li-ajli ahli mamlakatī wa-dawlatī liʾallā yamīlū ilayhi wa-sawfa tarayna mā yakūnu
sentences.l: and I did not bestow-favour on him and make-pleasant his mind except for-the-sake-of the people of my kingdom and my state, lest they incline toward him; and you will see what will be.
sentences.i: I showed him favour and humoured him only for the sake of the people of my kingdom and my realm, so that they should not lean toward him. You shall see what comes of it.
sentences.n: ṭayyaba khāṭirahu, “to set someone's mind at ease, humour him”. dawla, “reign, state”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَرَكَهَا وَخَرَجَ يُدَبِّرُ أَمْرَ مُلْكِهِ هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma tarakahā wa-kharaja yudabbiru amra mulkihi hādhā mā kāna min amri al-maliki Sāsāna
sentences.l: Then he left her and went-out managing the affair of his kingdom. This is what was of the affair of the king Sāsān.
sentences.i: Then he left her and went out to see to the business of his kingdom. So much for King Sāsān.
sentences.n: hādhā mā kāna min amri …, “this is what there was of the matter of …”, the storyteller's formula for leaving one thread of the story; it is answered by wa-ammā mā kāna min amri …, “and as for the matter of …”, which takes up the other.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَإِنَّهُ أَقْبَلَ عَلَى أُمِّهِ فِي ثَانِي يَوْمٍ وَقَالَ لَهَا يَا أُمِّي إِنِّي عَزَمْتُ عَلَى شَنِّ الْغَارَاتِ وَقَطْعِ الطُّرُقَاتِ وَسَوْقِ الْخَيْلِ وَالنَّعَمِ وَالْعَبِيدِ وَالْمَمَالِيكِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri Kāna Mā Kāna fa-innahu aqbala ʿalā ummihi fī thānī yawmin wa-qāla lahā yā ummī innī ʿazamtu ʿalā shanni al-ghārāti wa-qaṭʿi al-ṭuruqāti wa-sawqi al-khayli wa-al-naʿami wa-al-ʿabīdi wa-al-mamālīki
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of Kān Mā Kān, he came to his mother on the second day and said to her: O my mother, I have resolved on the launching of raids, and the cutting of the roads, and the driving-off of the horses and the cattle and the slaves and the mamelukes;
sentences.i: As for Kān Mā Kān, the next day he came to his mother and said: Mother, I have made up my mind to go raiding and to waylay the roads, driving off horses and herds, slaves and mamelukes.
sentences.n: fī thānī yawm, “on the second day”, i.e. the next day. shann al-ghārāt, “launching raids”, and qaṭʿ al-ṭuruqāt, “cutting the roads”, i.e. highway robbery, the Bedouin road to wealth, spoken of without shame; the pair rhyme in -āt. naʿam, livestock, above all camels. mamālīk, “mamelukes”, bought slaves trained as soldiers.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا كَثُرَ مَالِي وَحَسُنَ حَالِي خَطَبْتُ بِنْتَ عَمِّي قَضَى فَكَانَ مِنْ عَمِّي الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā kathura mālī wa-ḥasuna ḥālī khaṭabtu binta ʿammī Qaḍā Fakāna min ʿammī al-maliki Sāsāna
sentences.l: and when my wealth becomes-much and my state becomes-fair, I will ask-in-marriage the daughter of my uncle, Qaḍā Fakān, from my uncle the king Sāsān.
sentences.i: And when my wealth has grown and my fortunes are fair, I shall ask my uncle King Sāsān for the hand of my cousin Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.n: mālī / ḥālī, a small rhyme. khaṭabtu, a perfect after idhā, has future sense. Qaḍā Fakān is his bint ʿamm, “cousin”, in the strict sense, being Sharrkān's daughter; Sāsān, the husband of her mother Nuzhat al-Zamān, is called ʿamm, “uncle”, more loosely.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي إِنَّ أَمْوَالَ النَّاسِ غَيْرُ سَائِبَةٍ لَكَ لِأَنَّ دُونَهَا ضَرْبَ الصِّفَاحِ وَطَعْنَ الرِّمَاحِ وَرِجَالٌ تَأْكُلُ السِّبَاعَ وَتُوحِشُ الْبِقَاعَ وَتَقْتَنِصُ الْأُسُودَ وَتَصِيدُ الْفُهُودَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu yā waladī inna amwāla al-nāsi ghayru sāʾibatin laka li-anna dūnahā ḍarba al-ṣifāḥi wa-ṭaʿna al-rimāḥi wa-rijālun taʾkulu al-sibāʿa wa-tūḥishu al-biqāʿa wa-taqtaniṣu al-usūda wa-taṣīdu al-fuhūda
sentences.l: And she said to him: O my son, the possessions of the people are not left-loose for you, because before-them is the striking of the broad-blades and the thrusting of the spears, and men who eat the beasts-of-prey, and make-desolate the places, and snare the lions, and hunt the leopards.
sentences.i: She answered: My son, other men's wealth is not lying loose for you to take. Between you and it stand the strokes of broad blades and the thrusts of lances, and men who devour wild beasts, who leave whole regions desolate, who trap lions and hunt down leopards.
sentences.n: sāʾiba, “roaming loose, ownerless”, said of a she-camel turned out to graze at will; hence goods free to anyone who takes them. dūnahā, “before it, barring the way to it”. ṣifāḥ, broad swords (pl. of ṣafīḥa). The speech is sajʿ in rhyming pairs: ṣifāḥ / rimāḥ, sibāʿ / biqāʿ, usūd / fuhūd. wa-rijālun, “and men”: after li-anna Classical wants the accusative rijālan, but the print has no alif of tanwīn, so the word is pointed as a fresh nominative, as the spoken language would take it. tūḥishu al-biqāʿ, “make the places desolate”, is taken as men who empty the land of life; it may rather mean that they make the wilds fearful.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ هَيْهَاتَ أَنْ أَرْجِعَ عَنْ عَزِيمَتِي إِلَّا إِذَا بَلَغْتُ مُنْيَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Kāna Mā Kāna hayhāta an arjiʿa ʿan ʿazīmatī illā idhā balaghtu munyatī
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to her: Far-be-it that I turn-back from my resolve, except when I have-reached my desire.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān replied: Never shall I turn back from my resolve until I have won my heart's desire.
sentences.n: hayhāta, “far be it, how remote!”. ʿazīmatī / munyatī, a rhyme.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَرْسَلَ الْعَجُوزَ إِلَى قَضَى فَكَانَ يُعْلِمُهَا أَنَّهُ سَائِرٌ يَتَسَبَّبُ لَهَا مَهْرًا يَصْلُحُ لَهَا وَقَالَ لِلْعَجُوزِ لَابُدَّ أَنْ تَسْأَلَهَا حَتَّى تَأْتِيَنِي مِنْهَا بِجَوَابٍ
sentences.tr: thumma arsala al-ʿajūza ilā Qaḍā Fakāna yuʿlimuhā annahu sāʾirun yatasabbabu lahā mahran yaṣluḥu lahā wa-qāla li-al-ʿajūzi lā budda an tasʾalahā ḥattā taʾtiyanī minhā bi-jawābin
sentences.l: Then he sent the old-woman to Qaḍā Fakān, informing her that he was setting-out, seeking-the-means for her of a bride-price befitting her; and he said to the old-woman: There is no escape that you ask her, so that you bring-me from her an answer.
sentences.i: Then he sent the old woman to Qaḍā Fakān to tell her that he was setting out to win a bride-price worthy of her, and he said to the old woman: You must ask her, and bring me back her answer.
sentences.n: yatasabbabu, form V from sabab, “means”: “to go about procuring, to earn”; with lahā mahran, “to earn a bride-price for her”. tasʾalahā and taʾtiyanī are masculine forms, although he is speaking to the old woman; Classical would have tasʾalīhā and taʾtīnī. Middle Arabic often lets the masculine stand for the feminine in address like this. lābudda is printed as one word here.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً ثُمَّ ذَهَبَتْ إِلَيْهَا وَرَجَعَتْ إِلَيْهِ بِالْجَوَابِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنَّهَا تَأْتِي إِلَيْكَ فِي نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan thumma dhahabat ilayhā wa-rajaʿat ilayhi bi-al-jawābi wa-qālat lahu innahā taʾtī ilayka fī niṣfi al-layli
sentences.l: And she said to him: Hearing and obedience. Then she went to her and returned to him with the answer, and said to him: She will come to you in the middle of the night.
sentences.i: She said to him: With hearing and obedience. Then she went to Qaḍā Fakān and came back to him with the answer, telling him: She will come to you at midnight.

sentences.t: فَأَقَامَ سَهْرَانًا إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ فَأَخَذَهُ الْقَلَقُ فَلَمْ يَشْعُرْ إِلَّا وَهِيَ دَاخِلَةٌ عَلَيْهِ وَهِيَ تَقُولُ رُوحِي لَكَ الْفِدَاءُ مِنَ السَّهَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-aqāma sahrānan ilā niṣfi al-layli fa-akhadhahu al-qalaqu fa-lam yashʿur illā wa-hiya dākhilatun ʿalayhi wa-hiya taqūlu rūḥī laka al-fidāʾu mina al-sahari
sentences.l: And he remained wakeful until the middle of the night, and restlessness took him; and he did not perceive but that she was coming-in upon him, and she saying: My soul be-the-ransom for you from the wakefulness!
sentences.i: So he sat up awake until midnight, and grew restless; and before he knew it she was coming in to him, saying: May my soul be your ransom for this long waking!
sentences.n: sahrānan, “wakeful”: sahrān takes no tanwīn in Classical (sahrāna); the print's alif gives it the tanwīn of the spoken language, and it is pointed as written. fa-lam yashʿur illā wa-, “he was not aware except that …”, the stock phrase for something that happens before one notices. rūḥī laka al-fidāʾ, “my soul is your ransom”, a lover's endearment; min al-sahar, “for (what you have suffered from) the wakefulness”.

sentences.t: فَنَهَضَ لَهَا قَائِمًا وَقَالَ يَا مُنْيَةَ الْقَلْبِ رُوحِي لَكِ الْفِدَاءُ مِنْ جَمِيعِ الْأَسْوَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-nahaḍa lahā qāʾiman wa-qāla yā munyata al-qalbi rūḥī laki al-fidāʾu min jamīʿi al-aswāʾi
sentences.l: And he rose for her, standing, and said: O desire of the heart, my soul be-the-ransom for you from all the evils!
sentences.i: He sprang to his feet for her and said: O my heart's desire, may my soul be your ransom against every ill!
sentences.n: He answers her endearment with the same words. aswāʾ, plural of sūʾ, “evil, harm”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَعْلَمَهَا بِمَا عَزَمَ عَلَيْهِ فَبَكَتْ فَقَالَ لَهَا لَا تَبْكِي يَا بِنْتَ الْعَمِّ فَأَنَا أَسْأَلُ الَّذِي حَكَمَ عَلَيْنَا بِالْفِرَاقِ أَنْ يَمُنَّ عَلَيْنَا بِالتَّلَاقِي وَالْوِفَاقِ
sentences.tr: thumma aʿlamahā bi-mā ʿazama ʿalayhi fa-bakat fa-qāla lahā lā tabkī yā binta al-ʿammi fa-anā asʾalu alladhī ḥakama ʿalaynā bi-al-firāqi an yamunna ʿalaynā bi-al-talāqī wa-al-wifāqi
sentences.l: Then he informed her of what he had resolved upon, and she wept; and he said to her: Do not weep, O daughter of the uncle, for I ask the One who decreed upon us the parting that He be-gracious to us with the meeting-again and the concord.
sentences.i: Then he told her what he had resolved, and she wept. He said to her: Do not weep, cousin; I pray the One who has decreed our parting to grant us the grace of meeting again in harmony.
sentences.n: lā tabkī, the feminine jussive (tabkīna loses its -na). alladhī ḥakama, “the One who decreed”, is God, named by His act. firāq / talāqī / wifāq, a rhyme.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ عَوَّلَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ عَلَى السَّفَرِ وَدَخَلَ عَلَي أُمِّهِ وَوَدَّعَهَا وَنَزَلَ مِنَ الْقَصْرِ وَتَقَلَّدَ بِسَيْفِهِ وَتَعَمَّمَ وَتَلَثَّمَ وَرَكِبَ جَوَادَهُ الْقَاتُولَ وَشَقَّ الْمَدِينَةَ وَهُوَ كَالْبَدْرِ حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَى بَابِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: thumma ʿawwala Kāna Mā Kāna ʿalā al-safari wa-dakhala ʿalā ummihi wa-waddaʿahā wa-nazala mina al-qaṣri wa-taqallada bi-sayfihi wa-taʿammama wa-talaththama wa-rakiba jawādahu al-Qātūla wa-shaqqa al-madīnata wa-huwa ka-al-badri ḥattā waṣala ilā bābi Baghdāda
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān set-his-mind on the journey, and went-in to his mother and bade-her-farewell, and went-down from the palace, and girded-himself with his sword, and turbaned-himself, and veiled-his-face, and mounted his steed al-Qātūl, and cleft the city, he being like the full-moon, until he reached the gate of Baghdad.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān resolved upon the journey. He went in to his mother and bade her farewell, came down from the palace, girded on his sword, wound his turban and drew the veil across his face, mounted his steed al-Qātūl, and rode through the city like the full moon until he came to the gate of Baghdad.
sentences.n: ʿawwala ʿalā, “to resolve on, set one's mind on”. The second ʿalā (“to his mother”) is printed with a dotted yāʾ, ʿly; kept as printed and pointed ʿalā. talaththama, “to put on the lithām”, the cloth drawn over the lower face by desert riders. The print marks the doubled letters of ʿawwala, waddaʿahā, taqallada, taʿammama and talaththama.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِرَفِيقِهِ صَبَّاحِ بْنِ رَمَّاحٍ خَارِجٌ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ فَلَمَّا رَأَٰهُ جَرَى فِي رِكَابِهِ وَحَيَّاهُ فَرَدَّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-rafīqihi Ṣabbāḥi ibni Rammāḥin khārijun mina al-madīnati fa-lammā raʾāhu jarā fī rikābihi wa-ḥayyāhu fa-radda ʿalayhi al-salāma
sentences.l: And behold, his companion Ṣabbāḥ ibn Rammāḥ, coming-out from the city; and when he saw him he ran at his stirrup and greeted him, and he returned to him the greeting.
sentences.i: And there was his comrade Ṣabbāḥ ibn Rammāḥ, coming out of the city. When Ṣabbāḥ saw him he ran up beside his stirrup and greeted him, and Kān Mā Kān returned his greeting.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold!”: bi- marks what suddenly comes into view. raʾāhu is printed rʾh, with hamza but without the madda of the usual spelling; the long vowel is supplied here with a dagger alif. jarā fī rikābihi, “ran at his stirrup”, running alongside a rider as a mark of respect.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ صَبَّاحٌ يَا أَخِي كَيْفَ صَارَ لَكَ هَذَا الْجَوَادُ وَهَذَا السَّيْفُ وَالثِّيَابُ وَأَنَا إِلَى الْآنَ لَا أَمْلِكُ غَيْرَ سَيْفِي وَتُرْسِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Ṣabbāḥun yā akhī kayfa ṣāra laka hādhā al-jawādu wa-hādhā al-sayfu wa-al-thiyābu wa-anā ilā al-āna lā amliku ghayra sayfī wa-tursī
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ said to him: O my brother, how did this steed come-to-be yours, and this sword and the clothes, while I until now do not possess other than my sword and my shield?
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ said to him: Brother, how did you come by this horse, this sword and these clothes, while I to this day own nothing but my sword and my shield?

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مَا يَرْجِعُ الصَّيَّادُ بِصَيْدٍ إِلَّا عَلَى قَدْرِ نِيَّتِهِ وَبَعْدَ فِرَاقِكَ بِسَاعَةٍ حَصَلَتْ لِيَ السَّعَادَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Kāna Mā Kāna mā yarjiʿu al-ṣayyādu bi-ṣaydin illā ʿalā qadri niyyatihi wa-baʿda firāqika bi-sāʿatin ḥaṣalat liya al-saʿādatu
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: The hunter does not return with a catch except according-to the measure of his intent; and an hour after your parting, good-fortune came to me.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān answered: A hunter brings home game only in the measure of his intent. And within an hour of our parting, fortune came my way.
sentences.n: The print has يزجع, a misprint for يرجع, corrected here. The saying means that what a man gains answers to what he sets out to gain. baʿda firāqika bi-sāʿatin, “an hour after parting from you”: bi- gives the measure of the interval.

sentences.t: وَهَلْ لَكَ أَنْ تَأْتِيَ مَعِي وَتُخْلِصَ النِّيَّةَ فِي صُحْبَتِي وَتُسَافِرَ مَعِي فِي هَذِهِ الْبَرِّيَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-hal laka an taʾtiya maʿī wa-tukhliṣa al-niyyata fī ṣuḥbatī wa-tusāfira maʿī fī hādhihi al-barriyyati
sentences.l: And is there for you that you come with me, and make-pure the intent in my companionship, and journey with me in this wilderness?
sentences.i: Will you come with me, give yourself wholeheartedly to my company, and travel with me through this wilderness?
sentences.n: hal laka an …?, “have you a mind to …?”, a courteous invitation. akhlaṣa al-niyya, “to make one's intention pure”, i.e. to be wholehearted and loyal.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَرَبِّ الْكَعْبَةِ مَا بَقِيتُ أُنَادِيكَ إِلَّا مَوْلَايَ ثُمَّ جَرَى قُدَّامَ الْجَوَادِ وَسَيْفُهُ عَلَى عَاتِقِهِ وَجِرَابُهُ بَيْنَ كَتِفَيْهِ وَكَانَ مَا كَانَ وَرَاءَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-rabbi al-kaʿbati mā baqītu unādīka illā mawlāya thumma jarā quddāma al-jawādi wa-sayfuhu ʿalā ʿātiqihi wa-jirābuhu bayna katifayhi wa-Kāna Mā Kāna warāʾahu
sentences.l: So he said: By the Lord of the Kaʿba, I-will-not-remain calling-you except “my master”. Then he ran before the steed, and his sword on his shoulder and his bag between his shoulder-blades, and Kān Mā Kān behind him.
sentences.i: “By the Lord of the Kaʿba,” said Ṣabbāḥ, “from now on I shall call you nothing but ‘my master’.” Then he ran on ahead of the horse, his sword on his shoulder and his bag slung between his shoulder-blades, with Kān Mā Kān riding behind him.
sentences.n: wa-rabbi al-kaʿba, “by the Lord of the Kaʿba”, an oath; the wa- here is the wāw of swearing, which puts its noun in the genitive. mā baqītu unādīka illā, literally “I have not remained calling you except”: the past tense with mā is a vow about the future, “I shall never again call you anything but”. The clauses wa-sayfuhu … wa-jirābuhu … are circumstantial (ḥāl) clauses: “with his sword … and his bag …”.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَغْرَقُوا فِى الْبَرِّ أَرْبَعَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَهُمَا يَأْكُلَانِ مِنْ صَيْدِ الْغِزْلَانِ وَيَشْرَبَانِ مِنْ مَاءِ الْعُيُونِ
sentences.tr: wa-istaghraqū fī al-barri arbaʿata ayyāmin wa-humā yaʾkulāni min ṣaydi al-ghizlāni wa-yashrabāni min māʾi al-ʿuyūni
sentences.l: And they spent-fully in the open-country four days, and they-two eating from the hunting of the gazelles and drinking from the water of the springs.
sentences.i: They spent four whole days in the open desert, eating the gazelles they hunted and drinking from the springs.
sentences.n: istaghraqū, “they took up (a span of time) completely”, is plural although there are only two travellers; the very next clause switches to the dual (humā yaʾkulāni … yashrabāni). This loose agreement, plural verb for two people, is common in Middle Arabic. al-barr is the open land, the desert, as opposed to settled country.

sentences.t: وَفِى الْيَوْمِ الْخَامِسِ أَشْرَفَا عَلَى تَلٍّ عَالٍ تَحْتَهُ مَرَابِعُ وَغَدِيرٌ سَيَّاحٌ فِيهَا إِبِلٌ وَبَقَرٌ وَغَنَمٌ وَخُيُولٌ مَلَأَتِ الرَّوَابِيَ وَالْبِطَاحَ وَأَوْلَادُهَا الصِّغَارُ تَلْعَبُ حَوْلَ الْمُرَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī al-yawmi al-khāmisi ashrafā ʿalā tallin ʿālin taḥtahu marābiʿu wa-ghadīrun sayyāḥun fīhā ibilun wa-baqarun wa-ghanamun wa-khuyūlun malaʾati al-rawābiya wa-al-biṭāḥa wa-awlāduhā al-ṣighāru talʿabu ḥawla al-murāḥi
sentences.l: And on the fifth day they-two looked-down from a high hill, beneath it spring-pastures and a flowing pool, in-them camels and cattle and sheep and horses that filled the hillocks and the flat-valleys, and their young little-ones playing around the night-fold.
sentences.i: On the fifth day they came out upon a high hill, and below it lay spring pastures and a running stream, with camels, cattle, sheep and horses filling the knolls and the broad valley floors, and their little young ones frolicking about the folds.
sentences.n: ashrafa ʿalā, “to come up over, look down upon” a place from a height. marābiʿ (sing. marbaʿ) are spring pastures and camping grounds. ghadīr sayyāḥ, a pool or stream “flowing freely”. The rhyme falls on -āḥ: sayyāḥ, biṭāḥ, murāḥ. al-murāḥ is the place where camels and flocks are brought back to rest at night. Note the bare noun after the hill: tallin ʿālin, “a high hill”, with ʿālin the shortened form of ʿālī that indefinite nouns of this pattern take.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى ذَلِكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ زَادَتْ بِهِ الْأَفْرَاحُ وَامْتَلَأَ صَدْرُهُ بِالِانْشِرَاحِ وَعَوَّلَ عَلَي الْقِتَالِ لِيَأْخُذَ النِّيَاقَ وَالْجِمَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā dhālika Kāna Mā Kāna zādat bihi al-afrāḥu wa-imtalaʾa ṣadruhu bi-al-inshirāḥi wa-ʿawwala ʿalā al-qitāli li-yaʾkhudha al-niyāqa wa-al-jimāla
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān saw that, the joys increased in-him and his breast filled with the opening-wide, and he resolved on the fighting, to take the she-camels and the camels.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān saw this his delight grew, his heart swelled with gladness, and he resolved to fight for the she-camels and the camels and carry them off.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose again: afrāḥ / inshirāḥ, then qitāl / jimāl. inshirāḥ al-ṣadr, “the expanding of the breast”, is the Arabic image for joy and ease of heart. ʿawwala ʿalā, “to set one's mind on, determine upon”. The print spells the preposition ʿalā here with a dotted yāʾ (علي), a habit of the edition; it is read ʿalā.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِصَبَّاحٍ انْزِلْ بِنَا عَلَى هَذَا الْمَالِ الَّذِي عَنْ أَهْلِهِ وَحِيدٌ وَقَاتِلْ مَعِى الْقَرِيبَ وَالْبَعِيدَ حَتَّى يَكُونَ لَنَا فِي أَخْذِ الْمَالِ نَصِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla li-Ṣabbāḥin inzil binā ʿalā hādhā al-māli alladhī ʿan ahlihi waḥīdun wa-qātil maʿī al-qarība wa-al-baʿīda ḥattā yakūna lanā fī akhdhi al-māli naṣībun
sentences.l: So he said to Ṣabbāḥ: Go-down with us upon this wealth which is alone from its people, and fight with me the near and the far, so-that there be for us in the taking of the wealth a share.
sentences.i: “Come down with me upon these herds,” he said to Ṣabbāḥ, “left here far from their owners, and fight at my side against all comers, near and far, so that we may have our share in taking them.”
sentences.n: māl, “property, wealth”, means livestock here, as it often does among Bedouin. inzil binā, literally “descend with us”, is “let us go down”. ʿan ahlihi waḥīd, “alone, apart from its owners”, i.e. unguarded. The rhyme runs waḥīd / baʿīd, then naṣīb.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ صَبَّاحٌ يَا مَوْلَايَ إِنَّ أَصْحَابَ هَؤُلَاءِ خَلْقٌ كَثِيرُونَ وَفِيهِمْ أَبْطَالٌ مِنْ فُرْسَانٍ وَرِجَالٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Ṣabbāḥun yā mawlāya inna aṣḥāba hāʾulāʾi khalqun kathīrūna wa-fīhim abṭālun min fursānin wa-rijālin
sentences.l: So Ṣabbāḥ said: O my master, the owners of these are many people, and among them are heroes, of horsemen and foot-men.
sentences.i: “My master,” said Ṣabbāḥ, “the owners of these beasts are a great many, and there are champions among them, both horse and foot.”
sentences.n: khalq, “creation, people”, is a collective singular, yet takes the plural adjective kathīrūn: agreement by sense. fursān wa-rijāl, “riders and men on foot”, the usual pairing for an armed company.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ رَمَيْنَا أَرْوَاحَنَا فِي هَذَا الْخَطْبِ الْجَسِيمِ فَإِنَّنَا نَكُونُ مِنْ هَوْلِهِ عَلَى خَطَرٍ عَظِيمٍ وَمَا يَرْجِعُ أَحَدٌ مِنَّا لِأَهْلِهِ سَلِيمًا وَيَنْخَرِمُ مِنِ ابْنَةِ عَمِّهِ يَتِيمًا
sentences.tr: wa-in ramaynā arwāḥanā fī hādhā al-khaṭbi al-jasīmi fa-innanā nakūnu min hawlihi ʿalā khaṭarin ʿaẓīmin wa-mā yarjiʿu aḥadun minnā li-ahlihi salīman wa-yankharimu min ibnati ʿammihi yatīman
sentences.l: And if we throw our souls into this grave affair, then we shall be, from its terror, in great danger; and not one of us will return to his people safe, and he will be cut-off from his uncle's daughter, bereft.
sentences.i: “If we fling ourselves into so grave a business, its terrors will put us in great peril: not one of us will come home safe to his people, and each will be torn from his cousin and left bereft.”
sentences.n: The print has تكون, a misprint for نكون, corrected here: after fa-innanā, “then we”, the verb must be first-person plural, and only a dot separates the two. The sajʿ rhymes jasīm / ʿaẓīm / salīman / yatīman. The last clause is doubtful. inkharama means “to be breached, notched, cut off”; read so, it says that the man who goes will be cut off from his cousin (for Ṣabbāḥ, Najma, whom he hopes to marry), left yatīm, “bereft, orphaned”. The verb may instead be a slip for yuḥramu, “be deprived of”, which gives much the same sense; we keep the print and read it as it stands. As often in this text, mā with the present (mā yarjiʿu) simply negates the future.

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَعَلِمَ أَنَّهُ جَبَانٌ فَتَرَكَهُ وَانْحَدَرَ مِنَ الرَّابِيَةِ عَازِمًا عَلَى شَنِّ الْغَارَاتِ وَصَاحَ وَتَرَنَّمَ وَأَنْشَدَ بِهَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika Kāna Mā Kāna wa-ʿalima annahu jabānun fa-tarakahu wa-inḥadara mina al-rābiyati ʿāziman ʿalā shanni al-ghārāti wa-ṣāḥa wa-tarannama wa-anshada bi-hādhihi al-abyāti
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān laughed and knew that he was a coward, so he left him and went-down from the hillock, resolved upon the launching of raids, and shouted and chanted and recited these verses:
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān laughed, knowing him for a coward, and left him. He rode down the hill bent on raiding, shouting and chanting, and recited these lines:
sentences.n: shann al-ghārāt, “the pouring-out of raids”, is the stock phrase for launching an attack. anshada bi-, “to recite”: this text regularly puts bi- before the verses recited, where Classical would take them as a direct object.

sentences.t:
وَآلِ نُعْمَانَ نَحْنُ ذُو الْهِمَمِ * وَالسَّادَةُ الضَّارِبُوْنَ فِى الْقِمَمِ
قَوْمٌ اِذَا مَا الْهِيَاجُ قَامَ لَهُمْ * قَامُوْا باَسْوَاقِهِ عَلَى قَدَمِ
تَنَامُ عَيْنُ الْفَقِيْرِ بَيْنَهُمُ * وَلَا يَرَى قُبْحَ صُوْرَةِ الْعَدَمِ
وَاِنَّنِي اَرْتَجِيْ مُعَاوَنَةً * مِنْ مَالِكِ الْمُلْكِ بَارِئِ النَّسَمِ
sentences.tr:
wa-āli Nuʿmāna naḥnu dhū al-himami * wa-al-sādatu al-ḍāribūna fī al-qimami
qawmun idhā mā al-hiyāju qāma lahum * qāmū bi-aswāqihi ʿalā qadami
tanāmu ʿaynu al-faqīri baynahumu * wa-lā yarā qubḥa ṣūrati al-ʿadami
wa-innanī artajī muʿāwanatan * min māliki al-mulki bāriʾi al-nasami
sentences.l:
And of the house of Nuʿmān are we, the possessors of high-aims * and the lords, the strikers upon the skull-tops.
A people who, whenever the battle-fury rises for them, * stand-up to its markets upon (their) feet.
The eye of the poor-man sleeps among them, * and he does not see the ugliness of the face of want.
And I, I hope for aid * from the Possessor of the Kingdom, Creator of the living-souls.
sentences.i:
Of Nuʿmān's house are we, men of high resolve, * lords who strike home upon the crowns of heads;
a people who, when the fury of war comes on, * stand up to meet it, firm upon their feet.
The poor man sleeps in peace among us * and never sees the ugly face of want.
And I look for help from the Lord of all dominion, * who made every living soul.
sentences.n: Metre munsariḥ, rhyme -imi. The print's pointing is copied as it stands. In line 1 it points wa-āli, genitive, which is hard to construe; the sense is plainly “we of the house of Nuʿmān”, and dhū, singular “possessor of”, stands for the plural dhawū, “possessors of”. In line 2 the print sets a fatḥa over the bāʾ of باَسْوَاقِهِ, apparently marking the alif after it; read bi-aswāqihi. The “markets” of war (aswāq al-ḥarb) are the press of battle, where blows are traded, and qāma ʿalā qadam, “to stand on a foot”, means to rise to a thing ready and in earnest. mālik al-mulk, “Possessor of the Kingdom”, echoes Qurʾān 3:26; al-nasam, “breathing creatures”, are all living souls.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ حَمَلَ عَلَي تِلْكَ النُّوقِ مِثْلَ الْجَمَلِ الْهَائِجِ وَسَاقَ جَمِيعَ الْإِبِلِ وَالْبَقَرِ وَالْغَنَمِ وَالْخَيْلِ قُدَّامَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu ḥamala ʿalā tilka al-nūqi mithla al-jamali al-hāʾiji wa-sāqa jamīʿa al-ibili wa-al-baqari wa-al-ghanami wa-al-khayli quddāmahu
sentences.l: Then he charged upon those she-camels like the raging camel, and drove all the camels and the cattle and the sheep and the horses before him.
sentences.i: Then he fell upon the she-camels like a rutting camel and drove all the camels, cattle, sheep and horses before him.
sentences.n: ḥamala ʿalā, “to charge, make an onslaught upon”, the regular verb for an attack in battle. thumma innahu, “then he”, is the storyteller's usual way to open a new step. al-jamal al-hāʾij is a camel in rut or in fury, proverbially dangerous.

sentences.t: فَبَادَرَتْ إِلَيْهِ الْعَبِيدُ بِالسُّيُوفِ الصِّقَالِ وَالرِّمَاحِ الطِّوَالِ وَفِي أَوَائِلِهِمْ فَارِسٌ تُرْكِيٌّ إِلَّا أَنَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْحَرْبِ وَالْكِفَاحِ عَارِفٌ بِأَعْمَالِ سُمْرِ الْقَنَا وَبِيضِ الصِّفَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-bādarat ilayhi al-ʿabīdu bi-al-suyūfi al-ṣiqāli wa-al-rimāḥi al-ṭiwāli wa-fī awāʾilihim fārisun turkiyyun illā annahu shadīdu al-ḥarbi wa-al-kifāḥi ʿārifun bi-aʿmāli sumri al-qanā wa-bīḍi al-ṣifāḥi
sentences.l: And the slaves hastened to him with the polished swords and the long lances, and in their forefront a Turkish horseman, except that he (was) strong of war and combat, knowing in the workings of the brown spear-shafts and the white broad-blades.
sentences.i: The slaves rushed at him with burnished swords and long lances, and at their head rode a Turkish horseman, a fierce man in war and fighting, well practised with the tawny spear and the bright broad blade.
sentences.n: illā annahu, literally “except that he”, here only joins on a further remark about the Turk, “and what is more, he was”; it marks no real exception. The rhyme pairs ṣiqāl / ṭiwāl and kifāḥ / ṣifāḥ. sumr al-qanā, “the brown (shafts of) spears”, and bīḍ al-ṣifāḥ, “the white broad blades” (ṣifāḥ, plural of ṣafīḥa), are a stock pair for lance and sword. bi-aʿmāl can also be read bi-iʿmāl, “in the plying of”; the sense is the same. fa-bādarat … al-ʿabīdu: the feminine verb with a broken plural is normal.

sentences.t: فَحَمَلَ عَلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ لَوْ عَلِمْتَ لِمَنْ هَذَا الْمَالُ مَا فَعَلْتَ هَذِهِ الْفِعَالَ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥamala ʿalā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-qāla lahu waylaka law ʿalimta li-man hādhā al-mālu mā faʿalta hādhihi al-fiʿāla
sentences.l: And he charged upon Kān Mā Kān and said to him: Woe to you! If you knew to whom this wealth (belongs), you would not have done these doings.
sentences.i: He bore down on Kān Mā Kān and cried, “Woe to you! If you knew whose herds these are, you would never have done such a thing.
sentences.n: waylaka, “woe to you”, an angry rebuke rather than a curse in earnest. law … mā faʿalta, “if … you would not have done”: the answer to law is put in the past and negated with mā. mālu / fiʿāla keep the rhyme going.

sentences.t: اعْلَمْ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْأَمْوَالَ لِلْعِصَابَةِ الرُّومِيَّةِ وَالْأَبْطَالِ الْبَحْرِيَّةِ وَالْفِرْقَةِ الْجَرْكَسِيَّةِ الَّذِينَ مَّا فِيهِمْ إِلَّا كُلُّ بَطَلٍ عَابِسٍ وَهُمْ مِائَةُ فَارِسٍ الَّذِينَ خَرَجُوا عَنْ طَاعَةِ كُلِّ سُلْطَانٍ
sentences.tr: iʿlam anna hādhihi al-amwāla li-al-ʿiṣābati al-rūmiyyati wa-al-abṭāli al-baḥriyyati wa-al-firqati al-jarkasiyyati alladhīna mā fīhim illā kullu baṭalin ʿābisin wa-hum miʾatu fārisin alladhīna kharajū ʿan ṭāʿati kulli sulṭānin
sentences.l: Know that these wealths belong to the Greek band and the sea-heroes and the Circassian troop, those among whom there is none but every grim hero, and they are a hundred horsemen, those who have gone out from the obedience of every sultan.
sentences.i: Know that these herds belong to the Greek band, the heroes from over the sea, and the Circassian troop, among whom there is not a man who is not a grim champion. They are a hundred horsemen, and they have thrown off the obedience of every sultan.
sentences.n: al-rūmiyya, “Rūmī”, Byzantine Greek or, loosely, Christian European; al-baḥriyya, “of the sea”, men who came by sea or from the coast; al-jarkasiyya, “Circassian”. The three adjectives rhyme in -iyya. The print sets a shadda on the mīm of mā (مّا), which has no grammatical reason; it is kept and the word read as plain mā, “there is not”. alladhīna is repeated awkwardly after miʾatu fārisin, a loose relative typical of this text: it refers back to the whole band.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ سُرِقَ مِنْهُمْ حِصَانٌ وَحَلَفُوا أَنْ لَا يَرْجِعُوا مِنْ هُنَا إِلَّا بِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad suriqa minhum ḥiṣānun wa-ḥalafū an lā yarjiʿū min hunā illā bihi
sentences.l: And a stallion has been stolen from them, and they have sworn that they will not return from here except with it.
sentences.i: A stallion has been stolen from them, and they have sworn not to go back from here without it.”
sentences.n: The stolen stallion is al-Qātūl, the horse Kān Mā Kān is riding, as his answer makes plain.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ صَاحَ قَائِلًا يَا لِئَامُ هَذَا هُوَ الْحِصَانُ الَّذِي تَعْنُونَ وَأَنْتُمْ لَهُ طَالِبُونَ وَفِي قِتَالِي بِسَبَبِهِ رَاغِبُونَ فَبَارِزُونِي كُلُّكُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ وَشَأْنَكُمْ وَمَا تُرِيدُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Kāna Mā Kāna hādhā al-kalāma ṣāḥa qāʾilan yā liʾāmu hādhā huwa al-ḥiṣānu alladhī taʿnūna wa-antum lahu ṭālibūna wa-fī qitālī bi-sababihi rāghibūna fa-bārizūnī kullukum ajmaʿūna wa-shaʾnakum wa-mā turīdūna
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard this speech, he shouted, saying: O base-ones, this is the stallion which you mean, and you for it are seekers, and in fighting-me on-account-of it are desirous; so come-out-to-duel-me, all of you together, and (to) your business and what you want!
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard this he shouted, “You curs, this is the very stallion you mean, the one you are hunting for, and on its account you are eager to fight me. So come out against me, every one of you together, and do what you will!”
sentences.n: liʾām, plural of laʾīm, “mean, base, ignoble”, a heavy insult. The rhyme in -ūn runs through the whole speech: taʿnūn, ṭālibūn, rāghibūn, ajmaʿūn, turīdūn. bāraza, “to come out to single combat with”. wa-shaʾnakum wa-mā turīdūna, “(see to) your business and what you want”, is an accusative of challenge, “have at it, do as you please”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَرَخَ بَيْنَ أُذُنَيِ الْقَاتُولِ فَخَرَجَ عَلَيْهِمْ مِثْلَ الْغُولِ
sentences.tr: thumma ṣarakha bayna udhunayi al-Qātūli fa-kharaja ʿalayhim mithla al-ghūli
sentences.l: Then he shouted between the two ears of al-Qātūl, and it went-out upon them like the ghoul.
sentences.i: Then he gave a shout between al-Qātūl's ears, and the horse burst out upon them like a ghoul.
sentences.n: The print has فخرح, a misprint for فخرج, corrected here; the two letters differ only by a dot. al-Qātūl, “the Killer”, is the stallion's name. The ghoul (ghūl) is the desert demon of Arab lore; Qātūl / ghūl rhyme.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ عَطَفَ عَلَى الْفَارِسِ فَطَعَنَهُ وَرَمَاهُ وَأَخْرَجَ كُلَاهُ وَمَالَ عَلَى ثَانٍ وَثَالِثٍ وَرَابِعٍ أَعْدَمَهُمُ الْحَيَاةَ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra Kāna Mā Kāna ʿaṭafa ʿalā al-fārisi fa-ṭaʿanahu wa-ramāhu wa-akhraja kulāhu wa-māla ʿalā thānin wa-thālithin wa-rābiʿin aʿdamahumu al-ḥayāta
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān went-on: he wheeled upon the horseman, and speared-him and threw-him-down and brought-out his kidneys; and he turned upon a second and a third and a fourth, he made-them-lack life.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān wheeled upon the horseman, ran him through and flung him down with his kidneys spilled; and he turned upon a second, a third and a fourth, and bereft them of life.
sentences.n: ṣāra, “became”, here only sets the action going (“he went and …”); Classical would follow it with an imperfect (ṣāra yaʿṭifu), and its use before a perfect is loose narrative style. kulā is the plural of kulya, “kidney”: the thrust goes clean through. aʿdamahumu al-ḥayāta, “he made them lack life”: aʿdama takes two objects, the person and what he is robbed of; the clause stands without “and”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ هَابَتْهُ الْعَبِيدُ فَصَاحَ عَلَيْهِمْ يَا أَوْلَادَ الزَّوَانِي سُوقُوا الْمَالَ وَالْخُيُولَ وَإِلَّا خَضَبْتُ مِنْ دِمَائِكُمْ سِنَانِي
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika hābathu al-ʿabīdu fa-ṣāḥa ʿalayhim yā awlāda al-zawānī sūqū al-māla wa-al-khuyūla wa-illā khaḍabtu min dimāʾikum sinānī
sentences.l: And at that the slaves feared-him, and he shouted at them: O sons of the adulteresses, drive the goods and the horses, or-else I-have-dyed from your blood my spearhead!
sentences.i: At that the slaves grew afraid of him, and he shouted at them, “You sons of whores, drive on the goods and the horses, or I will dye my spearhead in your blood!”
sentences.n: hābathu al-ʿabīdu, “the slaves feared him”: a broken plural of persons may take a feminine singular verb. al-zawānī is the plural of zāniya, “adulteress, whore”. wa-illā, “and if not”, i.e. “or else”; the perfect khaḍabtu after it has a future sense, “I shall have dyed”.

sentences.t: فَسَاقُوا الْمَالَ وَأَخَذُوا فِي الِانْطِلَاقِ فَانْحَدَرَ إِلَيْهِ صَبَّاحٌ وَأَعْلَنَ بِالصِّيَاحِ وَزَادَتْ بِهِ الْأَفْرَاحُ
sentences.tr: fa-sāqū al-māla wa-akhadhū fī al-inṭilāqi fa-inḥadara ilayhi Ṣabbāḥun wa-aʿlana bi-al-ṣiyāḥi wa-zādat bihi al-afrāḥu
sentences.l: So they drove the goods and took to setting-off; and Ṣabbāḥ came-down to him and made-loud the shouting, and the joys increased in him.
sentences.i: So they drove the goods and set off, and Ṣabbāḥ came down to him crying aloud, his joy swelling within him.
sentences.n: akhadhū fī, “they took to”, i.e. they began. The rhymed prose (sajʿ) chimes on Ṣabbāḥ, al-ṣiyāḥ, al-afrāḥ. aʿlana bi-, “to make public, raise (the voice) in”.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِغُبَارٍ طَلَعَ وَطَارَ حَتَّى سَدَّ الْأَقْطَارَ وَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهِ مِائَةُ فَارِسٍ مِثْلُ اللُّيُوثِ الْعَوَابِسِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-ghubārin ṭalaʿa wa-ṭāra ḥattā sadda al-aqṭāra wa-bāna min taḥtihi miʾatu fārisin mithlu al-luyūthi al-ʿawābisi
sentences.l: And behold, a dust rose and flew until it blocked the horizons, and there appeared from under it a-hundred horseman like the frowning lions.
sentences.i: And lo, a cloud of dust rose and flew up until it shut out the horizons, and from beneath it there came into view a hundred horsemen like scowling lions.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks what appears. After “hundred” Arabic counts with a singular noun, miʾatu fārisin; the print spells the number مائة, with a silent alif. Rhymes: ṭāra / al-aqṭāra, fārisin / al-ʿawābisi.

sentences.t: فَهَرَبَ صَبَّاحٌ وَطَلَعَ عَلَى أَعْلَى الرَّابِيَةِ وَتَرَكَ الْبِطَاحَ وَصَارَ يَتَفَرَّجُ عَلَى الْكِفَاحِ وَقَالَ مَا أَنَا فَارِسٌ إِلَّا فِى اللَّعِبِ وَالْمُزَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-haraba Ṣabbāḥun wa-ṭalaʿa ʿalā aʿlā al-rābiyati wa-taraka al-biṭāḥa wa-ṣāra yatafarraju ʿalā al-kifāḥi wa-qāla mā anā fārisun illā fī al-laʿibi wa-al-muzāḥi
sentences.l: And Ṣabbāḥ fled and climbed onto the top of the hillock and left the flatlands, and set-about looking-on at the fray, and said: I am not a horseman except in play and jest.
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ fled, climbed to the top of the hill and left the plain below, and there he settled down to watch the fight, saying, “I am a horseman only in play and in jest.”
sentences.n: yatafarraju ʿalā, “to look on at, enjoy the sight of”, a verb still used in Egyptian Arabic for watching a show. The rhyme in -āḥ runs on: al-biṭāḥ, al-kifāḥ, al-muzāḥ. The print marks the doubled lām of illā.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمِائَةَ فَارِسٍ أَحَاطُوا بِكَانَ مَا كَانَ وَدَارُوا بِهِ مِنْ كُلِّ جَانِبٍ وَمَكَانٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-miʾata fārisin aḥāṭū bi-Kāna Mā Kāna wa-dārū bihi min kulli jānibin wa-makānin
sentences.l: Then the hundred horseman surrounded Kān Mā Kān and circled about him from every side and place.
sentences.i: Then the hundred horsemen surrounded Kān Mā Kān and closed round him on every side.
sentences.n: al-miʾata fārisin, “the hundred horseman”: putting the article on the number and leaving the counted noun bare is Middle Arabic (Classical miʾatu fārisin, or al-fursānu al-miʾa). Rhyme: Kān / makān.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ فَارِسٌ مِنْهُمْ وَقَالَ لَهُ إِلَى أَيْنَ تَمْضِى بِهَذَا الْمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama ilayhi fārisun minhum wa-qāla lahu ilā ayna tamḍī bi-hādhā al-māli
sentences.l: And a horseman of them advanced to him and said to him: To where are you going-off with these goods?
sentences.i: One of them rode forward and said to him, “And where would you be going with these goods?”
sentences.n: The print has اى اين, a misprint for الى اين, corrected here. ilā ayna, “to where”, i.e. whither. maḍā bi-, “to go off with, carry away”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ آخُذُهُ وَأَذْهَبُ بِهِ وَأَحْرِمُكَ مِنْهُ فَدُونَكَ وَالْقِتَالَ وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ مِنْ دُونِهِ أَسَدٌ أَرْوَعُ وَبَطَلٌ سَمَيْدَعٌ وَسَيْفٌ أَيْنَمَا مَالَ قَطَعَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Kāna Mā Kāna ākhudhuhu wa-adhhabu bihi wa-aḥrimuka minhu fa-dūnaka wa-al-qitāla wa-iʿlam anna min dūnihi asadun arwaʿu wa-baṭalun samaydaʿun wa-sayfun aynamā māla qaṭaʿa
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: I take-it and go with it and deprive you of it; so there-you-are, and the fighting! And know that short of it is a lion awe-inspiring, and a hero lordly, and a sword that, wherever it inclines, cuts.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān answered, “I am taking them and going off with them, and you shall have none of them; so come on, and let us fight! And know that between you and them stands a dread lion, a lordly champion, a sword that cuts wherever it swings.”
sentences.n: dūnaka, literally “before you, within your reach”, is a challenge: “there it is, come and take it”; wa-al-qitāla, “and the fighting”, is pointed here as governed by it. min dūnihi, “on this side of it”, i.e. standing between you and it. asadun, baṭalun and sayfun are nominative: the print writes no alif of the accusative, so the noun of anna, held back behind min dūnihi, is not put in the accusative as Classical requires; this is Middle Arabic. arwaʿ, “one whose looks inspire awe”; samaydaʿ, “a noble, generous chief” (Lane). The three clauses rhyme: arwaʿ / samaydaʿ / qaṭaʿ.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْفَارِسُ ذَلِكَ الْكَلَامَ نَظَرَ إِلَيْهِ فَوَجَدَهُ فَارِسًا كَالْأَسَدِ الضِّرْغَامِ إِلَّا أَنَّ وَجْهَهُ كَالْقَمَرِ الطَّالِعِ لَيْلَةَ أَرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ وَالشَّجَاعَةُ تَلُوحُ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-fārisu dhālika al-kalāma naẓara ilayhi fa-wajadahu fārisan ka-al-asadi al-ḍirghāmi illā anna wajhahu ka-al-qamari al-ṭāliʿi laylata arbaʿata ʿashara wa-al-shajāʿatu talūḥu bayna ʿaynayhi
sentences.l: And when the horseman heard that speech, he looked at him and found him a horseman like the fierce lion, except that his face was like the moon rising the night of fourteen, and the courage gleams between his eyes.
sentences.i: When the horseman heard these words he looked at him and found him a rider like a ravening lion, save that his face was like the moon rising on the fourteenth night, with courage shining between his eyes.
sentences.n: ḍirghām, “a fierce lion”, doubles asad as an epithet; rhyme al-kalām / al-ḍirghām. laylata arbaʿata ʿashara, “the night of fourteen”, the night of the full moon: Classical would make the number feminine to agree with layla (arbaʿa ʿashrata), so the form here is Middle Arabic. The print marks the doubled lām of illā.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ الْفَارِسُ هُوَ الْمُقَدَّمَ عَلَى الْمِائَةِ فَارِسٍ وَاسْمُهُ كَهْرْدَاشُ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-fārisu huwa al-muqaddama ʿalā al-miʾati fārisin wa-ismuhu Kahrdāshu
sentences.l: And that horseman, he was the one set-over the hundred horseman, and his name was Kahrdāsh.
sentences.i: This horseman was the captain of the hundred, and his name was Kahrdāsh.
sentences.n: Kahrdāsh, the leader of the band, appears here for the first time; the name is not Arabic, and its pointing is ours. al-muqaddam ʿalā, “the one put in front of”, i.e. the commander of.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى إِلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ مَعَ كَمَالِ فُرُوسِيَّتِهِ بَدِيعَ الْمَحَاسِنِ يُشْبِهُ حُسْنُهُ حُسْنَ مَعْشُوقَةٍ لَهُ يُقَالُ لَهَا فَاتِنُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā ilā Kāna Mā Kāna maʿa kamāli furūsiyyatihi badīʿa al-maḥāsini yushbihu ḥusnuhu ḥusna maʿshūqatin lahu yuqālu lahā Fātinu
sentences.l: And when he saw to Kān Mā Kān, with the perfection of his horsemanship, wondrous of charms, his beauty resembling the beauty of a beloved of his who was called Fātin,
sentences.i: And when he looked upon Kān Mā Kān and saw him, for all his perfect horsemanship, marvellously handsome, his beauty like that of a woman he loved, whose name was Fātin,
sentences.n: raʾā ilā, “he saw to”: raʾā takes a direct object and needs no ilā, so this looks like a crossing with naẓara ilā, “he looked at”; the print's reading is kept as the text gives it. This “when” waits a long time for its answer: the story turns aside to tell of Fātin, and the main clause comes only with fa-ẓanna, “he thought”, below. Fātin, “enchanting, alluring”, is a new name here.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ مِنْ أَجْمَلِ النِّسَاءِ وَجْهًا قَدْ أَعْطَاهَا اللَّهُ مِنَ الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ وَكَرَمِ الْخِصَالِ وَمِنْ كُلِّ مَعْنًى لَطِيفٍ مَا يَعْجِزُ عَنْ وَصْفِهِ اللِّسَانُ وَيَشْغَلُ قَلْبَ كُلِّ إِنْسَانٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat min ajmali al-nisāʾi wajhan qad aʿṭāhā Allāhu mina al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli wa-karami al-khiṣāli wa-min kulli maʿnan laṭīfin mā yaʿjizu ʿan waṣfihi al-lisānu wa-yashghalu qalba kulli insānin
sentences.l: And she was of the most beautiful of the women in face; God had given her, of beauty and comeliness and nobility of qualities, and of every fine meaning, what the tongue is powerless to describe and which occupies the heart of every human.
sentences.i: She was among the fairest-faced of women: God had granted her such beauty and grace, such nobility of nature and every delicate charm, as no tongue can describe, and as would take hold of every heart.
sentences.n: maʿnan laṭīf, “a fine meaning”, here a subtle grace or charm. mā, “what”, is the object of aʿṭāhā; the min-phrases set in front of it say what it consists of. Rhymes: al-jamāl / al-khiṣāl, al-lisān / insān.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ فُرْسَانُ الْقَوْمِ تَخْشَي سَطْوَتَهَا وَأَبْطَالُ ذَاكَ الْقُطْرِ تَخَافُ مِنْ هَيْبَتِهَا وَحَلَفَتْ أَنَّهَا لَا تَتَزَوَّجُ وَلَا تُمَلِّكُ نَفْسَهَا إِلَّا مَنْ يَقْهَرُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kānat fursānu al-qawmi takhshā saṭwatahā wa-abṭālu dhāka al-quṭri takhāfu min haybatihā wa-ḥalafat annahā lā tatazawwaju wa-lā tumalliku nafsahā illā man yaqharuhā
sentences.l: And the horsemen of the people feared her assault, and the heroes of that region were afraid of her awe; and she swore that she would not marry, and would not make-owner of herself any but whoever overpowers her.
sentences.i: The horsemen of her people dreaded her onslaught, and the champions of that land stood in awe of her; and she had sworn that she would never marry, nor give herself to any man but one who could overcome her.
sentences.n: The print spells takhshā, “fears”, with a dotted yāʾ (تخشي) where alif maqṣūra is usual; the spelling is kept. Broken plurals of persons, fursān and abṭāl, take feminine singular verbs. tumalliku nafsahā, “give possession of herself to”: Form II of malaka takes two objects, here the man and herself; the plain lā tamliku nafsahā, “she would not be mistress of herself”, fits illā man less well, but the print leaves either open.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ كَهْرْدَاشُ مِنْ جُمْلَةِ خُطَّابِهَا فَقَالَتْ لِأَبِيهَا مَا يَقْرَبُنِي إِلَّا مَنْ يَقْهَرُنِي فِى الْمَيْدَانِ وَمَوْقِفِ الْحَرْبِ وَالطِّعَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna Kahrdāshu min jumlati khuṭṭābihā fa-qālat li-abīhā mā yaqrabunī illā man yaqharunī fī al-maydāni wa-mawqifi al-ḥarbi wa-al-ṭiʿāni
sentences.l: And Kahrdāsh was of the number of her suitors; and she said to her father: None comes-near me except whoever overpowers me in the field and the standing-place of war and the spear-thrusting.
sentences.i: Kahrdāsh was among her suitors; and she said to her father, “None shall come near me but one who overcomes me on the field, where war is waged and spears are thrust.”
sentences.n: min jumlati, “among the whole number of”, i.e. one of. khuṭṭāb, “suitors”, plural of khāṭib; the print marks its doubled ṭāʾ, and the doubled lām of illā. yaqrabunī, “comes near me”, a decent way of saying “has me as a husband”. Rhyme: al-maydān / al-ṭiʿān.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا بَلَغَ كَهْرْدَاشَ هَذَا الْقَوْلُ اخْتَشَى أَنْ يُقَاتِلَ جَارِيَةً وَخَافَ مِنَ الْعَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā balagha Kahrdāsha hādhā al-qawlu ikhtashā an yuqātila jāriyatan wa-khāfa mina al-ʿāri
sentences.l: And when this saying reached Kahrdāsh, he was-ashamed to fight a girl, and he feared the disgrace.
sentences.i: When this saying reached Kahrdāsh, he shrank from fighting a girl and feared the shame of it.
sentences.n: The print has جاربة, a misprint for جارية, corrected here. jāriya is here simply “a girl, a young woman”. balagha Kahrdāsha hādhā al-qawlu: the object stands before the subject. ikhtashā, Form VIII of khashiya, “to fear”, in later Arabic “to feel shy, be ashamed” (Egyptian ikhtasha); both senses fit.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ بَعْضُ خَوَاصِّهِ أَنْتَ كَامِلُ الْخِصَالِ فِى الْحُسْنِ وَالْجَمَالِ فَلَوْ قَاتَلْتَهَا وَكَانَتْ أَقْوَى مِنْكَ فَإِنَّكَ تَغْلِبُهَا لِأَنَّهَا إِذَا رَأَتْ حُسْنَكَ وَجَمَالَكَ تَنْهَزِمُ قُدَّامَكَ حَتَّى تَمْلِكَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu baʿḍu khawāṣṣihi anta kāmilu al-khiṣāli fī al-ḥusni wa-al-jamāli fa-law qātaltahā wa-kānat aqwā minka fa-innaka taghlibuhā li-annahā idhā raʾat ḥusnaka wa-jamālaka tanhazimu quddāmaka ḥattā tamlikahā
sentences.l: And one of his intimates said to him: You are perfect of qualities in beauty and comeliness; so if you fought her, and she were stronger than you, then you overcome her, because she, when she sees your beauty and your comeliness, is-routed before you, until you possess her.
sentences.i: But one of his intimates said to him, “You are perfect in every quality of beauty and grace. Were you to fight her, even if she were the stronger, you would get the better of her; for when she sees your beauty and grace she will give way before you, and you will have her.
sentences.n: baʿḍu khawāṣṣihi, “some of his intimates”, i.e. one of them. fa-law qātaltahā … fa-innaka taghlibuhā, “if you fought her … then you overcome her”: Classical would answer law with la-ghalabtahā; the present tense after fa-inna is Middle Arabic. Likewise tanhazimu, “she gives way”, answers idhā without a linking fa-. The print spells raʾat with its hamza. ḥattā tamlikahā, “so that you possess her”, as conqueror and as husband.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّ النِّسَاءَ لَهُنَّ غَرَضٌ فِى الرِّجَالِ وَلَا يَخْفَى عَنْكَ هَذِهِ الْأَحْوَالُ
sentences.tr: li-anna al-nisāʾa lahunna gharaḍun fī al-rijāli wa-lā yakhfā ʿanka hādhihi al-aḥwālu
sentences.l: Because the women, to them is a desire in the men, and these matters are not hidden from you.
sentences.i: For women have a hankering after men, and such things are no secret to you.”
sentences.n: gharaḍ, “aim, purpose”, here “a liking, a desire”. lā yakhfā … hādhihi al-aḥwālu: a masculine verb may stand before a feminine plural subject when the verb comes first. Rhyme: al-rijāl / al-aḥwāl, picking up al-khiṣāl / al-jamāl.

sentences.t: فَأَبَى كَهْرْدَاشُ وَامْتَنَعَ مِنْ قِتَالِهَا وَاسْتَمَرَّ عَلَى امْتِنَاعِهِ مِنَ الْقِتَالِ إِلَى أَنْ جَرَتْ لَهُ مَعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ هَذِهِ الْأَفْعَالُ
sentences.tr: fa-abā Kahrdāshu wa-imtanaʿa min qitālihā wa-istamarra ʿalā imtināʿihi mina al-qitāli ilā an jarat lahu maʿa Kāna Mā Kāna hādhihi al-afʿālu
sentences.l: But Kahrdāsh refused and held-back from fighting her, and persisted in his holding-back from the fighting, until there ran-their-course for him with Kān Mā Kān these doings.
sentences.i: But Kahrdāsh refused, would not fight her, and held firm in that refusal until these things befell him with Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: The print marks the doubled rāʾ of istamarra. jarat lahu … hādhihi al-afʿālu, “these doings ran their course for him”, i.e. until this encounter came about.

sentences.t: فَظَنَّ أَنَّهُ مَحْبُوبَتُهُ فَاتِنُ فَهَابَ وَقَدْ عَشِقَتْهُ لَمَّا سَمِعَتْ بِحُسْنِهِ وَشَجَاعَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ẓanna annahu maḥbūbatuhu Fātinu fa-hāba wa-qad ʿashiqathu lammā samiʿat bi-ḥusnihi wa-shajāʿatihi
sentences.l: And he thought that he was his beloved Fātin, and he was-awed; and she had fallen-in-love with him when she heard of his beauty and his courage.
sentences.i: And he took him for his beloved Fātin, and was overawed; for she had fallen in love with him when she heard of his beauty and his valour.
sentences.n: Here at last is the answer to “when he saw” above: fa-ẓanna, “he thought”. annahu maḥbūbatuhu, “that he was his beloved”: Kahrdāsh takes the rider before him for Fātin herself. In wa-qad ʿashiqathu the subject is feminine, so it is Fātin who had fallen in love with “him”; the him is most naturally Kahrdāsh, whose beauty his companion has just praised, though it could be read of Kān Mā Kān. samiʿa bi-, “to hear of”.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ إِلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ وَيْلَكِ يَا فَاتِنُ قَدْ أَتَيْتِنِي لِتُرِينِي شَجَاعَتَكِ فَانْزِلِي عَنْ جَوَادِكِ حَتَّى أَتَحَدَّثَ مَعَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama ilā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-qāla waylaki yā Fātinu qad ataytinī li-turīnī shajāʿataki fa-inzilī ʿan jawādiki ḥattā ataḥaddatha maʿaki
sentences.l: And he advanced to Kān Mā Kān and said: Woe-to-you, O Fātin! You have come to me to show me your courage; so get-down from your steed, so that I may talk with you.
sentences.i: Then he rode up to Kān Mā Kān and said, “Woe to you, Fātin! You have come out to show me your courage; now get down from your horse, so that I may talk with you.
sentences.n: The speaker is Kahrdāsh, who still takes the veiled rider for Fātin, a woman: so every “you” here is feminine — waylaki, ataytinī, turīnī, inzilī, jawādiki, maʿaki. The masculine and feminine forms of several of these words are written alike, and the pointing follows his mistake. waylaki, “woe to you”, is a rough form of address, here half taunt and half familiarity.

sentences.t: فَإِنِّي قَدْ سُقْتُ هَذِهِ الْأَمْوَالَ وَخُنْتُ الرَّفِيقَ وَقَطَعْتُ الطَّرِيقَ عَلَى الْفُرْسَانِ وَالْأَبْطَالِ كُلُّ هَذَا لِحُسْنِكِ وَجَمَالِكِ الَّذِي مَا لَهُ مَثِيلٌ وَتَزَوَّجِينِي حَتَّى تَخْدُمَكِ بَنَاتُ الْمُلُوكِ وَتَصِيرِى مَلِكَةَ هَذِهِ الْأَقْطَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-innī qad suqtu hādhihi al-amwāla wa-khuntu al-rafīqa wa-qaṭaʿtu al-ṭarīqa ʿalā al-fursāni wa-al-abṭāli kullu hādhā li-ḥusniki wa-jamāliki alladhī mā lahu mathīlun wa-tazawwajīnī ḥattā takhdumaki banātu al-mulūki wa-taṣīrī malikata hādhihi al-aqṭāri
sentences.l: For I have driven-off these goods, and betrayed the companion, and cut the road upon the horsemen and the heroes — all this for your beauty and your loveliness, which has no like; and marry-me, so that the daughters of the kings may serve you and you become queen of these regions.
sentences.i: For I have driven off these riches, betrayed my comrade, and waylaid horsemen and champions — all of it for the sake of your beauty and your loveliness, which has no equal. Marry me, and the daughters of kings shall wait on you, and you shall be queen of all these lands.”
sentences.n: suqtu, “I drove (off)”, from sāqa, to drive cattle or plunder before one; amwāl, “goods, wealth”, here the captured herds and loot. qaṭaʿa al-ṭarīq ʿalā, “to cut the road upon”, is the regular phrase for highway robbery. The verb tazawwajīnī is an imperative, “marry me!”, joined with wa- to what goes before — a lurch from boast to proposal. wa-taṣīrī is written with final ى, the edition’s habit for final yāʾ; it is subjunctive after ḥattā, which is why the feminine ending has no nūn.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ صَارَتْ نِيرَانُ غَيْظِهِ فِي اضْطِرَامٍ وَنَادَى وَيْلَكَ يَا كَلْبَ الْأَعْجَامِ دَعْ عَنْكَ فَاتِناً وَمَا بِهِ تَرْتَابُ وَتَقَدَّمْ إِلَى الطَّعْنِ وَالضِّرَابِ فَعَنْ قَرِيبٍ تَبْقَى عَلَى التُّرَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Kāna Mā Kāna hādhā al-kalāma ṣārat nīrānu ghayẓihi fī iḍṭirāmin wa-nādā waylaka yā kalba al-aʿjāmi daʿ ʿanka Fātinan wa-mā bihi tartābu wa-taqaddam ilā al-ṭaʿni wa-al-ḍirābi fa-ʿan qarībin tabqā ʿalā al-turābi
sentences.l: And when Kān Mā Kān heard this speech, the fires of his rage became in a-blaze, and he called-out: Woe-to-you, O dog of the barbarians! Leave from-you Fātin and what you are uneasy about, and come-forward to the thrusting and the striking — for in a-short-while you will remain upon the dust.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān heard these words, the fires of his wrath blazed up, and he cried, “Woe to you, you dog of the barbarians! Put Fātin out of your mind, and all your fretting with her, and come on to the thrust and the blow — for soon enough you will lie in the dust.”
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: iḍṭirām / aʿjām, then tartāb / ḍirāb / turāb. aʿjām, “non-Arabs, barbarians”, is a standard insult for a non-Arab foe. wa-mā bihi tartābu, literally “and that over which you are unsettled”: irtāba is “to doubt, be uneasy”; the sense seems to be “and whatever has you so stirred up” — the phrase is a little loose and our reading is a guess. The print gives Fātin the tanwīn (fātinan), declining the name as an ordinary adjective (“a seductive one”) rather than as a woman’s name, which would take no tanwīn; the mark is kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ جَالَ وَصَالَ وَمَدَّ وَاسْتَطَالَ فَلَمَّا نَظَرَهُ كَهْرْدَاشُ عَلِمَ أَنَّهُ فَارِسٌ هُمَامٌ وَبَطَلٌ ضِرْغَامٌ وَتَبَيَّنَ لَهُ خَطَأُ ظَنِّهِ حَيْثُ لَاحَ لَهُ عِذَارٌ أَخْضَرُ فَوْقَ خَدِّهِ كَآسِ نَبَتَ خِلَالَ وَرْدٍ أَحْمَرَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu jāla wa-ṣāla wa-madda wa-istaṭāla fa-lammā naẓarahu Kahrdāshu ʿalima annahu fārisun humāmun wa-baṭalun ḍirghāmun wa-tabayyana lahu khaṭaʾu ẓannihi ḥaythu lāḥa lahu ʿidhārun akhḍaru fawqa khaddihi ka-āsi nabata khilāla wardin aḥmara
sentences.l: Then he wheeled and charged, and stretched and reached-far; and when Kahrdāsh saw-him, he knew that he was a high-minded horseman and a lion-like hero, and the error of his supposition became-clear to him, since there gleamed to him a green cheek-down above his cheek, like myrtle that has sprouted amid a red rose.
sentences.i: Then he wheeled and charged, lunging and reaching far; and when Kahrdāsh looked at him, he knew him for a noble horseman and a lion of a champion. His mistake was plain to him now, for he caught sight of the green down above the youth’s cheek, like myrtle sprung up among red roses.
sentences.n: jāla wa-ṣāla, “he wheeled about and attacked”, is a stock jingling pair for a horseman showing his skill; madda wa-istaṭāla, “stretched out and reached far”, adds two more. naẓarahu, “saw him”, takes a direct object where Classical prose usually says naẓara ilayhi — a Middle Arabic habit. ʿidhār is the first down on a young man’s cheek, the sign that this is a beardless youth and no woman; poets call it green and compare it to myrtle (ās) on the rose of the cheek. The print points the word kāsi with a bare kasra where Classical would give the tanwīn (ka-āsin); the print’s mark is kept.

sentences.t: فَهَابَ مِنْ كَرَّتِهِ وَقَالَ لِلَّذِينَ مَعَهُ وَيْلَكُمْ لِيَحْمِلْ وَاحِدٌ مِنْكُمْ عَلَيْهِ وَيُظْهِرْ لَهُ السَّيْفَ الْبَتَّارَ وَالرُّمْحَ الْخَطَّارَ وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ قِتَالَ الْجَمَاعَةِ لِلْوَاحِدِ عَارٌ وَلَوْ كَانَ فَارِساً شُجَاعاً وَقَرْماً مَنَّاعاً
sentences.tr: fa-hāba min karratihi wa-qāla li-alladhīna maʿahu waylakum li-yaḥmil wāḥidun minkum ʿalayhi wa-yuẓhir lahu al-sayfa al-battāra wa-al-rumḥa al-khaṭṭāra wa-iʿlamū anna qitāla al-jamāʿati li-al-wāḥidi ʿārun wa-law kāna fārisan shujāʿan wa-qarman mannāʿan
sentences.l: And he feared his onset, and said to those who were with him: Woe-to-you! Let one of you charge upon him and show him the cutting sword and the quivering lance; and know that the fighting of the band against the one is a disgrace, even if he were a brave horseman and a warding chieftain.
sentences.i: He grew wary of the youth’s onset, and said to the men with him, “Out on you! Let one of you charge him and show him the keen sword and the quivering spear — and know that for a whole troop to fight one man is a shame, however brave a horseman he may be, and however stout a champion.”
sentences.n: hāba min, “to stand in awe of, be wary of”. li-yaḥmil … wa-yuẓhir: the lām of command with the jussive, “let one … charge, and let him show”. battār, “cutting”, and khaṭṭār, “quivering, swaying” (of a supple lance), are stock epithets; the pairs rhyme (battār / khaṭṭār / ʿār, shujāʿan / mannāʿan). qarm is properly a stallion kept for breeding, hence a lordly chief; mannāʿ, “one who wards off, defends stoutly”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ حَمَلَ عَلَيْهِ فَارِسٌ ضَيْغَمٌ وَتَحْتَهُ جَوَادٌ أَدْهَمُ بِتَحْجِيلٍ وَغُرَّةٍ كَالدِّرْهَمِ يُحَيِّرُ الْعَقْلَ وَالنَّاظِرَ كَأَنَّهُ الْأَبْجَرُ الَّذِي كَانَ لِعَنْتَرَ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ḥamala ʿalayhi fārisun ḍayghamun wa-taḥtahu jawādun adhamu bi-taḥjīlin wa-ghurratin ka-al-dirhami yuḥayyiru al-ʿaqla wa-al-nāẓira ka-annahu al-Abjaru alladhī kāna li-ʿAntara kamā qāla fīhi al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And at that, a lion horseman charged upon him, and beneath him a black steed with white-feet and a blaze like the dirham, bewildering the mind and the beholder, as-if it were al-Abjar that belonged to ʿAntar, as the poet said of it:
