sentences.i: At that a lion of a horseman charged him, mounted on a black steed with white stockings and a blaze like a silver dirham, a horse to dazzle the mind and the eye, as if it were al-Abjar, ʿAntar’s own steed — even as the poet says of such a horse:
sentences.n: ḍaygham, “lion”, used like an adjective after fāris. adham, “black” (of a horse); taḥjīl, white markings on the legs; ghurra, a white blaze on the forehead, here round and bright “like the dirham”, the silver coin. al-Abjar was the famous horse of ʿAntar ibn Shaddād, the black warrior-poet of pre-Islamic legend.

sentences.t:
قَدْ جَاءَكَ الْمُهْرُ الَّذِى نَزَلَ الْوَغَى * جَزْلَانَ يَخْلِطُ اَرْضَهُ بِسَمَائِهِ
وَكَاَنَّمَا لَطَمَ الصَّبَاحُ جَبِينَهُ * وَاقْتَصَّ مِنْهُ فَخَاضَ فِي اَحْشَائِهِ
sentences.tr:
qad jāʾaka al-muhru alladhī nazala al-waghā * jazlāna yakhliṭu arḍahu bi-samāʾihi
wa-ka-annamā laṭama al-ṣabāḥu jabīnahu * wa-iqtaṣṣa minhu fa-khāḍa fī aḥshāʾihi
sentences.l:
There-has-come to you the colt that went-down into the fray * exulting, mixing its earth with its sky;
and as-though the morning had slapped its forehead * and it took-retaliation from it, and waded into its entrails.
sentences.i:
Here comes the colt that rode down into the fray, exulting, * mingling its earth and its heaven as it goes;
as though the dawn had struck it on the brow, * and it took its revenge, and plunged deep into the dawn’s own bowels.
sentences.n: Metre kāmil, rhyme -āʾihi. The conceit: the horse is black, and its white blaze is the mark where the dawn slapped its forehead; in revenge the black horse plunged into the dawn’s entrails — that is, it carries the night in its body and the morning on its brow. “Mixing its earth with its sky” is the dust it raises into the air, or its leaping from ground to sky. The print writes the hamza seats as alif with fatḥa (اَرْضَهُ, وَكَاَنَّمَا, اَحْشَائِهِ); its pointing is kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَحَمَلَ عَلَي كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَابْتَدَرَ وَتَجَاوَلَا فِى الْحَرْبِ بُرْهَةً مِنَ الزَّمَانِ وَتَضَارَبَا ضَرْباً يُحَيِّرُ الْأَفْكَارَ وَيُعْشِى الْأَبْصَارَ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥamala ʿalā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-ibtadara wa-tajāwalā fī al-ḥarbi burhatan mina al-zamāni wa-taḍārabā ḍarban yuḥayyiru al-afkāra wa-yuʿshī al-abṣāra
sentences.l: And he charged upon Kān Mā Kān and rushed-forward, and the two wheeled-about-each-other in the war a while of time, and the two exchanged-blows with a striking that bewilders the thoughts and dims the eyes.
sentences.i: He bore down on Kān Mā Kān and rushed at him, and the two of them wheeled about each other in combat for a good while, trading blows that would bewilder the mind and dazzle the sight.
sentences.n: The print spells ʿalā here with a dotted final yāʾ (علي), a variant spelling of the same word; it is kept. tajāwalā and taḍārabā are dual verbs of the reciprocal form VI: “they circled each other”, “they struck at each other”. afkār / abṣār rhyme.

sentences.t: فَسَبَقَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ بِضَرْبَةِ بَطَلٍ شُجَاعٍ فَقَطَعَتْ مِنْهُ الْعِمَامَةَ وَالْمِغْفَرَ وَإِلَى رَأْسِهِ وَصَلَتْ فَمَالَ عَنِ الْجَوَادِ كَأَنَّهُ الْبَعِيرُ إِذَا انْحَدَرَ
sentences.tr: fa-sabaqahu Kāna Mā Kāna bi-ḍarbati baṭalin shujāʿin fa-qaṭaʿat minhu al-ʿimāmata wa-al-mighfara wa-ilā raʾsihi waṣalat fa-māla ʿani al-jawādi ka-annahu al-baʿīru idhā inḥadara
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān got-ahead-of-him with the stroke of a brave hero, and it cut from him the turban and the helmet, and to his head it reached; and he leaned-off from the steed as-though he were the camel when it goes-down.
sentences.i: But Kān Mā Kān was quicker, and dealt him the stroke of a valiant champion, which sheared through his turban and his helmet and bit down into his head; and he toppled from his horse like a camel going down.
sentences.n: The print has فقطت, a misprint for فقطعت, corrected here. The subject of qaṭaʿat and waṣalat is the stroke (ḍarba, feminine). mighfar is the mail coif or helmet worn under or over the turban. wa-ilā raʾsihi waṣalat puts the phrase “to his head” first for emphasis: “and right to his head it went”. raʾs is printed without its hamza (راسه), the edition’s usual spelling.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ الثَّانِي وَحَمَلَ عَلَيْهِ وَكَذَا الثَّالِثُ وَالرَّابِعُ وَالْخَامِسُ فَفَعَلَ بِهِمْ كَالْأَوَّلِ
sentences.tr: thumma taqaddama ilayhi al-thānī wa-ḥamala ʿalayhi wa-ka-dhā al-thālithu wa-al-rābiʿu wa-al-khāmisu fa-faʿala bihim ka-al-awwali
sentences.l: Then the second advanced to him and charged upon him, and likewise the third and the fourth and the fifth, and he did with them as-with the first.
sentences.i: Then the second came out against him and charged, and after him the third, the fourth and the fifth; and he dealt with each of them as he had with the first.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَمَلَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْبَاقُونَ وَقَدِ اشْتَدَّ بِهِمُ الْقَلَقُ وَزَادَتْ بِهِمُ الْحُرَقُ فَمَا كَانَ إِلَّا سَاعَةٌ حَتَّى الْتَقَطَهُمْ بِسِنَانِ رُمْحِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥamalat ʿalayhi al-bāqūna wa-qadi ishtadda bihimu al-qalaqu wa-zādat bihimu al-ḥuraqu fa-mā kāna illā sāʿatun ḥattā iltaqaṭahum bi-sināni rumḥihi
sentences.l: Then the remaining-ones charged upon him, and the agitation had grown-severe in them and the burnings had increased in them; and there was not but an hour until he picked-them-off with the point of his lance.
sentences.i: Then the rest of them charged him all together, their alarm now grown sharp and their anguish burning ever hotter; and within the hour he had picked them off, one by one, on the point of his spear.
sentences.n: ḥamalat … al-bāqūna: a feminine verb with a masculine plural subject, a looseness of agreement common in this Arabic (the group treated as a collective). ḥuraq, plural of ḥurqa, “burning, anguish”; qalaq / ḥuraq make a rhyme. mā kāna illā sāʿatun ḥattā, “there was only an hour before”, is the stock way of saying how fast it happened. The print marks the shadda in illā. iltaqaṭa, “to pick up, pick off one by one”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ كَهْرْدَاشُ إِلَى هَذِهِ الْفِعَالِ خَافَ مِنَ الِارْتِحَالِ وَعَرَفَ أَنَّ عِنْدَهُ ثَبَاتَ الْجَنَانِ وَاعْتَقَدَ أَنَّهُ أَوْحَدُ الْأَبْطَالِ وَالْفُرْسَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara Kahrdāshu ilā hādhihi al-fiʿāli khāfa mina al-irtiḥāli wa-ʿarafa anna ʿindahu thabāta al-janāni wa-iʿtaqada annahu awḥadu al-abṭāli wa-al-fursāni
sentences.l: And when Kahrdāsh looked at these deeds, he feared the departing, and knew that he had firmness of the heart, and believed that he was the unique-one of the heroes and the horsemen.
sentences.i: When Kahrdāsh saw these feats, he feared that his own last journey was at hand; he knew that the youth had a heart that would not waver, and he was persuaded that here was the peerless one among all champions and horsemen.
sentences.n: khāfa mina al-irtiḥāl, literally “he feared the departure”: irtiḥāl, “setting out on a journey”, is a common euphemism for death, and that is how we take it here; it could also mean he feared to turn and flee. Rhymed prose: fiʿāl / irtiḥāl, then janān / fursān. thabāt al-janān, “steadiness of heart”, i.e. a cool nerve.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِكَانَ مَا كَانَ قَدْ وَهَبْتُ لَكَ دَمَكَ وَدَمَ أَصْحَابِي فَخُذْ مِنَ الْمَالِ مَا شِئْتَ وَاذْهَبْ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِكَ فَقَدْ رَحِمْتُكَ لِحُسْنِ ثَبَاتِكَ وَالْحَيَوٰةُ أَوْلَى بِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla li-Kāna Mā Kāna qad wahabtu laka damaka wa-dama aṣḥābī fa-khudh mina al-māli mā shiʾta wa-idhhab ilā ḥāli sabīlika fa-qad raḥimtuka li-ḥusni thabātika wa-al-ḥayātu awlā bika
sentences.l: And he said to Kān Mā Kān: I have granted to you your blood and the blood of my companions; so take of the wealth what you wish, and go to the state of your way, for I have pitied you for the goodness of your steadfastness, and life is more-fitting for you.
sentences.i: And he said to Kān Mā Kān, “I make you a gift of your life and of my comrades’ blood. Take what you will of the plunder and go your way; I have taken pity on you for the fine stand you have made, and life becomes you better than death.”
sentences.n: wahabtu laka damaka, “I have given you your blood”, i.e. I spare your life — and he waives vengeance for the men he has lost. idhhab ilā ḥāli sabīlika, “go off about your business”, a fixed phrase. al-ḥayāt is printed الحيوة, the old spelling with wāw (as in the Qurʾān), read ḥayāt; we point it with the small alif.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ لَا عَدِمْتَ مُرُوَّةَ الْكِرَامِ وَلَٰكِنِ اتْرُكْ عَنْكَ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ وَفُزْ بِنَفْسِكَ وَلَا تَخْشَ الْمَلَامَ وَلَا تُطْمِعْ نَفْسَكَ فِي رَدِّ الْغَنِيمَةِ وَاسْلُكْ لِنَجَاةِ نَفْسِكَ طَرِيقَةً مُسْتَقِيمَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Kāna Mā Kāna lā ʿadimta muruwwata al-kirāmi wa-lākini utruk ʿanka hādhā al-kalāma wa-fuz bi-nafsika wa-lā takhsha al-malāma wa-lā tuṭmiʿ nafsaka fī raddi al-ghanīmati wa-usluk li-najāti nafsika ṭarīqatan mustaqīmatan
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: May you not lack the manliness of the noble! But leave from-you this talk, and escape with your soul, and do not fear the blame; and do not make your soul covet the return of the booty, and take for the saving of your soul a straight path.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān answered, “May you never want for the chivalry of noble men! But leave off this talk: save your own skin and never mind the reproach, and do not let yourself hope to get the plunder back. Take the straight road, and save your life.”
sentences.n: lā ʿadimta, “may you not lose / not lack”, a polite formula of thanks, here with an edge of mockery. muruwwa, “manliness, chivalrous virtue”, is printed مروة without its hamza (Classical murūʾa); we read the unhamzated form muruwwa, which the lexicons also give. fuz bi-nafsika, “win safety with your own self”, i.e. escape alive. tuṭmiʿ nafsaka, “make yourself covet”, causative form IV. Rhymed prose: kirām / kalām / malām, then ghanīma / mustaqīma.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ اشْتَدَّ بِكَهْرْدَاشَ الْغَضَبُ وَحَصَلَ عِنْدَهُ مَا يُوجِبُ الْعَطَبَ فَقَالَ لِكَانَ مَا كَانَ وَيْلَكَ لَوْ عَرَفْتَ مَنْ أَنَا مَا نَطَقْتَ بِهَذَا الْكَلَامِ فِي حَوْمَةِ الزِّحَامِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ishtadda bi-Kahrdāsha al-ghaḍabu wa-ḥaṣala ʿindahu mā yūjibu al-ʿaṭaba fa-qāla li-Kāna Mā Kāna waylaka law ʿarafta man anā mā naṭaqta bi-hādhā al-kalāmi fī ḥawmati al-ziḥāmi
sentences.l: And at that the anger grew-severe in Kahrdāsh, and there came-about in him what necessitates ruin; and he said to Kān Mā Kān: Woe-to-you! If you knew who I am, you would not have uttered this speech in the thick of the press.
sentences.i: At that Kahrdāsh’s anger rose to a pitch, and there came over him a fury fit to bring on destruction, and he said to Kān Mā Kān, “Woe to you! If you knew who I am, you would never have spoken such words in the thick of the fight.
sentences.n: ghaḍab / ʿaṭab and kalām / ziḥām rhyme. mā yūjibu al-ʿaṭab, “what entails ruin”, i.e. a rage that would destroy someone. ḥawmat al-ziḥām, “the thick of the crush”, the heart of the battle.

sentences.t: فَاسْأَلْ عَنِّي فَأَنَا الْأَسَدُ الْبَطَّاشُ الْمَعْرُوفُ بِكَهْرْ دَاشَ الَّذِي نَهَبَ الْمُلُوكَ الْكِبَارَ وَقَطَعَ الطَّرِيقَ عَلَى جَمِيعِ السُّفَّارِ وَأَخَذَ أَمْوَالَ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: fa-isʾal ʿannī fa-anā al-asadu al-baṭṭāshu al-maʿrūfu bi-Kahr Dāsha alladhī nahaba al-mulūka al-kibāra wa-qaṭaʿa al-ṭarīqa ʿalā jamīʿi al-suffāri wa-akhadha amwāla al-tujjāri
sentences.l: So ask about me: for I am the lion, the violent-striker, the one known as Kahrdāsh, who plundered the great kings, and cut the road upon all the travellers, and took the wealth of the merchants.
sentences.i: Ask who I am! I am the fierce-handed lion known as Kahrdāsh, who has plundered great kings, waylaid every traveller on the road, and stripped the merchants of their goods.
sentences.n: The print here sets the name in two words, كهر داش; the spacing is kept. baṭṭāsh, “one who seizes and strikes violently”. kibār / suffār / tujjār rhyme; suffār, “travellers”, is plural of sāfir, and the print marks its shadda.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا الْحِصَانُ الَّذِي تَحْتَكَ طَلِبَتِي وَأُرِيدُ أَنْ تُعَرِّفَنِي كَيْفَ وَصَلْتَ إِلَيْهِ حَتَّى اسْتَوْلَيْتَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā al-ḥiṣānu alladhī taḥtaka ṭalibatī wa-urīdu an tuʿarrifanī kayfa waṣalta ilayhi ḥattā istawlayta ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And this stallion which is under you is my quest; and I want you to inform me how you reached it, so that you got-possession of it.
sentences.i: This stallion under you is the prize I was after, and I want you to tell me how you came at him and made yourself his master.”
sentences.n: ṭaliba, “the thing sought, one’s object”. The ḥiṣān is the horse al-Qātūl, which Kahrdāsh had seized from the old woman’s party.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ هَذَا الْجَوَادَ كَانَ سَائِراً إِلَى عَمِّي الْمَلِكِ سَا سَانَ وَقَائِدَتُهُ عَجُوزٌ كَبِيرَةٌ وَمَعَهَا عَشَرَةُ عَبِيدٍ يَخْدُمُونَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla iʿlam anna hādhā al-jawāda kāna sāʾiran ilā ʿammī al-maliki Sā Sāna wa-qāʾidatuhu ʿajūzun kabīratun wa-maʿahā ʿasharatu ʿabīdin yakhdumūnahā
sentences.l: And he said: Know that this steed was going to my uncle, the king Sāsān, and its leader an old-woman, aged, and with her ten slaves serving her.
sentences.i: He said, “Know that this horse was on its way to my uncle, King Sāsān, led by an aged crone with ten slaves to wait on her.
sentences.n: Sāsān, the king who has seized the throne of Baghdad, is Kān Mā Kān’s uncle by marriage, the husband of his aunt Nuzhat al-Zamān. The print sets his name as two words, سا سان; the spacing is kept. qāʾidatuhu, “its leader”, the one leading the horse by its halter.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ تَعَدَّيْتَ عَلَيْهَا وَأَخَذْتَهُ مِنْهَا وَلَنَا عِنْدَهَا ثَأْرٌ مِنْ جِهَةِ جَدِّي الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ وَعَمِّي الْمَلِكِ شَرَّكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-anta taʿaddayta ʿalayhā wa-akhadhtahu minhā wa-lanā ʿindahā thaʾrun min jihati jaddī al-maliki ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni wa-ʿammī al-maliki Sharrkāna
sentences.l: And you transgressed against her and took it from her; and we have with her a blood-vengeance on the side of my grandfather, the king ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, and my uncle, the king Sharrkān.
sentences.i: You fell upon her and took him from her. And we have a blood-debt to settle with that woman, for my grandfather King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān and for my uncle King Sharrkān.”
sentences.n: thaʾr, “blood-revenge”, is printed ثار without its hamza. ʿindahā, “with her”: she owes it to them. The old woman is the one who brought about the deaths of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān and of Sharrkān earlier in the tale.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ كَهْرْدَاشُ وَيْلَكَ وَمَنْ أَبُوكَ لَا أُمَّ لَكَ فَقَالَ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي كَانَ مَا كَانَ ابْنُ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Kahrdāshu waylaka wa-man abūka lā umma laka fa-qāla iʿlam annī Kāna Mā Kāna ibnu Ḍawʾi al-Makāni ibni ʿUmara ibni al-Nuʿmāni
sentences.l: And Kahrdāsh said: Woe-to-you! And who is your father — no mother to you? And he said: Know that I am Kān Mā Kān, son of Ḍawʾ al-Makān, son of ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān.
sentences.i: “Woe to you,” said Kahrdāsh, “and who is your father, you motherless wretch?” He answered, “Know that I am Kān Mā Kān, son of Ḍawʾ al-Makān, son of ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān.”
sentences.n: lā umma laka, “may you have no mother”, an old Arab imprecation, often half admiring; here rough contempt. The name Kān Mā Kān does not decline, so the case shows on ibn: ibnu, nominative, in apposition to him, and then ibni, genitive, in apposition to Ḍawʾ al-Makān.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَهْرْدَاشُ هَذَا الْخِطَابَ قَالَ لَا يُسْتَنْكَرُ عَلَيْكَ الْكَمَالُ وَالْجَمْعُ بَيْنَ الْفُرُوسِيَّةِ وَالْجَمَالِ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ تَوَجَّهْ بِأَمَانٍ فَإِنَّ أَبَاكَ كَانَ صَاحِبَ فَضْلٍ عَلَيْنَا وَإِحْسَانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Kahrdāshu hādhā al-khiṭāba qāla lā yustankaru ʿalayka al-kamālu wa-al-jamʿu bayna al-furūsiyyati wa-al-jamāli thumma qāla lahu tawajjah bi-amānin fa-inna abāka kāna ṣāḥiba faḍlin ʿalaynā wa-iḥsānin
sentences.l: And when Kahrdāsh heard this address, he said: Not deemed-strange in you is the perfection, and the joining between the horsemanship and the beauty. Then he said to him: Set-out in safety, for your father was a possessor of favour upon us and kindness.
sentences.i: When Kahrdāsh heard this, he said, “Then no wonder you are so accomplished, and join such horsemanship to such beauty!” And he said to him, “Go your way in safety, for your father was a man of great kindness and bounty towards us.”
sentences.n: lā yustankaru ʿalayka, “it is not to be thought strange in you”, passive of form X istankara, “to find strange, disapprove”. kamāl / jamāl rhyme, and amān / iḥsān. The print marks the shadda in tawajjah. Note the split phrase ṣāḥiba faḍlin ʿalaynā wa-iḥsānin, “a man of favour towards us, and of kindness”, with the rhyme word held to the end.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ أَنَا وَاللّٰهِ مَا أُوَقِّرُكَ يَا مُهَانُ حَتَّى أَتْهَرَكَ فِى حَوْمَةِ الْمَيْدَانِ فَاغْتَاظَ الْبَدَوِيُّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Kāna Mā Kāna anā wa-Allāhi mā uwaqqiruka yā muhānu ḥattā atharaka fī ḥawmati al-maydāni fa-ightāẓa al-badawiyyu
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: I, by God, will not honour you, O despised-one, until I [humble] you in the thick of the field. And the Bedouin was enraged.
sentences.i: But Kān Mā Kān said to him, “By God, I will show you no respect, you contemptible creature, until I have brought you low in the thick of the field!” At that the Bedouin flew into a rage.
sentences.n: The print has اتهرك, a word we cannot find in the lexicons; it is kept as printed and pointed atharaka only for want of better. The sense must be something like “humble, drive off”: likely candidates are anharaka, “I drive you back, rebuke you” (one dot moved, ت for ن), or aqharaka, “I overpower you”; we translate the sense and leave the letters. The print marks the shadda in uwaqqiruka, “I honour you”. muhān, “one held in contempt”, answers Kahrdāsh’s courtesy with an insult (maydān rhymes with muhān). Kahrdāsh is called al-badawī, “the Bedouin”: the robber chief of the desert, though his band and kin are not Arabs.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَمَلَ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا عَلَى صَاحِبِهِ وَتَصَايَحَا فَسَدَّتْ لَهُمَا الْخَيْلُ آذَانَهَا وَرَفَعَتْ أَذْنَابَهَا وَلَمْ يَزَالَا يَصْطَدِمَانِ حَتَّى ظَنَّ كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا أَنَّ السَّمَاءَ قَدِ انْشَقَّتْ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥamala kullun minhumā ʿalā ṣāḥibihi wa-taṣāyaḥā fa-saddat lahumā al-khaylu ādhānahā wa-rafaʿat adhnābahā wa-lam yazālā yaṣṭadimāni ḥattā ẓanna kullun minhumā anna al-samāʾa qadi inshaqqat
sentences.l: Then each-one of-them charged upon his companion, and they shouted-at-each-other, so the horses stopped-up their ears at-them and raised their tails; and they did not cease clashing until each-one of-them thought that the sky had split.
sentences.i: Then each charged at the other, and they raised such war-cries that the horses stopped their ears at them and lifted their tails; and they went on clashing until each of them thought the sky had split asunder.
sentences.n: ḥamala ʿalā, “to bear down upon, charge”. ṣāḥibihi, literally “his companion”, is the usual word for “the other one” in a duel. taṣāyaḥā, “they shouted at each other”: the sixth form gives the mutual sense. The horses “stopped their ears” (saddat ... ādhānahā) at the din of the two riders; lahumā, “at them”, names its cause.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ تَقَاتَلَا كَكِبَاشِ النِّطَاحِ وَاخْتَلَفَتْ بَيْنَهُمَا طَعَنَاتُ الرِّمَاحِ فَحَاوَلَهُ كَهْرْ دَاشُ بِطَعْنَةٍ فَزَاغَ عَنْهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ ثُمَّ كَرَّ عَلَيْهِ وَطَعَنَهُ فِي صَدْرِهِ فَأَطْلَعَ السِّنَانَ مِنْ ظَهْرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma baʿda dhālika taqātalā ka-kibāshi al-niṭāḥi wa-ikhtalafat baynahumā ṭaʿanātu al-rimāḥi fa-ḥāwalahu Kahr Dāshu bi-ṭaʿnatin fa-zāgha ʿanhā Kāna Mā Kāna thumma karra ʿalayhi wa-ṭaʿanahu fī ṣadrihi fa-aṭlaʿa al-sināna min ẓahrihi
sentences.l: Then after that they fought like rams of butting, and the thrusts of the spears went-back-and-forth between them; and Kahr Dāsh tried-for-him with a thrust, but Kān Mā Kān swerved from it, then wheeled upon him and thrust him in his chest, and made the spearhead come-out from his back.
sentences.i: After that they fought like butting rams, and spear-thrusts passed to and fro between them. Kahrdāsh aimed a thrust at him, but Kān Mā Kān swerved aside from it, then wheeled upon him and drove his spear into his chest so that the point came out through his back.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-niṭāḥ / al-rimāḥ. kibāsh al-niṭāḥ, “rams of butting”, fighting rams. The print splits the name here into two words, كهر داش; a few lines on it sets كهرداش as one. ḥāwalahu bi-ṭaʿna, “he attempted him with a thrust”. zāgha ʿan, “to swerve from, dodge”. karra, “to wheel round and attack again”; the print marks its doubled rāʾ. aṭlaʿa is the causative of ṭalaʿa, “to come out”: he made the spearhead come out of his back.

sentences.t: وَجَمَعَ الْخَيْلَ وَالْأَسْلَابَ وَصَاحَ فِى الْعَبِيدِ دُونَكُمْ وَالسَّوْقَ الشَّدِيدَ
sentences.tr: wa-jamaʿa al-khayla wa-al-aslāba wa-ṣāḥa fī al-ʿabīdi dūnakum wa-al-sawqa al-shadīda
sentences.l: And he gathered the horses and the spoils, and shouted at the slaves: “At-it! And the hard driving!”
sentences.i: He gathered up the horses and the spoils and cried out to the slaves, “To it, and drive them hard!”
sentences.n: ṣāḥa fī, “to shout at”. dūnakum, literally “before you”, is an interjection meaning “take it, set to it”; al-sawqa al-shadīda, “the hard driving”, is in the accusative as the thing they are urged to: “get on with driving hard”. The slaves are those of Kahrdāsh's band, now Kān Mā Kān's to command.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ عِنْدَ ذَلِكَ صَبَّاحٌ وَجَاءَ إِلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ أَحْسَنْتَ يَا فَارِسَ الزَّمَانِ إِنِّي دَعَوْتُ لَكَ وَقَدِ اسْتَجَابَ رَبِّي دُعَائِي
sentences.tr: fa-nazala ʿinda dhālika Ṣabbāḥun wa-jāʾa ilā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-qāla lahu aḥsanta yā fārisa al-zamāni innī daʿawtu laka wa-qadi istajāba rabbī duʿāʾī
sentences.l: So Ṣabbāḥ came-down at that, and came to Kān Mā Kān and said to him: “You-did-well, O horseman of the age! I prayed for you, and my Lord has answered my prayer.”
sentences.i: At that Ṣabbāḥ came down and went to Kān Mā Kān and said, “Well done, O knight of the age! I prayed for you, and my Lord has answered my prayer.”
sentences.n: nazala, “came down”: Ṣabbāḥ comes down from where he had kept out of the fight. aḥsanta, “you have done well”, the ordinary word of praise. fāris al-zamān, “the horseman of the age”, the champion of his time.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ صَبَّاحًا قَطَعَ رَأْسَ كَهْرْدَاشَ فَضَحِكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ يَا صَبَّاحُ كُنْتُ أَظُنُّ أَنَّكَ فَارِسُ الْحَرْبِ وَالْكِفَاحِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Ṣabbāḥan qaṭaʿa raʾsa Kahrdāsha fa-ḍaḥika Kāna Mā Kāna wa-qāla lahu waylaka yā Ṣabbāḥu kuntu aẓunnu annaka fārisu al-ḥarbi wa-al-kifāḥi
sentences.l: Then Ṣabbāḥ cut-off the head of Kahrdāsh; and Kān Mā Kān laughed and said to him: “Woe-to-you, O Ṣabbāḥ! I used-to think that you were the horseman of war and combat.”
sentences.i: Then Ṣabbāḥ cut off Kahrdāsh's head, and Kān Mā Kān laughed and said, “Confound you, Ṣabbāḥ! I took you for a champion of war and battle.”
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then (it was that)”, the narrator's usual way of moving the story on. The laugh is mockery: Ṣabbāḥ is brave enough to behead a man already dead. waylaka, “woe to you”, here a teasing rebuke rather than a curse. al-kifāḥ rhymes with Ṣabbāḥ.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ لَا تَنْسَ عَبْدَكَ مِنْ هَذِهِ الْغَنِيمَةِ لَعَلِّي أَصِلُ بِسَبَبِهَا إِلَى زَوَاجِ بِنْتِ عَمِّي نَجْمَةَ فَقَالَ لَهُ لَابُدَّ لَكَ فِيهَا مِنْ نَصِيبٍ وَلَكِنْ كُنْ مُحَافِظًا عَلَى الْغَنِيمَةِ وَالْعَبِيدِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu lā tansa ʿabdaka min hādhihi al-ghanīmati laʿallī aṣilu bi-sababihā ilā zawāji binti ʿammī Najmata fa-qāla lahu lā budda laka fīhā min naṣībin wa-lākin kun muḥāfiẓan ʿalā al-ghanīmati wa-al-ʿabīdi
sentences.l: And he said to him: “Do-not forget your slave from this booty; perhaps I may arrive by-means-of-it at marriage to the daughter of my paternal-uncle, Najma.” And he said to him: “There-is-no-escape: for you in it is a share; but be guarding over the booty and the slaves.”
sentences.i: “Do not forget your servant when this booty is shared,” said Ṣabbāḥ; “perhaps by it I may win my cousin Najma in marriage.” “You shall certainly have a share of it,” said Kān Mā Kān, “but keep watch over the booty and the slaves.”
sentences.n: ʿabdaka, “your slave”, the humble way of saying “me”. Najma is Ṣabbāḥ's cousin, bint ʿammī, “my father's brother's daughter”, whom he hopes to marry once he has the bride-price. lā budda laka fīhā min naṣīb, “there is no escaping a share for you in it”, that is, you are sure of a share; the print runs lā budda together as one word here.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ سَارَ مُتَوَجِّهًا إِلَى الدِّيَارِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ سَائِرًا بِاللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ حَتَّى أَشْرَفَ عَلَى مَدِينَةِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Kāna Mā Kāna sāra mutawajjihan ilā al-diyāri wa-lam yazal sāʾiran bi-al-layli wa-al-nahāri ḥattā ashrafa ʿalā madīnati Baghdāda
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān went-off, heading to the home-lands, and did not cease travelling by night and day until he overlooked the city of Baghdad.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān set off for home, and journeyed on by night and day until he came in sight of the city of Baghdad.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-diyār / al-nahār. al-diyār, “the dwellings”, is home. ashrafa ʿalā, “to look down upon, come within sight of”.

sentences.t: وَعَلِمَتْ بِهِ جَمِيعُ الْأَجْنَادِ وَرَؤَا مَا مَعَهُ مِنَ الْغَنِيمَةِ وَالْأَمْوَالِ وَرَأْسَ كَهْرْدَاشَ عَلَى رُمْحِ صَبَّاحٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿalimat bihi jamīʿu al-ajnādi wa-raʾaw mā maʿahu mina al-ghanīmati wa-al-amwāli wa-raʾsa Kahrdāsha ʿalā rumḥi Ṣabbāḥin
sentences.l: And all the troops knew of him, and they saw what was with him of the booty and the wealth, and the head of Kahrdāsh on the spear of Ṣabbāḥ.
sentences.i: All the troops learned of his coming, and saw the booty and riches he brought with him, and Kahrdāsh's head on Ṣabbāḥ's spear.
sentences.n: ʿalimat ... jamīʿu al-ajnād: a feminine verb with “all the troops”, agreeing with the plural as a collective. The print spells raʾaw, “they saw”, as رؤا, the hamza on a wāw-seat standing for the plural's -aw; it is read raʾaw.

sentences.t: وَعَرَفَ التُّجَّارُ رَأْسَ كَهْرْدَاشَ فَفَرِحُوا وَقَالُوا لَقَدْ أَرَاحَ اللَّهُ الْخَلْقَ مِنْهُ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ قَاطِعَ الطَّرِيقِ وَتَعَجَّبُوا مِنْ قَتْلِهِ وَدَعَوْا لِقَاتِلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿarafa al-tujjāru raʾsa Kahrdāsha fa-fariḥū wa-qālū laqad arāḥa Allāhu al-khalqa minhu li-annahu kāna qāṭiʿa al-ṭarīqi wa-taʿajjabū min qatlihi wa-daʿaw li-qātilihi
sentences.l: And the merchants recognised the head of Kahrdāsh and rejoiced, and said: “God has indeed given-rest to the people from him, for he was a cutter of the road”; and they marvelled at his killing, and prayed for his killer.
sentences.i: The merchants knew Kahrdāsh's head and were glad. “God has rid mankind of him at last,” they said, “for he was a highway robber”; and they marvelled that he had been slain, and called down blessings on the man who slew him.
sentences.n: arāḥa ... min, “to give rest from, relieve of”. qāṭiʿ al-ṭarīq, “cutter of the road”, a highwayman. daʿā li-, “to pray for, bless”.

sentences.t: وَأَتَتْ أَهْلُ بَغْدَادَ إِلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ يَسْأَلُونَ بِمَاجَرَى لَهُ مِنَ الْأَخْبَارِ فَأَخْبَرَهُمْ بِمَاجَرَى فَهَابَتْهُ جَمِيعُ الرِّجَالِ وَخَافَتْهُ الْفُرْسَانُ وَالْأَبْطَالُ
sentences.tr: wa-atat ahlu Baghdāda ilā Kāna Mā Kāna yasʾalūna bi-mājarā lahu mina al-akhbāri fa-akhbarahum bi-mājarā fa-hābathu jamīʿu al-rijāli wa-khāfathu al-fursānu wa-al-abṭālu
sentences.l: And the people of Baghdad came to Kān Mā Kān, asking about what-had-happened to him of tidings; and he told them what-had-happened, and all the men held him in awe, and the horsemen and the champions feared him.
sentences.i: The people of Baghdad came to Kān Mā Kān to ask him all that had befallen him, and he told them; and every man stood in awe of him, and the knights and champions feared him.
sentences.n: atat ahlu: a feminine verb with ahl, “people”, taken as a collective. yasʾalūna bi-, “asking about”: bi- where Classical prefers ʿan. The print runs bi-mā jarā together as one word, بماجرى, both times. Rhymed prose: al-rijāl / al-abṭāl.

sentences.t: وَسَاقَ مَا مَعَهُ إِلَى أَنْ أَوْصَلَهُ تَحْتَ الْقَصْرِ وَرَكَزَ الرُّمْحَ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ رَأْسُ كَهْرْدَاشَ إِلَى بَابِ الْقَصْرِ وَوَهَبَ لِلنَّاسِ وَأَعْطَاهُمُ الْخَيْلَ وَالْجِمَالَ فَأَحَبَّهُ أَهْلُ بَغْدَادَ وَمَالَتْ إِلَيْهِ الْقُلُوبُ
sentences.tr: wa-sāqa mā maʿahu ilā an awṣalahu taḥta al-qaṣri wa-rakaza al-rumḥa alladhī ʿalayhi raʾsu Kahrdāsha ilā bābi al-qaṣri wa-wahaba li-al-nāsi wa-aʿṭāhumu al-khayla wa-al-jimāla fa-aḥabbahu ahlu Baghdāda wa-mālat ilayhi al-qulūbu
sentences.l: And he drove what was with him until he brought-it beneath the palace, and planted the spear on which was the head of Kahrdāsh at the gate of the palace, and gave-freely to the people, and gave them the horses and the camels; so the people of Baghdad loved him, and the hearts inclined to him.
sentences.i: He drove all he had brought until he had it beneath the palace, and planted the spear that bore Kahrdāsh's head by the palace gate; and he made gifts to the people, bestowing on them the horses and the camels, so that the people of Baghdad loved him and all hearts were drawn to him.
sentences.n: The print has اغطاهم, a misprint for اعطاهم, corrected here. awṣalahu, “he brought it to”, causative of waṣala, “to arrive”. rakaza ... ilā bāb al-qaṣr, “planted ... up to the palace gate”: ilā where Classical would say ʿinda, “at”. wahaba li-, “to make a gift to”; the print marks the doubled bāʾ of aḥabbahu.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَقْبَلَ عَلَى صَبَّاحٍ وَأَنْزَلَهُ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَمَاكِنِ الْفِسَاحِ وَأَعْطَاهُ شَيْأً مِنَ الْغَنِيمَةِ ثُمَّ دَخَلَ عَلَى أُمِّهِ وَأَخْبَرَهَا بِمَا جَرَى لَهُ فِي سَفَرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma aqbala ʿalā Ṣabbāḥin wa-anzalahu fī baʿḍi al-amākini al-fisāḥi wa-aʿṭāhu shayʾan mina al-ghanīmati thumma dakhala ʿalā ummihi wa-akhbarahā bi-mā jarā lahu fī safarihi
sentences.l: Then he turned-to Ṣabbāḥ and lodged him in some-one of the spacious places, and gave him something of the booty; then he went-in to his mother and told her what had happened to him on his journey.
sentences.i: Then he saw to Ṣabbāḥ, lodged him in a spacious dwelling and gave him a portion of the booty; after which he went in to his mother and told her all that had befallen him on his journey.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā, “to turn toward, attend to”. anzalahu, “he lodged him”, literally “made him alight”. al-fisāḥ, plural of fasīḥ, “roomy”; it rhymes with Ṣabbāḥ. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ, the hamza on an alif-seat with no further alif for the tanwīn.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ وَصَلَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ خَبَرُهُ فَقَامَ مِنْ مَجْلِسِهِ وَاخْتَلَى بِخَوَاصِّهِ وَقَالَ لَهُمُ اعْلَمُوا أَنِّي أُرِيدُأَنْ أَبُوحَ لَكُمْ بِسِرِّي وَأُبْدِيَ لَكُمْ مَكْنُونَ أَمْرِي
sentences.tr: wa-qad waṣala ilā al-maliki khabaruhu fa-qāma min majlisihi wa-ikhtalā bi-khawāṣṣihi wa-qāla lahumu iʿlamū annī urīdu an abūḥa lakum bi-sirrī wa-ubdiya lakum maknūna amrī
sentences.l: And his news had reached the king; so he rose from his sitting-place and went-apart with his intimates, and said to them: “Know that I want to disclose to you my secret, and reveal to you the hidden-part of my affair.
sentences.i: Word of him had meanwhile reached the king, who rose from his council, withdrew with his closest men, and said to them, “Know that I mean to open my secret to you, and lay bare what I have kept hidden.
sentences.n: The king is Sāsān, who rules in Baghdad since the death of Ḍawʾ al-Makān, Kān Mā Kān's father. khawāṣṣ, “the special ones”, a ruler's inner circle. The print runs urīdu an together as one word, اريدان. bāḥa bi-, “to divulge”; maknūn, “hidden, stored away”. sirrī / amrī close on the same sound.

sentences.t: اِعْلَمُوا أَنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ هُوَ الَّذِي يَكُونُ سَبَبًا لِانْقِلَاعِنَا مِنْ هَذِهِ الْأَوْطَانِ لِأَنَّهُ قَتَلَ كَهْرْدَاشَ مَعَ أَنَّهُ لَهُ قَبَائِلُ مِنَ الْأَكْرَادِ وَالْأَتْرَاكِ وَأَمْرُنَا مَعَهُ آيِلٌ إِلَى الْهَلَاكِ
sentences.tr: iʿlamū anna Kāna Mā Kāna huwa alladhī yakūnu sababan li-inqilāʿinā min hādhihi al-awṭāni li-annahu qatala Kahrdāsha maʿa annahu lahu qabāʾilu mina al-akrādi wa-al-atrāki wa-amrunā maʿahu āʾilun ilā al-halāki
sentences.l: Know that Kān Mā Kān, he is the-one who will-be a cause for our uprooting from these homelands; for he killed Kahrdāsh, although he has tribes of the Kurds and the Turks; and our affair with him is tending toward destruction.
sentences.i: Know that Kān Mā Kān is the man who will be the cause of our being torn up out of these lands. He has killed Kahrdāsh, though Kahrdāsh had tribes of Kurds and Turks behind him; and with him about, our cause is heading for ruin.
sentences.n: maʿa annahu lahu qabāʾil, “although he has tribes”: annahu lahu doubles the pronoun, a Middle Arabic habit. The “he” is most likely Kahrdāsh, whose Kurdish and Turkish kin will want revenge; the king fears the trouble Kān Mā Kān draws down on them. āʾil ilā, “coming round to, ending in”. Rhymed prose: al-atrāk / al-halāk.

sentences.t: وَأَكْثَرُ جَيْشِنَا مِنْ أَقَارِبِهِ وَقَدْ عَلِمْتُمْ بِمَا فَعَلَ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ فَإِنَّهُ جَحَدَ مَعْرُوفِي بَعْدَ الْإِحْسَانِ وَخَانَنِي فِى الْأَيْمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-aktharu jayshinā min aqāribihi wa-qad ʿalimtum bi-mā faʿala al-wazīru Dandānu fa-innahu jaḥada maʿrūfī baʿda al-iḥsāni wa-khānanī fī al-aymāni
sentences.l: And most of our army are of his kinsmen; and you have known what the vizier Dandān did: for he denied my kindness after the benefaction, and betrayed me in the oaths.
sentences.i: Most of our army are his kin; and you know what the vizier Dandān has done — how he has met my kindness with ingratitude after all my favours, and broken faith with me in his sworn oaths.
sentences.n: “His kinsmen”: Kān Mā Kān's, grandson of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, whose house the army had served. jaḥada maʿrūfī, “he denied my kindness”, he was ungrateful. al-aymān, “the oaths” (plural of yamīn), is read so for the rhyme with al-iḥsān; the letters would also allow al-īmān, “faith”.

sentences.t: وَبَلَغَنِي أَنَّهُ جَمَعَ عَسَاكِرَ الْبُلْدَانِ وَقَصَدَ أَنْ يُسَلْطِنَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ لِأَنَّ السَّلْطَنَةَ كَانَتْ لِأَبِيهِ وَجَدِّهِ وَلَا شَكَّ أَنَّهُ قَاتِلِي بِلَا مُحَالَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-balaghanī annahu jamaʿa ʿasākira al-buldāni wa-qaṣada an yusalṭina Kāna Mā Kāna li-anna al-salṭanata kānat li-abīhi wa-jaddihi wa-lā shakka annahu qātilī bi-lā muḥālatin
sentences.l: And it-has-reached me that he has gathered the armies of the lands, and intends to make-sultan Kān Mā Kān, because the sultanate was his father's and grandfather's; and there is no doubt that he is my-killer without fail.”
sentences.i: And I hear that he has gathered the armies of the provinces and means to make Kān Mā Kān sultan, since the sultanate was his father's and his grandfather's; and beyond all doubt he will be the death of me.”
sentences.n: yusalṭina, “to make sultan”, a verb coined from sulṭān. “His father and grandfather” are Ḍawʾ al-Makān and King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. qātilī, “my killer”, the participle for what is sure to happen. bi-lā muḥāla, “without fail, inevitably”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ خَوَاصُّ مَمْلَكَتِهِ مِنْهُ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ قَالُوا لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ إِنَّهُ أَقَلُّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَلَوْلَا أَنَّنَا عَلِمْنَا بِأَنَّهُ تَرْبِيَتُكَ لَمْ يُقْبِلْ عَلَيْهِ مِنَّا أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa khawāṣṣu mamlakatihi minhu hādhā al-kalāma qālū lahu ayyuhā al-maliku innahu aqallu min dhālika wa-lawlā annanā ʿalimnā bi-annahu tarbiyatuka lam yuqbil ʿalayhi minnā aḥadun
sentences.l: And when the intimates of his kingdom heard from him this speech, they said to him: “O king, he is less than that; and were-it-not that we knew that he is your rearing, not one of us would-have turned toward him.
sentences.i: When the chief men of his kingdom heard this from him, they said, “O king, he is too slight a man for that; and had we not known that he was reared in your house, not one of us would have given him any countenance.
sentences.n: The print has واولا, a misprint for ولولا, corrected here. aqallu min dhālika, “less than that”, too small a matter to fear. tarbiyatuka, “your rearing”, the verbal noun standing for the person reared: “your foster-son”. lam yuqbil ʿalayhi, “would not have turned to him”, received or favoured him; after lawlā Classical would mark the answer with la-, which is missing here.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّنَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ إِنْ شِئْتَ قَتْلَهُ قَتَلْنَاهُ وَإِنْ شِئْتَ بُعْدَهُ أَبْعَدْنَاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam annanā bayna yadayka in shiʾta qatlahu qatalnāhu wa-in shiʾta buʿdahu abʿadnāhu
sentences.l: And know that we are between your hands: if you wish his killing, we kill-him; and if you wish his distance, we put-him-far-away.”
sentences.i: Know that we are at your command: if you want him killed, we will kill him, and if you want him gone, we will send him far away.”
sentences.n: bayna yadayka, “between your hands”, at your disposal. buʿdahu, “his being far off”, the plain verbal noun of baʿuda set beside the causative abʿadnāhu, “we put him far away”; Classical would say ibʿādahu, “his removal”. Read so, the two clauses match: qatlahu qatalnāhu / buʿdahu abʿadnāhu.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَهُمْ قَالَ إِنَّ قَتْلَهُ هُوَ الصَّوَابُ وَلَكِنْ لَابُدَّ مِنْ أَخْذِ الْمِيثَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kalāmahum qāla inna qatlahu huwa al-ṣawābu wa-lākin lā budda min akhdhi al-mīthāqi
sentences.l: And when he heard their speech, he said: “His killing, it is the right-course; but there-is-no-escape from taking the covenant.”
sentences.i: When he heard what they said, he answered, “To kill him is the right course; but first I must have your sworn covenant.”
sentences.n: akhdh al-mīthāq, “the taking of the covenant”, binding them by oath. lā budda is again run together in the print.

sentences.t: فَتَحَالَفُوا عَلَى أَنَّهُمْ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ يَقْتُلُوا كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَإِذَا أَتَى الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ سَمِعَ بِقَتْلِهِ تَضْعُفُ قُوَّتُهُ عَمَّا هُوَ عَازِمٌ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-taḥālafū ʿalā annahum lā budda an yaqtulū Kāna Mā Kāna fa-idhā atā al-wazīru Dandānu samiʿa bi-qatlihi taḍʿufu quwwatuhu ʿammā huwa ʿāzimun ʿalayhi
sentences.l: So they swore-together on that they must-needs kill Kān Mā Kān: so when the vizier Dandān comes, he hears of his killing, his strength weakens from what he is resolved upon.
sentences.i: So they swore together that they would kill Kān Mā Kān without fail, so that when the vizier Dandān came and heard he was dead, his strength would fail him for the thing he had resolved on.
sentences.n: taḥālafū, “they swore to one another”. The last clause is loosely strung: fa-idhā atā ... samiʿa ... taḍʿufu, “when he comes, he hears ..., his strength weakens”, three verbs with no wa- or fa- between them, where Classical would write fa-idhā atā ... wa-samiʿa ... ḍaʿufat. It gives the plotters' reckoning: with Kān Mā Kān dead, Dandān's plan to make him sultan has nothing to stand on.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَعْطَوْهُ الْعَهْدَ وَالْمِيثَاقَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ أَكْرَمَهُمْ غَايَةَ الْإِكْرَامِ ثُمَّ دَخَلَ بَيْتَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aʿṭawhu al-ʿahda wa-al-mīthāqa ʿalā dhālika akramahum ghāyata al-ikrāmi thumma dakhala baytahu
sentences.l: And when they gave him the pledge and the covenant on that, he honoured them the utmost of honouring; then he went-into his house.
sentences.i: When they had given him their pledge and covenant to that, he honoured them to the utmost, and then withdrew into his own house.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ تَفَرَّقَ عَنْهُ الرُّأَسَاءُ وَامْتَنَعَتِ الْعَسَاكِرُ مِنَ الرُّكُوبِ وَالنُّزُولِ حَتَّى يُبْصِرُوا مَا يَكُونُ لِأَنَّهُمْ رَأَوْا غَالِبَ الْعَسْكَرِ مَعَ الْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-qad tafarraqa ʿanhu al-ruʾasāʾu wa-imtanaʿati al-ʿasākiru mina al-rukūbi wa-al-nuzūli ḥattā yubṣirū mā yakūnu li-annahum raʾaw ghāliba al-ʿaskari maʿa al-wazīri Dandāna
sentences.l: And the chiefs had scattered from him, and the armies held-back from mounting and dismounting until they should see what would-be, because they saw the greater-part of the army with the vizier Dandān.
sentences.i: By now the chief men had fallen away from him, and the troops would neither ride out nor stand down until they saw how matters would go, for they saw that the greater part of the army was with the vizier Dandān.
sentences.n: al-ruʾasāʾ, “the chiefs”: the print spells it الرأساء, the hamza on an alif-seat, where the usual spelling is رؤساء. al-rukūb wa-al-nuzūl, “mounting and dismounting”, any move at all: the troops would commit themselves to nothing. ghālib, “the greater part”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ ذَلِكَ الْخَبَرَ وَصَلَ إِلَى قَضَى فَكَانَ فَحَصَلَ عِنْدَهَا غَمٌّ زَائِدٌ وَأَرْسَلَتْ إِلَى الْعَجُوزِ الَّتِي عَادَتُهَا أَنْ تَأْتِيَهَا مِنْ عِنْدِ ابْنِ عَمِّهَا بِالْأَخْبَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna dhālika al-khabara waṣala ilā Qaḍā Fakāna fa-ḥaṣala ʿindahā ghammun zāʾidun wa-arsalat ilā al-ʿajūzi allatī ʿādatuhā an taʾtiyahā min ʿindi ibni ʿammihā bi-al-akhbāri
sentences.l: Then that news reached Qaḍā Fakān, and there-came-about with her an exceeding grief; and she sent to the old-woman whose custom was that she come to her from her paternal-uncle's son with the tidings.
sentences.i: Then the news reached Qaḍā Fakān, and she was stricken with grief beyond measure; and she sent for the old woman whose habit it was to bring her tidings from her cousin.
sentences.n: The print has رائد, a misprint for زائد, corrected here. Qaḍā Fakān, Sharrkān's daughter, is Kān Mā Kān's cousin (ibn ʿammihā, “her father's brother's son”) and the girl he loves. ḥaṣala ʿindahā ghamm, “grief came to be with her”, a common Middle Arabic way of saying she felt it. ʿādatuhā an taʾtiyahā, “whose custom was to come to her”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا حَضَرَتْ عِنْدَهَا أَمَرَتْهَا أَنْ تَذْهَبَ إِلَيْهِ وَتُخْبِرَهُ بِالْخَبَرِ فَلَمَّا وَصَلَتْ إِلَيْهِ الْعَجُوزُ سَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ فَفَرِحَ بِهَا وَأَخْبَرَتْهُ بِالْخَبَرِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ḥaḍarat ʿindahā amarathā an tadhhaba ilayhi wa-tukhbirahu bi-al-khabari fa-lammā waṣalat ilayhi al-ʿajūzu sallamat ʿalayhi fa-fariḥa bihā wa-akhbarathu bi-al-khabari
sentences.l: And when she was-present with her, she commanded her that she go to him and inform him of the news. And when the old-woman reached him, she greeted him, and he rejoiced in her, and she informed him of the news.
sentences.i: When the old woman came, Qaḍā Fakān bade her go to him and tell him what was afoot. So the old woman went to him and greeted him, and he was glad to see her; and she told him the news.
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to be glad of, rejoice at”: glad of her coming.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ ذَلِكَ قَالَ بَلِّغِي بِنْتَ عَمِّي سَلَامِي وَقُولِي لَهَا إِنَّ الْأَرْضَ لِلَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ يُورِثُهَا مَنْ يَشَاءُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ وَمَا أَحْسَنَ قَوْلَ الْقَائِلِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa dhālika qāla ballighī binta ʿammī salāmī wa-qūlī lahā inna al-arḍa li-llāhi ʿazza wa-jalla yūrithuhā man yashāʾu min ʿibādihi wa-mā aḥsana qawla al-qāʾili
sentences.l: And when he heard that, he said: “Convey to the daughter of my paternal-uncle my greeting, and say to her: ‘The earth is God's, mighty and majestic is He; He gives-it-as-inheritance to whom He wills of His servants.’ And how fine is the saying of the sayer:
sentences.i: When he heard it he said, “Take my greeting to my cousin, and say to her: ‘The earth is God's, mighty and glorious is He; He gives it for an inheritance to whichever of His servants He will.’ And how well the poet put it:
sentences.n: ballighī, “make it reach”, the feminine imperative, with two objects: the person and the thing conveyed; the print marks the doubled lām. inna al-arḍa li-llāhi yūrithuhā man yashāʾu min ʿibādihi echoes the Qurʾān (7:128). mā aḥsana ..., the verb of wonder: “how fine is ...!”

sentences.t:
اَلْمُلْكُ لِلّٰهِ مَنْ يَظْفَرْ بِنَيْلِ مُنًى * يَرْدُدْهُ نَهْرًا وَتَضْمَنْ نَفْسُهُ الدَّرَكَا
لَوْ كَانَ لِي اَوْ لِغَيْرِي قَدْرُ اَنْمُلَةٍ * مِنَ الْبَسِيطَةِ كَانَ الْاَمْرُ مُشْتَرَكَا
sentences.tr:
al-mulku li-llāhi man yaẓfar bi-nayli munan * yardudhu nahran wa-taḍman nafsuhu al-darakā
law kāna lī aw li-ghayrī qadru anmulatin * mina al-basīṭati kāna al-amru mushtarakā
sentences.l:
The sovereignty is God's: whoever triumphs in the attaining of a wish * returns-it [by] a river (perforce?), and his soul stands-surety-for the liability.
If there were to me or to other-than-me the measure of a fingertip * of the wide-earth, the matter would-be shared.
sentences.i:
Dominion belongs to God: whoever wins the wish he sought * must give it back perforce, his soul held to account;
Were I or any other lord of a fingertip's breadth * of the wide earth, then the sovereignty would be shared.
sentences.n: Metre basīṭ, rhyming in -akā (al-darakā / mushtarakā). The print points both lines, and its marks are kept as printed. نَهْرًا, “a river”, makes no sense here; the likeliest reading is قَهْرًا, “by force, perforce”, one dot away, and we translate so, but the print's word stands. al-darak, “liability, consequence”: the soul is answerable for what it took. al-basīṭa, “the flat expanse”, is the earth. The thought: the world is God's alone, and any power a man holds is lent and will be taken back — which is why Kān Mā Kān will not grieve over the throne.

sentences.t: فَرَجَعَتِ الْعَجُوزُ إِلَى بِنْتِ عَمِّهِ وَأَخْبَرَتْهَا بِمَا قَالَهُ وَأَعْلَمَتْهَا بِأَنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ أَقَامَ فِى الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-rajaʿati al-ʿajūzu ilā binti ʿammihi wa-akhbarathā bi-mā qālahu wa-aʿlamathā bi-anna Kāna Mā Kāna aqāma fī al-madīnati
sentences.l: So the old-woman returned to the daughter of his paternal-uncle, and informed her of what he had said, and let her know that Kān Mā Kān had settled in the city.
sentences.i: So the old woman went back to his cousin, told her what he had said, and let her know that Kān Mā Kān had taken up residence in the city.
sentences.n: bint ʿammihi, “the daughter of his paternal uncle”, is his cousin Qaḍā Fakān. The print spells fī with final ى here (فى), as it often does; the pointing follows the print's letters. aʿlama bi-, “to inform someone of”, takes the bi- of the thing made known.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ سَان سَانَ صَارَ يَنْتَظِرُ خُرُوجَهُ مِنْ بَغْدَادَ لِيُرْسِلَ وَرَاءَهُ مَنْ يَقْتُلُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika Sān Sāna ṣāra yantaẓiru khurūjahu min Baghdāda li-yursila warāʾahu man yaqtuluhu
sentences.l: Then the king Sāsān began waiting for his going-out from Baghdad, so-that he might send after him one-who would kill him.
sentences.i: Meanwhile King Sāsān kept watching for him to leave Baghdad, meaning to send someone after him to kill him.
sentences.n: The print splits the name as سان سان, two words; it is Sāsān, the usurper on the throne of Baghdad, and the spacing is kept. ṣāra yantaẓiru, “he became waiting”: ṣāra with an imperfect marks an action that begins and goes on.

sentences.t: فَاتَّفَقَ أَنَّهُ خَرَجَ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنَصِ وَخَرَجَ صَبَّاحٌ مَعَهُ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ لَا يُفَارِقُهُ لَيْلًا وَلَا نَهَارًا
sentences.tr: fa-ittafaqa annahu kharaja ilā al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi wa-kharaja Ṣabbāḥun maʿahu li-annahu kāna lā yufāriquhu laylan wa-lā nahāran
sentences.l: And it happened that he went-out to the hunting and the chase, and Ṣabbāḥ went-out with him, because he would not part from him by night nor by day.
sentences.i: Now it chanced that he rode out to hunt and course game, and Ṣabbāḥ went with him, for he never left his side by night or by day.
sentences.n: al-ṣayd wa-al-qanaṣ, “hunting and the chase”, a stock pair of near-synonyms. fa-ittafaqa anna, “and it happened that”, introduces a chance turn of events.

sentences.t: فَاصْطَادَ عَشْرَ غَزَالَاتٍ وَفِيهِنَّ غَزَالَةٌ كَحْلَاءُ الْعُيُونِ صَارَتْ تَتَلَفَّتُ يَمِينًا وَشِمَالًا فَأَطْلَقَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-iṣṭāda ʿashra ghazālātin wa-fīhinna ghazālatun kaḥlāʾu al-ʿuyūni ṣārat tatalaffatu yamīnan wa-shimālan fa-aṭlaqahā
sentences.l: And he caught ten gazelles, and among-them a gazelle dark-of-the-eyes who kept turning right and left; so he set her free.
sentences.i: He took ten gazelles, and among them was a doe with eyes dark as if lined with kohl, who kept looking about her to right and left; and he let her go.
sentences.n: kaḥlāʾ al-ʿuyūn, “kohl-dark of eyes”: kaḥlāʾ is the feminine of akḥal, whose eyelids look naturally darkened as with kohl, a beauty in women and gazelles alike. tatalaffatu, “turn this way and that, keep looking round”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ صَبَّاحٌ لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ أَطْلَقْتَ هٰذِهِ الْغَزَالَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Ṣabbāḥun li-ayyi shayʾin aṭlaqta hādhihi al-ghazālata
sentences.l: Then Ṣabbāḥ said to him: For what thing did you set-free this gazelle?
sentences.i: Ṣabbāḥ asked him, “Why did you let this gazelle go?”

sentences.t: فَضَحِكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَأَطْلَقَ الْبَاقِيَ وَقَالَ لَهُ إِنَّ مِنَ الْمُرُوَّةِ إِطْلَاقَ الْغَزَالَاتِ الَّتِي لَهَا أَوْلَادٌ وَمَا تَتَلَفَّتُ تِلْكَ الْغَزَالَةُ إِلَّا لِأَنَّ لَهَا أَوْلَادًا فَأَطْلَقْتُهَا وَأَطْلَقْتُ الْبَاقِيَ فِي كَرَامَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ḍaḥika Kāna Mā Kāna wa-aṭlaqa al-bāqiya wa-qāla lahu inna mina al-muruwwati iṭlāqa al-ghazālāti allatī lahā awlādun wa-mā tatalaffatu tilka al-ghazālatu illā li-anna lahā awlādan fa-aṭlaqtuhā wa-aṭlaqtu al-bāqiya fī karāmatihā
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān laughed and set-free the rest, and said to him: Truly, of manly-virtue is the setting-free of the gazelles that have young; and that gazelle does not turn-about except because she has young; so I set her free, and I set free the rest in honour-of-her.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān laughed and let the rest go too, and said to him, “It is a part of true manliness to spare gazelles that have young. That doe kept looking about her only because she has fawns, so I let her go, and let the others go for her sake.”
sentences.n: muruwwa, “manly virtue, chivalry”, the whole code of generous conduct; the print spells it المروة without the hamza of the fuller form muruwwa/murūʾa. lahā awlād, “she has offspring”, of a mother animal. fī karāmatihā, “in her honour”, i.e. as a courtesy to her. The print marks the doubled lām of illā (الّا).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ صَبَّاحٌ أَطْلِقْنِي حَتَّى أَرُوحَ إِلَى أَهْلِي فَضَحِكَ وَضَرَبَهُ بِعَقِبِ الرُّمْحِ عَلَى قَلْبِهِ فَوَقَعَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ يَلْتَوِي كَالثُّعْبَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Ṣabbāḥun aṭliqnī ḥattā arūḥa ilā ahlī fa-ḍaḥika wa-ḍarabahu bi-ʿaqibi al-rumḥi ʿalā qalbihi fa-waqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍi yaltawī ka-al-thuʿbāni
sentences.l: Then Ṣabbāḥ said to him: Set-me-free, so-that I may go to my family. And he laughed and struck him with the butt of the lance on his heart, and he fell to the ground writhing like the serpent.
sentences.i: Then Ṣabbāḥ said, “Let me go too, so that I can go home to my people.” Kān Mā Kān laughed and struck him over the heart with the butt of his lance, and he fell to the ground writhing like a snake.
sentences.n: Ṣabbāḥ turns the lesson into a joke: if mercy is owed to those with a family waiting, let him go home as well. ʿaqib al-rumḥ, “the heel of the lance”, its butt end, so the blow is rough play rather than a wound. yaltawī, “twisting about”, a circumstantial verb describing how he lay.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُمَا كَذٰلِكَ وَإِذَا بِغَبَرَةٍ ثَائِرَةٍ وَخَيْلٍ تَرْكُضُ وَبَانَ مِنْ تَحْتِهَا فُرْسَانٌ وَشُجْعَانٌ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā humā ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-ghabaratin thāʾiratin wa-khaylin tarkuḍu wa-bāna min taḥtihā fursānun wa-shujʿānun
sentences.l: And while the two of them were thus, and behold, a dust-cloud rising and horses galloping, and there appeared from beneath it horsemen and brave-ones.
sentences.i: While they were so engaged, a cloud of dust rose up and horses came galloping, and out from under it appeared horsemen, warriors bold.
sentences.n: fa-baynamā … wa-idhā bi-, “while … behold!”: the stock way the Nights brings in a sudden arrival; the bi- after idhā merely marks what appears. fursān wa-shujʿān, “horsemen and brave men”, rhymes in -ān, a touch of sajʿ.

sentences.t: وَسَبَبُ ذٰلِكَ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ سَاسَانَ أَخْبَرَهُ جَمَاعَةٌ أَنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ خَرَجَ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنَصِ فَأَرْسَلَ أَمِيرًا مِنَ الدَّيْلَمِ يُقَالُ لَهُ جَامِعٌ
sentences.tr: wa-sababu dhālika anna al-malika Sāsāna akhbarahu jamāʿatun anna Kāna Mā Kāna kharaja ilā al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi fa-arsala amīran mina al-Daylami yuqālu lahu Jāmiʿun
sentences.l: And the cause of that was that the king Sāsān — a company informed him that Kān Mā Kān had gone-out to the hunting and the chase; so he sent an emir of the Daylam who was called Jāmiʿ,
sentences.i: The reason was this: some people had told King Sāsān that Kān Mā Kān had ridden out to hunt, and he sent an emir of the Daylam named Jāmiʿ,
sentences.n: anna al-malika Sāsāna akhbarahu jamāʿatun, “that King Sāsān, a group told him”: the king is set at the head and picked up again by the pronoun -hu, a topic-first construction common in this prose. The Daylam are the people of the highlands south of the Caspian, famed as soldiers; Jāmiʿ is one of their emirs.

sentences.t: وَمَعَهُ عِشْرُونَ فَارِسًا وَدَفَعَ لَهُمُ الْمَالَ ثُمَّ أَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يَقْتُلُوا كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-maʿahu ʿishrūna fārisan wa-dafaʿa lahumu al-māla thumma amarahum an yaqtulū Kāna Mā Kāna
sentences.l: and with him twenty horsemen, and he paid to them the money, then commanded them that they kill Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: with twenty horsemen, paid them their money, and ordered them to kill Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: dafaʿa lahum al-māl, “he handed them the money”: dafaʿa li- for “pay to” is the ordinary usage of the Nights.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرُبُوا مِنْهُ حَمَلُوا عَلَيْهِ وَحَمَلَ عَلَيْهِمْ فَقَتَلَهُمْ عَنْ آخِرِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qarubū minhu ḥamalū ʿalayhi wa-ḥamala ʿalayhim fa-qatalahum ʿan ākhirihim
sentences.l: And when they drew-near to him they charged upon him, and he charged upon them, and he killed them to the last of them.
sentences.i: When they came near him they charged him, and he charged them in turn and killed them to the last man.
sentences.n: ḥamala ʿalā, “to charge (at)”, literally “to bear down upon”. ʿan ākhirihim, “to the last of them”, i.e. every one.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِالْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ رَكِبَ وَسَارَ وَلَحِقَ بِالْعَسْكَرِ فَوَجَدَهُمْ مَقْتُولِينَ فَتَعَجَّبَ وَرَجَعَ وَإِذْ بِأَهَالِيهَا قَبَضُوا عَلَيْهِ وَشَدُّوا وِثَاقَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-al-maliki Sāsāna rakiba wa-sāra wa-laḥiqa bi-al-ʿaskari fa-wajadahum maqtūlīna fa-taʿajjaba wa-rajaʿa wa-idh bi-ahālīhā qabaḍū ʿalayhi wa-shaddū withāqahu
sentences.l: And behold, the king Sāsān mounted and went and caught-up with the troop, and found them slain; and he wondered and returned, and behold, its people seized him and bound his bonds tight.
sentences.i: And then King Sāsān himself rode out, overtook the troop, and found them dead; amazed, he turned back, and lo, the people of the city laid hands on him and bound him fast.
sentences.n: The story moves very fast here. wa-idh bi- is used just as wa-idhā bi- is, “and behold”. ahālīhā, “its people”: the feminine -hā has no stated antecedent in this sentence; the likeliest sense is the people of the city (al-madīna), who turn on the usurper, but the reference is unclear and the text may be abridged. shaddū withāqahu, “they made his bonds fast”, a set phrase for tying a captive.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ تَوَجَّهَ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَتَوَجَّهَ مَعَهُ صَبَّاحٌ الْبَدَوِيُّ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Kāna Mā Kāna tawajjaha baʿda dhālika min dhālika al-makāni wa-tawajjaha maʿahu Ṣabbāḥun al-badawiyyu
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān set-out after that from that place, and set-out with him Ṣabbāḥ the Bedouin.
sentences.i: After that Kān Mā Kān went on from that place, and Ṣabbāḥ the Bedouin went with him.
sentences.n: tawajjaha, “to turn one's face, head (somewhere)”, the common verb for setting off.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ سَائِرٌ إِذْ رَأَى فِي طَرِيقِهِ شَابًّا عَلَى بَابِ دَارٍ فَأَلْقَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ فَرَدَّ الشَّابُّ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa sāʾirun idh raʾā fī ṭarīqihi shābban ʿalā bābi dārin fa-alqā Kāna Mā Kāna ʿalayhi al-salāma fa-radda al-shābbu ʿalayhi al-salāma
sentences.l: And while he was journeying, then he saw on his way a young-man at the door of a house; so Kān Mā Kān cast upon him the greeting, and the young-man returned the greeting to him.
sentences.i: As he went on his way he saw a young man at the door of a house. Kān Mā Kān greeted him, and the young man returned his greeting.
sentences.n: alqā ʿalayhi al-salām, “he cast the greeting upon him”, and radda ʿalayhi al-salām, “he returned the greeting”, are the set phrases for giving and answering al-salāmu ʿalaykum.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَخَلَ الدَّارَ وَخَرَجَ وَمَعَهُ قَصْعَتَانِ إِحْدَيٰهُمَا فِيهَا لَبَنٌ وَالثَّانِيَةُ فِيهَا ثَرِيدٌ وَالسَّمْنُ فِي جَوَانِبِهَا يَمُوجُ
sentences.tr: thumma dakhala al-dāra wa-kharaja wa-maʿahu qaṣʿatāni iḥdāhumā fīhā labanun wa-al-thāniyatu fīhā tharīdun wa-al-samnu fī jawānibihā yamūju
sentences.l: Then he went-into the house and came-out, and with him two bowls, one-of-them in-it milk and the second in-it tharīd, and the clarified-butter in its sides surging.
sentences.i: Then he went into the house and came out carrying two great bowls, one of milk and the other of tharīd, with the butter swimming round its edges.
sentences.n: qaṣʿa, a large wooden bowl for serving. The print writes iḥdāhumā with yāʾ and a small upright alif (احديٰهما), the old spelling of a long ā written on yāʾ. tharīd is bread broken into broth, usually with meat, the Prophet's favourite dish; samn is clarified butter, ghee. yamūju, “surging, rippling”: the butter is so plentiful it seems to swell like waves.

sentences.t: وَوَضَعَ الْقَصْعَتَيْنِ قُدَّامَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ تَفَضَّلْ عَلَيْنَا بِالْأَكْلِ مِنْ زَادِنَا
sentences.tr: wa-waḍaʿa al-qaṣʿatayni quddāma Kāna Mā Kāna wa-qāla lahu tafaḍḍal ʿalaynā bi-al-akli min zādinā
sentences.l: And he set the two bowls before Kān Mā Kān and said to him: Do-us-the-favour of the eating from our provision.
sentences.i: He set the two bowls before Kān Mā Kān and said, “Do us the kindness of eating of our food.”
sentences.n: tafaḍḍal ʿalaynā bi-, “be gracious to us with”, the courteous host's way of pressing a guest; the print marks the doubled ḍād of tafaḍḍal. zād, properly “provisions for a journey”, here simply food.

sentences.t: فَامْتَنَعَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ مِنَ الْأَكْلِ فَقَالَ لَهُ الشَّابُّ مَالَكَ أَيُّهَا الْإِنْسَانُ لَا تَأْكُلُ فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِنَّهُ عَلَيَّ نَذْرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-imtanaʿa Kāna Mā Kāna mina al-akli fa-qāla lahu al-shābbu mā laka ayyuhā al-insānu lā taʾkulu fa-qāla lahu Kāna Mā Kāna innahu ʿalayya nadhrun
sentences.l: But Kān Mā Kān refrained from the eating, and the young-man said to him: What is with-you, O you person, you do not eat? And Kān Mā Kān said to him: Truly there is upon me a vow.
sentences.i: But Kān Mā Kān held back from the food, and the young man said, “What ails you, good sir, that you do not eat?” Kān Mā Kān answered, “I am under a vow.”
sentences.n: mā laka lā taʾkulu, “what is it with you, you do not eat?”, i.e. why do you not eat; the print runs mā laka together as مالك. ayyuhā al-insān, “O human being”, a neutral address to a stranger. ʿalayya nadhr, “a vow is upon me”, the usual way of saying one is bound by a vow; the print marks the doubled yāʾ of ʿalayya.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشَّابُّ وَمَا سَبَبُ نَذْرِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shābbu wa-mā sababu nadhrika
sentences.l: And the young-man said to him: And what is the cause of your vow?
sentences.i: “And what is the reason for your vow?” the young man asked.

sentences.t: فَقَٰلَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ سَاسَانَ غَصَبَ مُلْكِي ظُلْمًا وَعُدْوَانًا مَعَ أَنَّ ذٰلِكَ الْمُلْكَ كَانَ لِأَبِي وَجَدِّي مِنْ قَبْلِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Kāna Mā Kāna iʿlam anna al-malika Sāsāna ghaṣaba mulkī ẓulman wa-ʿudwānan maʿa anna dhālika al-mulka kāna li-abī wa-jaddī min qablī
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: Know that the king Sāsān usurped my kingdom in wrong and aggression, although that kingdom was my father's and my grandfather's before me.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān told him, “Know that King Sāsān seized my kingdom by injustice and violence, though it belonged to my father and my grandfather before me.
sentences.n: The print writes qāla defectively as قل, as it often does; it is pointed here with a small alif. ẓulman wa-ʿudwānan, “wrongfully and aggressively”, a set pair. The print marks the doubled dāl of jaddī.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَوْلَى عَلَيْهِ قَهْرًا بَعْدَ مَوْتِ أَبِي وَلَمْ يَعْتَبِرْنِي لِصِغَرِ سِنِّي فَنَذَرْتُ أَنَّنِي لَا آكُلُ لِأَحَدٍ زَادًا حَتَّى أَشْفِيَ فُؤَادِي مِنْ غَرِيمِي
sentences.tr: fa-istawlā ʿalayhi qahran baʿda mawti abī wa-lam yaʿtabirnī li-ṣighari sinnī fa-nadhartu annanī lā ākulu li-aḥadin zādan ḥattā ashfiya fuʾādī min gharīmī
sentences.l: And he took-possession of it by force after the death of my father, and took no account of me for the smallness of my age; so I vowed that I would not eat of anyone's provision until I heal my heart of my adversary.
sentences.i: He seized it by force when my father died and paid me no heed because I was so young. So I vowed to eat no man's food until I had taken my heart's satisfaction of my enemy.”
sentences.n: lam yaʿtabirnī, “he did not reckon with me”, did not count me as a rival. shafā fuʾādahu min, “to heal one's heart of”, to take revenge on someone. gharīm, properly “creditor, opponent at law”, here simply “enemy”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشَّابُّ أَبْشِرْ فَقَدْ وَفَّى اللّٰهُ نَذْرَكَ وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ مَسْجُونٌ فِي مَكَانٍ وَأَظُنُّهُ أَنْ يَمُوتَ قَرِيبًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shābbu abshir fa-qad waffā Allāhu nadhraka wa-iʿlam annahu masjūnun fī makānin wa-aẓunnuhu an yamūta qarīban
sentences.l: And the young-man said to him: Rejoice! For God has fulfilled your vow; and know that he is imprisoned in a place, and I think him that he will die soon.
sentences.i: The young man said, “Take heart, for God has fulfilled your vow. Know that he is held prisoner in a certain place, and I think he will soon be dead.”
sentences.n: abshir, “receive good news, rejoice”. waffā nadhraka, “has fulfilled your vow”, i.e. brought about what you vowed to wait for; the bare letters could also be read wafā, “has kept”, with much the same sense. aẓunnuhu an yamūta, “I think him that he will die”: Classical would say aẓunnu annahu yamūtu; this mixing of the object pronoun with an an-clause is Middle Arabic.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فِي أَيِّ بَيْتٍ هُوَ مُعْتَقَلٌ فَقَالَ لَهُ فِي تِلْكَ الْقُبَّةِ الْعَالِيَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Kāna Mā Kāna fī ayyi baytin huwa muʿtaqalun fa-qāla lahu fī tilka al-qubbati al-ʿāliyati
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to him: In which house is he held-captive? And he said to him: In that high dome.
sentences.i: “In what building is he held?” asked Kān Mā Kān. “In that lofty domed chamber,” he answered.
sentences.n: muʿtaqal, “held in confinement”. qubba, a domed building or pavilion, often a tent-like chamber of state. The print marks the doubled yāʾ of ayyi.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِلَى قُبَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍ وَرَأَى النَّاسَ فِي تِلْكَ الْقُبَّةِ يَدْخُلُونَ وَعَلَى سَاسَانَ يَلْطِمُونَ وَهُوَ يَتَجَرَّعُ غُصَصَ الْمَنُونِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara Kāna Mā Kāna ilā qubbatin ʿāliyatin wa-raʾā al-nāsa fī tilka al-qubbati yadkhulūna wa-ʿalā Sāsāna yalṭimūna wa-huwa yatajarraʿu ghuṣaṣa al-manūni
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān looked toward a high dome, and saw the people into that dome entering, and over Sāsān slapping-their-faces, and he gulping the chokings of death.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān looked at a tall dome and saw people going in and out of it, beating their faces in grief over Sāsān, while he swallowed the bitter draughts of death.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: yadkhulūn / yalṭimūn / al-manūn. laṭama, “to slap (one's own face)”, the gesture of mourning. yatajarraʿu ghuṣaṣa al-manūn, “he gulps down the chokings of death”: ghuṣaṣ are the lumps that stick in the throat, al-manūn is fate or death. The print marks the doubled rāʾ of yatajarraʿu.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَمَشَى حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَى تِلْكَ الْقُبَّةِ وَعَايَنَ مَا فِيهَا ثُمَّ عَادَ إِلَى مَوْضِعِهِ وَقَعَدَ عَلَى الْأَكْلِ وَأَكَلَ مَا تَيَسَّرَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma Kāna Mā Kāna wa-mashā ḥattā waṣala ilā tilka al-qubbati wa-ʿāyana mā fīhā thumma ʿāda ilā mawḍiʿihi wa-qaʿada ʿalā al-akli wa-akala mā tayassara
sentences.l: So Kān Mā Kān rose and walked until he arrived at that dome, and saw-with-his-own-eyes what was in it; then he returned to his place and sat-down to the eating, and ate what was easy.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān rose and walked until he reached the dome and saw for himself what was inside; then he went back to his place, sat down to the food, and ate what he could.
sentences.n: ʿāyana, “to see with one's own eyes”, to witness. akala mā tayassara, “he ate what came easily”, i.e. a moderate meal.

sentences.t: وَوَضَعَ مَا بَقِيَ مِنَ اللَّحْمِ فِي مِزْوَدِهِ ثُمَّ جَلَسَ فِي مَكَانِهِ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ جَالِسًا إِلَى أَنْ أَظْلَمَ اللَّيْلُ وَنَامَ الشَّابُّ الَّذِي ضَيَّفَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-waḍaʿa mā baqiya mina al-laḥmi fī mizwadihi thumma jalasa fī makānihi wa-lam yazal jālisan ilā an aẓlama al-laylu wa-nāma al-shābbu alladhī ḍayyafahu
sentences.l: And he put what remained of the meat in his provision-bag; then he sat in his place, and did not cease sitting until the night grew-dark, and the young-man who had hosted him slept.
sentences.i: He put what was left of the meat in his provision bag, then sat on where he was until night fell and the young man who had given him hospitality was asleep.
sentences.n: mizwad, a traveller's bag for provisions. The meat is that of the tharīd. ḍayyafa, “to receive as a guest”; the print marks its doubled yāʾ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ ذَهَبَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِلَى الْقُبَّةِ الَّتِي فِيهَا سَاسَانُ وَكَانَ حَوْلَهَا كِلَابٌ يَحْرُسُونَهَا
sentences.tr: thumma dhahaba Kāna Mā Kāna ilā al-qubbati allatī fīhā Sāsānu wa-kāna ḥawlahā kilābun yaḥrusūnahā
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān went to the dome in which was Sāsān; and there were around it dogs guarding it.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān went to the dome where Sāsān lay; it was ringed with dogs that guarded it.
sentences.n: yaḥrusūnahā, “they guard it”: the dogs take the plural ending used for people, -ūna, where Classical would use the feminine singular (taḥrusuhā) for animals; a common Middle Arabic feature. kāna before a plural subject stays singular, as it may.

sentences.t: فَوَثَبَ لَهُ كَلْبٌ مِنَ الْكِلَابِ فَرَمَى لَهُ قِطْعَةَ لَحْمٍ مِنَ الَّذِي فِي مِزْوَدِهِ وَمَا زَالَ يَرْمِي لِلْكِلَابِ لَحْمًا حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَى الْقُبَّةِ وَتَوَصَّلَ إِلَى أَنْ صَارَ عِنْدَ الْمَلِكِ سَاسَانَ
sentences.tr: fa-wathaba lahu kalbun mina al-kilābi fa-ramā lahu qiṭʿata laḥmin mina alladhī fī mizwadihi wa-mā zāla yarmī li-al-kilābi laḥman ḥattā waṣala ilā al-qubbati wa-tawaṣṣala ilā an ṣāra ʿinda al-maliki Sāsāna
sentences.l: And there leapt at him a dog of the dogs, so he threw to it a piece of meat from that-which was in his provision-bag; and he did not cease throwing meat to the dogs until he reached the dome, and made-his-way until he was beside the king Sāsān.
sentences.i: One of the dogs sprang at him, and he threw it a piece of meat from his bag; and he kept throwing meat to the dogs until he reached the dome and worked his way in until he stood by King Sāsān.
sentences.n: wathaba lahu, “leapt at him”. The li- of li-al-kilābi is “to”: he throws to the dogs. tawaṣṣala ilā, “to find a way through to, manage to reach”.

sentences.t: وَوَضَعَ يَدَهُ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ فَقَالَ لَهُ بِصَوْتٍ عَالٍ مَنْ أَنْتَ
sentences.tr: wa-waḍaʿa yadahu ʿalā raʾsihi fa-qāla lahu bi-ṣawtin ʿālin man anta
sentences.l: And he put his hand on his head, and he said to him in a loud voice: Who are you?
sentences.i: He laid his hand on Sāsān's head, and Sāsān cried out to him, “Who are you?”
sentences.n: The pronouns are left to context: Kān Mā Kān lays his hand on Sāsān's head, and it is Sāsān who cries out.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَنَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ الَّذِي سَعَيْتَ فِي قَتْلِهِ فَأَوْقَعَكَ اللّٰهُ فِي سُوءِ تَدْبِيرِكَ أَمَا يَكْفِيكَ أَخْذُ مُلْكِي وَمُلْكِ أَبِي وَجَدِّي حَتَّى تَسْعَى فِي قَتْلِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla anā Kāna Mā Kāna alladhī saʿayta fī qatlihi fa-awqaʿaka Allāhu fī sūʾi tadbīrika a-mā yakfīka akhdhu mulkī wa-mulki abī wa-jaddī ḥattā tasʿā fī qatlī
sentences.l: And he said: I am Kān Mā Kān, whom you strove for the killing of him; and God has made-you-fall into the evil of your scheming. Is it not enough for you, the taking of my kingdom and the kingdom of my father and my grandfather, that you strive for my killing?
sentences.i: He said, “I am Kān Mā Kān, whom you sought to have killed, and God has made you fall into your own evil plot. Was it not enough for you to take my kingdom, my father's and my grandfather's, without seeking my death as well?”
sentences.n: alladhī saʿayta fī qatlihi, “whom you strove in his killing”: the relative clause refers back with “his”, though the speaker means himself; Arabic allows this after a predicate noun. awqaʿahu fī sūʾ tadbīrihi, “made him fall into the evil of his own contriving”, i.e. his plot recoiled on him. The print points the first letter of a-mā, “is it not?”, with a fatḥa (اَما).

sentences.t: فَحَلَفَ سَاسَانُ الْأَيْمَانَ الْبَاطِلَةَ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَسْعَ فِي قَتْلِهِ وَأَنَّ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ غَيْرُ صَحِيحٍ فَصَفَحَ عَنْهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ اتَّبِعْنِي
sentences.tr: fa-ḥalafa Sāsānu al-aymāna al-bāṭilata annahu lam yasʿa fī qatlihi wa-anna hādhā al-kalāma ghayru ṣaḥīḥin fa-ṣafaḥa ʿanhu Kāna Mā Kāna wa-qāla lahu ittabiʿnī
sentences.l: Then Sāsān swore the false oaths that he had not striven for his killing, and that this talk was not true. So Kān Mā Kān pardoned him and said to him: Follow me.
sentences.i: Sāsān swore false oaths that he had never sought his death and that the report was untrue; and Kān Mā Kān forgave him and said, “Follow me.”
sentences.n: al-aymān, “oaths”, plural of yamīn (oath, also right hand). ṣafaḥa ʿan, “to pardon, overlook”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَا أَقْدِرُ أَنْ أَخْطُوَ خَطْوَةً وَاحِدَةً لِضَعْفِ قُوَّتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lā aqdiru an akhṭuwa khaṭwatan wāḥidatan li-ḍaʿfi quwwatī
sentences.l: And he said: I am not able to step a single step, for the weakness of my strength.
sentences.i: He said, “I cannot take a single step, my strength is so far gone.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِذَا كَانَ الْأَمْرُ كَذٰلِكَ نَأْخُذُ لَنَا فَرَسَيْنِ وَنَرْكَبُ أَنَا وَأَنْتَ وَنَطْلُبُ الْبَرَّ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Kāna Mā Kāna idhā kāna al-amru ka-dhālika naʾkhudhu lanā farasayni wa-narkabu anā wa-anta wa-naṭlubu al-barra
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said: If the matter is thus, we take for ourselves two horses, and we ride, I and you, and we seek the open-country.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān said, “If that is how things stand, we shall take two horses, you and I will ride, and we shall make for the open country.”
sentences.n: naʾkhudhu, “we (shall) take”: the answer to idhā comes without the fa- Classical would expect before it, as often in this prose. al-barr, “the open land”, the desert or countryside away from the town.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ فَعَلَ كَمَا قَالَ وَرَكِبَ هُوَ وَسَاسَانُ وَسَارَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ ثُمَّ صَلَّوُا الصُّبْحَ وَسَارُوا وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا كَذَلِكَ حَتَّى وَصَلُوا إِلَى بُسْتَانٍ فَجَلَسُوا فِيهِ يَتَحَدَّثُونَ
sentences.tr: thumma faʿala kamā qāla wa-rakiba huwa wa-Sāsānu wa-sārā ilā al-ṣabāḥi thumma ṣallawu al-ṣubḥa wa-sārū wa-lam yazālū ka-dhālika ḥattā waṣalū ilā bustānin fa-jalasū fīhi yataḥaddathūna
sentences.l: Then he did as he said, and he rode, he and Sāsān, and the-two went-on until the morning; then they prayed the dawn-prayer and went-on, and they did not cease thus until they arrived at a garden, and they sat in it talking-together.
sentences.i: Then he did as he had said. He and Sāsān mounted and rode through the night until morning; then they prayed the dawn prayer and rode on, and so they continued until they came to a garden, where they sat down and talked together.
sentences.n: The print has الصاح, a misprint for الصباح, corrected here. sārā, “the two of them went”, is dual, but ṣallaw and sārū, “they prayed, they went on”, are plural: the narrator slips from the pair to the whole company riding with them. al-ṣubḥ is both “dawn” and the dawn prayer; ṣallā al-ṣubḥ means to perform it. lam yazālū ka-dhālika ḥattā, “they did not cease so until”, is the stock formula for a journey that goes on without incident.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِلَى سَاسَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ هَلْ بَقِيَ فِي قَلْبِكَ مِنِّي أَمْرٌ تَكْرَهُهُ قَٰلَ سَاسَانُ لَا وَاللَّهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma Kāna Mā Kāna ilā Sāsāna wa-qāla lahu hal baqiya fī qalbika minnī amrun takrahuhu qāla Sāsānu lā wa-Allāhi
sentences.l: Then Kān Mā Kān rose to Sāsān and said to him: Has there remained in your heart from me a matter which you dislike? Sāsān said: No, by God.
sentences.i: Then Kān Mā Kān went over to Sāsān and said to him, “Is there anything of mine still lodged in your heart that you resent?” “No, by God,” said Sāsān.
sentences.n: The print has نكرهه, a misprint for تكرهه, corrected here. qāma ilā, “rose (and went) to”, is the usual way of saying someone got up and approached another. qāl Sāsān: the print spells qāla defectively, قل, as it often does; the small upright alif restores the long vowel without altering the letters.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اتَّفَقُوا عَلَى أَنَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ إِلَى بَغْدَادَ فَقَالَ صَبَّاحٌ الْبَدَوِيُّ أَنَا أَسْبِقُكُمَا لِأُ بَشِّرَ النَّاسَ فَسَبَقَ يُبَشِّرُ النِّسَاءَ وَالرِّجَالَ
sentences.tr: thumma ittafaqū ʿalā annahum yarjiʿūna ilā Baghdāda fa-qāla Ṣabbāḥun al-badawiyyu anā asbiqukumā li-u bashshira al-nāsa fa-sabaqa yubashshiru al-nisāʾa wa-al-rijāla
sentences.l: Then they agreed on that they would return to Baghdad. And Ṣabbāḥ the Bedouin said: I will go-ahead-of you-two to give-glad-tidings to the people. And he went-ahead, bringing-glad-tidings to the women and the men.
sentences.i: Then they agreed to return to Baghdad, and Ṣabbāḥ the Bedouin said, “I will ride on ahead of you both and give the people the good news.” So he went on ahead, bearing the glad tidings to women and men alike.
sentences.n: la bshr, li-ubashshira, “so that I may give glad tidings”: the print splits the word after the first alif, writing لا بشر as two words; the spacing is kept and the two halves are pointed as one verb. bashshara is to bring someone good news; Ṣabbāḥ rides ahead to announce the victors' return. asbiqukumā, “I will outstrip you two”, addresses Kān Mā Kān and Sāsān.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَتْ إِلَيْهِ النَّاسُ بِالدُّفُوفِ وَالْمَزَامِيرِ وَبَرَزَتْ قَضَى فَكَانَ وَهِيَ مِثْلُ الْبَدْرِ بَهِيِّ الْأَنْوَارِ فِي دَيَاجِى الِاعْتِكَارِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajat ilayhi al-nāsu bi-al-dufūfi wa-al-mazāmīri wa-barazat Qaḍā Fakāna wa-hiya mithlu al-badri bahiyyi al-anwāri fī dayājī al-iʿtikāri
sentences.l: And the people came-out to him with the tambourines and the pipes, and Qaḍā Fakān came-forth, and she was like the full-moon, splendid of the lights, in the darknesses of the thick-gloom.
sentences.i: The people came out to meet him with tambourines and pipes, and Qaḍā Fakān came forth, like the full moon in its radiant splendour amid the deepest darkness of the night.
sentences.n: kharajat al-nās, “the people (she) came out”: al-nās is treated as a feminine collective, which is common. bahiyy al-anwār, “splendid of lights”, describes the moon, and anwār rhymes with iʿtikār in a closing pair of sajʿ. dayājī (sing. daijūr/dayjūr) are thick darknesses; iʿtikār is the night's growing black and dense, so the phrase means “the depths of pitch-dark night”. The print writes dayājī with final ى.

sentences.t: فَقَابَلَهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَحَمَتِ الْأَرْوَاحُ لِلْأَرْوَاحِ وَاشْتَاقَتِ الْأَشْبَاحُ لِلْأَشْبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-qābalahā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-ḥamati al-arwāḥu li-al-arwāḥi wa-ishtāqati al-ashbāḥu li-al-ashbāḥi
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān met her, and the spirits grew-warm to the spirits, and the bodies longed for the bodies.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān met her face to face, and spirit kindled toward spirit, and body longed for body.
sentences.n: The word printed حمت is doubtful. As it stands it can only be read as ḥamat, a Middle Arabic shortening of ḥamiyat, “grew hot”, and it is translated so. But the parallel with ishtāqat, “longed”, strongly suggests ḥannat, “yearned” (وحنت), which differs from the print by one letter shape; since the change is not a matter of a dot, the print is kept here. ashbāḥ (sing. shabaḥ) are “figures, bodily forms”, set against arwāḥ, “spirits”: soul yearned for soul and body for body, in a rhymed pair.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَبْقَ لِأَهْلِ الْعَصْرِ حَدِيثٌ إِلَّا فِي كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَشَهِدَ لَهُ الْفُرْسَانُ أَنَّهُ أَشْجَعُ أَهْلِ الزَّمَانِ وَقَالُوا لَا يَصِحُّ أَنْ يَكُونَ سُلْطَانًا عَلَيْنَا إِلَّا كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَيَعُودُ إِلَيْهِ مُلْكُ جَدِّهِ كَمَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yabqa li-ahli al-ʿaṣri ḥadīthun illā fī Kāna Mā Kāna wa-shahida lahu al-fursānu annahu ashjaʿu ahli al-zamāni wa-qālū lā yaṣiḥḥu an yakūna sulṭānan ʿalaynā illā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-yaʿūdu ilayhi mulku jaddihi kamā kāna
sentences.l: And there did not remain for the people of the age talk except about Kān Mā Kān, and the horsemen bore-witness for him that he was the bravest of the people of the time, and they said: It is not fitting that a sultan over us be anyone but Kān Mā Kān, and the kingship of his grandfather returns to him as it was.
sentences.i: The people of that age talked of nothing but Kān Mā Kān. The horsemen bore witness that he was the bravest man of his time, and they said, “No one but Kān Mā Kān is fit to be sultan over us; let the kingdom of his grandfather return to him as it was.”
sentences.n: lam yabqa ... ḥadīth illā fī, “there remained no talk except of”, is the usual way of saying someone became the talk of the town. wa-yaʿūdu, “and (that) it returns”, is indicative where Classical, continuing the an-clause, would want the subjunctive yaʿūda; it is pointed as the text has it, a loose Middle Arabic continuation. Note the sajʿ on zamān and Kān, kān.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا سَاسَانُ فَإِنَّهُ دَخَلَ عَلَى نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ إِنِّي أَرَى النَّاسَ لَيْسَ لَهُمْ حَدِيثٌ إِلّاَ فِي كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَيَصِفُونَهُ بِأَوْصَافٍ يَعْجِزُ عَنْهَا اللِّسَانُ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā Sāsānu fa-innahu dakhala ʿalā Nuzhati al-Zamāni fa-qālat lahu innī arā al-nāsa laysa lahum ḥadīthun illā fī Kāna Mā Kāna wa-yaṣifūnahu bi-awṣāfin yaʿjizu ʿanhā al-lisānu
sentences.l: And as for Sāsān, he entered upon Nuzhat al-Zamān, and she said to him: I see the people, there is no talk for them except about Kān Mā Kān, and they describe him with descriptions which the tongue is unable to-do.
