sentences.i: As for Sāsān, he went in to Nuzhat al-Zamān, and she said to him, “I see that people talk of nothing but Kān Mā Kān, and they praise him in terms beyond the power of the tongue to tell.”
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “went in upon”, is used of entering someone's presence, especially a ruler's or a lady's. Nuzhat al-Zamān is Sāsān's wife and Kān Mā Kān's aunt. bi- with waṣafa gives the qualities ascribed: “describe him with descriptions”. ʿajaza ʿan, “to be incapable of”: the tongue falls short of them.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا لَيْسَ الْخَبَرُ كَالْعِيَانِ فَإِنِّي رَأَيْتُهُ وَلَمْ أَرَ فِيهِ صِفَةً مِنْ صِفَاتِ الْكَمَالِ وَمَا كُلُّ مَا يُسْمَعُ يُقَالُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā laysa al-khabaru ka-al-ʿiyāni fa-innī raʾaytuhu wa-lam ara fīhi ṣifatan min ṣifāti al-kamāli wa-mā kullu mā yusmaʿu yuqālu
sentences.l: And he said to her: The report is not like the eye-witnessing, for I have seen him and I did not see in him a quality from the qualities of perfection; and not all that is heard is said.
sentences.i: He said to her, “Hearsay is not the same as seeing with one's own eyes. I have seen him, and I saw in him not one of the marks of perfection. Not everything one hears deserves repeating.”
sentences.n: laysa al-khabar ka-al-ʿiyān, “report is not like eyewitness”, is a proverb, also current as a Prophetic saying. wa-mā kullu mā yusmaʿu yuqālu, “not everything that is heard is (to be) said”, is another stock saying: one should not pass on all one hears. Sāsān, who has just ridden back with Kān Mā Kān, is now running him down.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنَّ النَّاسَ يُقَلِّدُ بَعْضُهُمْ بَعْضًا فِي مَدْحِهِ وَمَحَبَّتِهِ وَأَجْرَى اللَّهُ عَلَى أَلْسِنَةِ النَّاسِ مَدْحَهُ حَتَّى مَالَتْ إِلَيْهِ قُلُوبُ أَهْلِ بَغْدَادَ وَالْوَزِيرِ دَنْدَانَ الْغَادِرِ الْخَوَّانِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākinna al-nāsa yuqallidu baʿḍuhum baʿḍan fī madḥihi wa-maḥabbatihi wa-ajrā Allāhu ʿalā alsinati al-nāsi madḥahu ḥattā mālat ilayhi qulūbu ahli Baghdāda wa-al-wazīri Dandāna al-ghādiri al-khawwāni
sentences.l: But the people, some of them imitate others in praising him and loving him; and God made his praise run upon the tongues of the people, until there inclined to him the hearts of the people of Baghdad and of the vizier Dandān, the treacherous, the perfidious.
sentences.i: “But people copy one another in praising him and loving him, and God has set his praise running on everyone's tongue, until the hearts of the people of Baghdad have leaned towards him, and the heart of the vizier Dandān too, that treacherous traitor.
sentences.n: yuqallidu baʿḍuhum baʿḍan, “some of them imitate others”: taqlīd is following another's lead without judging for oneself. ajrā Allāhu ʿalā alsinat al-nās, “God caused to run on people's tongues”, is a set phrase for universal renown. al-wazīr is read in the genitive, joined to ahl Baghdād: the hearts of the people and of the vizier; Sāsān heaps on him ghādir, “treacherous”, and khawwān, “arrant traitor”, the print marking its doubled wāw.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ جَمَعَ لَهُ عَسَاكِرَ مِنْ سَائِرِ الْبُلْدَانِ وَمَنِ الَّذِي يَكُونُ مَالِكَ الْأَقْطَارِ وَيَرْضَى أَنْ يَكُونَ تَحْتَ يَدِ حَاكِمٍ يَتِيمٍ مَالَهُ مِقْدَارٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qad jamaʿa lahu ʿasākira min sāʾiri al-buldāni wa-mani alladhī yakūnu mālika al-aqṭāri wa-yarḍā an yakūna taḥta yadi ḥākimin yatīmin mā lahu miqdārun
sentences.l: And he has gathered for him armies from all the lands. And who is he who is master of the regions and consents to be under the hand of a ruler, an orphan, who has no worth?
sentences.i: He has gathered troops for him from every land. And who that is master of the realms would consent to stand under the hand of an orphan ruler of no account?”
sentences.n: The print points the kasra on mani, carried over to the following alladhī; the mark is kept. mālik al-aqṭār, “owner of the regions”, is Sāsān himself, who holds the throne; the yatīm, “orphan”, is Kān Mā Kān, whose father Ḍawʾ al-Makān is dead. mā lahu miqdār, “who has no measure”, i.e. of no standing; the print runs mā and lahu together as ماله, kept as one word.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ وَعَلَى مَا ذَا عَوَّلْتَ فَقَالَ لَهَا عَوَّلْتُ عَلَى قَتْلِهِ وَيَرْجِعُ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ خَائِبًا فِي قَصْدِهِ وَيَدْخُلُ تَحْتَ أَمْرِي وَطَاعَتِي وَلَا يَبْقَى لَهُ إِلّاَ خِدْمَتِى
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Nuzhatu al-Zamāni wa-ʿalā mā dhā ʿawwalta fa-qāla lahā ʿawwaltu ʿalā qatlihi wa-yarjiʿu al-wazīru Dandānu khāʾiban fī qaṣdihi wa-yadkhulu taḥta amrī wa-ṭāʿatī wa-lā yabqā lahu illā khidmatī
sentences.l: And Nuzhat al-Zamān said to him: And upon what have you resolved? And he said to her: I have resolved upon killing him, and the vizier Dandān returns disappointed in his aim, and enters under my command and my obedience, and there remains not for him except my service.
sentences.i: Nuzhat al-Zamān said to him, “And what have you resolved to do?” He answered, “I have resolved to kill him. Then the vizier Dandān will be thwarted in his design, and will come under my command and my obedience, and nothing will be left him but to serve me.”
sentences.n: ʿawwala ʿalā, “to rely on, resolve on”: “what have you set your mind on?”; the print marks the doubled wāw on the first ʿawwalta only. mā dhā is printed as two words, as often. wa-yarjiʿu ... wa-yadkhulu, “and (then) Dandān returns ... and enters”: plain imperfects for the expected result, where Classical might use fa- with the subjunctive. khidmatī is spelled with final ى.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ إِنَّ الْغَدْرَ قَبِيحٌ بِالْأَجَانِبِ فَكَيْفَ بِالْأَقَارِبِ وَالصَّوَابُ أَنْ تُزَوِّجَهُ ابْنَتَكَ قَضَى فَكَانَ وَتَسْمَعَ مَا قِيلَ فِيمَا مَضَى مِنَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu Nuzhatu al-Zamāni inna al-ghadra qabīḥun bi-al-ajānibi fa-kayfa bi-al-aqāribi wa-al-ṣawābu an tuzawwijahu ibnataka Qaḍā Fakāna wa-tasmaʿa mā qīla fīmā maḍā mina al-zamāni
sentences.l: And Nuzhat al-Zamān said to him: Indeed treachery is ugly with strangers, so how with kinsmen? And the right-course is that you marry him to your daughter Qaḍā Fakān, and that you hear what was said in what has passed of the time:
sentences.i: Nuzhat al-Zamān said to him, “Treachery is foul even towards strangers; how much more towards kin! The right course is to give him your daughter Qaḍā Fakān in marriage, and to heed what was said in days gone by:
sentences.n: qabīḥ bi-, “ugly in regard to”: treachery is shameful even when done to strangers. fa-kayfa bi-, “then how (much more) with”, is the regular a fortiori turn. ajānib and aqārib rhyme. ibnataka, “your daughter”: Qaḍā Fakān is Nuzhat al-Zamān's own child, brought up in Sāsān's household, and she speaks of her as his.

sentences.t:
اِذَا رَفَعَ الزَّمَانُ عَلَيْكَ شَخْصًا * وَكُنْتَ اَحَقُّ مِنْهُ وَلَوْ تَصَاعَدْ
اَنِلْهُ حَقَّ رُتْبَتِهِ تَجِدْهُ * يُنِيلُكَ اِنْ دَنَوْتَ وَاِنْ تَبَاعَدْ
وَلَا تَقُلِ الَّذِي تَدْرِيهِ فِيهِ * تَكُنْ مِمَّنْ عَنِ الْحُسْنَى تَقَاعَدْ
فَكَمْ فِى الْخِدْرِ اَبْهَى مِنْ عَرُوسٍ * وَلٰكِنْ لِلْعَرُوسِ الدَّهْرُ سَاعَدْ
sentences.tr:
idhā rafaʿa al-zamānu ʿalayka shakhṣan * wa-kunta aḥaqqu minhu wa-law taṣāʿad
anilhu ḥaqqa rutbatihi tajidhu * yunīluka in danawta wa-in tabāʿad
wa-lā taquli alladhī tadrīhi fīhi * takun mimman ʿani al-ḥusnā taqāʿad
fa-kam fī al-khidri abhā min ʿarūsin * wa-lākin li-al-ʿarūsi al-dahru sāʿad
sentences.l:
When the time raises above you a person * and you were more-deserving than him, even if he ascended,
give him the due of his rank, you will find him * granting you, whether you draw-near or he be-far;
and do not say that which you know about him, * you will be of those who from the fairest-course have held-back.
For how many in the curtained-chamber are more-splendid than a bride, * but for the bride the time has helped.
sentences.i:
When Time exalts a man above you, * though you deserve it more than he, however high he climbs,
give him the honour due his rank, and you will find * he grants you favour, whether you come near or he be far.
Do not speak out the faults you know in him, * or you will be of those who fall short of the nobler way.
How many in the curtained room outshine the bride! * Yet it is the bride whom Fortune chose to favour.
sentences.n: Metre wāfir; rhyme in -āʿad, the final verbs in pause. The print's pointing is kept throughout. In line 1 it has aḥaqqu, “more deserving”, with a ḍamma, where the predicate of kunta should be accusative, aḥaqqa; the ḍamma is kept as printed. taṣāʿad, “he rose”, and tabāʿad, “he was distant”, are past forms of the sixth stem pausally shortened for the rhyme (or imperfects with a dropped ta-). anilhu, “grant him”, is the imperative of the fourth stem anāla, and yunīluka answers it: honour him and he will honour you. al-khidr is the curtained recess of the women's quarters, where unmarried girls are kept from view; the last line says that many a girl there is fairer than the bride, but it was the bride whom fortune favoured.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ سَاسَانُ مِنْهَا هَذَا الْكَلَامَ وَفَهِمَ الشِّعْرَ وَالنِّظَامَ قَامَ مُغْضَبًا مِنْ عِنْدِهَا وَقَالَ لَوْلَا أَنَّ قَتْلَكِ عَارٌ وَشَنَارٌ لَعَلَوْتُ بِالسَّيْفِ رَأْسَكِ وَأَخْمَدْتُ أَنْفَاسَكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa Sāsānu minhā hādhā al-kalāma wa-fahima al-shiʿra wa-al-niẓāma qāma mughḍaban min ʿindihā wa-qāla lawlā anna qatlaki ʿārun wa-shanārun la-ʿalawtu bi-al-sayfi raʾsaki wa-akhmadtu anfāsaki
sentences.l: And when Sāsān heard from her this speech, and understood the verse and the ordering, he rose angered from beside her and said: Were-it-not that killing-you is a shame and a disgrace, I would have come-down with the sword upon your head and snuffed-out your breaths.
sentences.i: When Sāsān heard her say this, and understood the verses and their drift, he rose from her side in anger and said, “Were it not that killing you would be a shame and a disgrace, I would bring the sword down on your head and stop your breath for good.”
sentences.n: al-shiʿr wa-al-niẓām, “the verse and the arrangement”: a rhyming pair meaning the poem and how it was put together, that is, its whole drift. ʿār wa-shanār, “shame and disgrace”, is another stock rhyming pair. ʿalawtu bi-al-sayfi raʾsaki, literally “I would have topped your head with the sword”: ʿalā with a direct object, “to come down on, to strike from above”. The pronouns are feminine: he is speaking to his wife.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ حَيْثُ غَضِبْتَ مِنِّي فَأَنَا أَمْزَحُ مَعَكَ ثُمَّ وَثَبَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَتْ رَأْسَهُ وَيَدَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ الصَّوَابُ مَا تَرَاهُ وَسَوْفَ أَتَدَبَّرُ أَنَا وَأَنْتَ فِي حِيلَةٍ نَقْتُلُهُ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat ḥaythu ghaḍibta minnī fa-anā amzaḥu maʿaka thumma wathabat ilayhi wa-qabbalat raʾsahu wa-yadayhi wa-qālat lahu al-ṣawābu mā tarāhu wa-sawfa atadabbaru anā wa-anta fī ḥīlatin naqtuluhu bihā
sentences.l: And she said: Since you have-become-angry with-me, then I am joking with-you. Then she sprang to him and kissed his head and his two-hands and said to him: The right is what you see, and I shall contrive, I and you, a stratagem we kill him by.
sentences.i: She said, “Since you are angry with me, know that I was only jesting.” Then she sprang to him, kissed his head and his hands, and said to him, “What you think is right. You and I together will work out a plan by which we can kill him.”
sentences.n: ḥaythu, properly “where”, is used here as in much Middle Arabic for “since, seeing that”. fa-anā amzaḥu maʿaka, literally “I am joking with you”: the present stands for “I was only joking”. atadabbaru anā wa-anta, “I shall contrive, I and you”: the verb agrees with the first speaker and the other is tacked on, a loose colloquial pattern; tadabbara fī, “to think something out, plan”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ مِنْهَا هَذَا الْكَلَامَ فَرِحَ وَقَالَ لَهَا عَجِّلِي بِالْحِيلَةِ وَفَرِّجِي كُرْبَتِي فَلَقَدْ ضَاقَ عَلَيَّ بَابُ الْحِيَلِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa minhā hādhā al-kalāma fariḥa wa-qāla lahā ʿajjilī bi-al-ḥīlati wa-farrijī kurbatī fa-la-qad ḍāqa ʿalayya bābu al-ḥiyali
sentences.l: And when he heard from her this speech he rejoiced and said to her: Hasten with the stratagem and relieve my distress, for indeed the door of stratagems has-grown-narrow upon-me.
sentences.i: When he heard her say this he was glad, and said to her, “Be quick with your plan and ease my trouble, for every door of contrivance has closed on me.”
sentences.n: ʿajjila bi-, “to hurry something on”. farraja kurbatan, “to dispel a distress”, is a common pairing. ḍāqa ʿalayya bābu al-ḥiyal, “the door of stratagems has grown narrow on me”: I am at the end of my resources. The print marks the doubled letters of ʿajjilī, farrijī and ʿalayya.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ سَوْفَ أَتَحَيَّلُ لَكَ عَلَى إِتْلَافِ مُهْجَتِهِ فَقَالَ لَهَا بِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ بِجَارِيَتِنَا الَّتِي اسْمُهَا بَاكُونُ فَإِنَّهَا فِي الْمَكْرِ ذَاتُ فُنُونٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu sawfa ataḥayyalu laka ʿalā itlāfi muhjatihi fa-qāla lahā bi-ayyi shayʾin fa-qālat lahu bi-jāriyatinā allatī ismuhā Bākūnu fa-innahā fī al-makri dhātu funūnin
sentences.l: And she said to him: I shall scheme for you toward the destroying of his heart's-blood. And he said to her: By what thing? And she said to him: By our slave-girl whose name is Bākūn, for she in cunning is possessed-of arts.
sentences.i: She said to him, “I will find a way to take his life for you.” He asked her, “By what means?” She answered, “By our slave woman named Bākūn, for she is a mistress of every art of cunning.”
sentences.n: taḥayyala ʿalā, “to use a trick against, scheme toward”. muhja, “heart's blood, lifeblood”, so itlāf muhjatihi is “the destruction of his life”. Bākūn, the slave woman, appears here for the first time. dhātu funūn, “possessed of (many) arts”, rhymes with Bākūn: a touch of sajʿ.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةُ مِنْ أَنْحَسِ الْعَجَائِزِ وَعَدَمُ الْخُبْثِ فِي مَذْهَبِهَا غَيْرُ جَائِزٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat hādhihi al-jāriyatu min anḥasi al-ʿajāʾizi wa-ʿadamu al-khubthi fī madhhabihā ghayru jāʾizin
sentences.l: And this slave-girl was among the most-ill-omened of old-women, and the absence of wickedness in her creed was not permissible.
sentences.i: This slave woman was one of the most baleful of old crones, and in her creed it was not lawful to be without malice.
sentences.n: A rhymed pair (sajʿ) on ʿajāʾiz / jāʾiz. anḥas, elative of naḥs, “ill-omened, sinister”. The second clause is a mock-legal joke: ʿadam al-khubth, “the absence of wickedness”, is “not permissible” (ghayr jāʾiz, the jurists' word) in her madhhab, her “school of law, creed”. The print has the hamza seat in al-ʿajāʾiz and jāʾiz.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ قَدْ رَبَّتْ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَقَضَى فَكَانَ غَيْرَأَنَّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ يَمِيلُ إِلَيْهَا كَثِيرًا وَمِنْ فَرْطِ مَيْلِهِ إِلَيْهَا كَانَ يَنَامُ تَحْتَ رِجْلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: wa-kānat qad rabbat Kāna Mā Kāna wa-Qaḍā Fakāna ghayra anna Kāna Mā Kāna yamīlu ilayhā kathīran wa-min farṭi maylihi ilayhā kāna yanāmu taḥta rijlayhā
sentences.l: And she had reared Kān Mā Kān and Qaḍā Fakān; except-that Kān Mā Kān inclined to her much, and from the excess of his inclining to her he used-to sleep beneath her two-feet.
sentences.i: She had brought up both Kān Mā Kān and Qaḍā Fakān, but Kān Mā Kān was especially fond of her, so much so that he would sleep at her feet.
sentences.n: The print runs ghayra anna, “except that, but”, together as one word, ghayrān; it is kept so. The names Kān Mā Kān and Qaḍā Fakān are sentences frozen into names and do not decline. kāna yanāmu, “he used to sleep”: kāna with the imperfect for habit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ سَاسَانُ مِنْ زَوْجَتِهِ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ قَالَ إِنَّ هَذَا الرَّائَ هُوَ الصَّوَابُ ثُمَّ أَحْضَرَ الْجَارِيَةَ بَاكُونَ وَحَدَّثَهَا بِمَا جَرَى وَأَمَرَهَا أَنْ تَسْعَى فِي قَتْلِهِ وَوَعَدَهَا بِكُلِّ جَمِيلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku Sāsānu min zawjatihi hādhā al-kalāma qāla inna hādhā al-raʾya huwa al-ṣawābu thumma aḥḍara al-jāriyata Bākūna wa-ḥaddathahā bi-mā jarā wa-amarahā an tasʿā fī qatlihi wa-waʿadahā bi-kulli jamīlin
sentences.l: And when King Sāsān heard from his wife this speech, he said: Indeed this opinion, it is the right. Then he summoned the slave-girl Bākūn and told her of what had-passed, and commanded her to strive in killing him, and promised her every fair-thing.
sentences.i: When King Sāsān heard this from his wife, he said, “This plan is the right one.” Then he summoned the slave woman Bākūn, told her all that had happened, ordered her to see to killing him, and promised her every kindness.
sentences.n: al-rāʾ is the print's spelling of al-raʾy, “opinion, plan”, with the hamza set on a yāʾ seat at the end; it is read al-raʾya, accusative after inna. saʿā fī, “to work at, set about”. waʿadahā bi-kulli jamīl, “promised her every good thing”: a stock phrase for lavish reward.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ أَمْرُكَ مُطَاعٌ وَلَكِنْ أُرِيدُ يَامَوْلَاىَ أَنْ تُعْطِيَنِي خِنْجَرًا قَدْ سُقِيَ بِمَاءِ الْهَلَاكِ لِأُعَجِّلَ لَكَ بِإِتْلَافِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu amruka muṭāʿun wa-lākin urīdu yā mawlāya an tuʿṭiyanī khinjaran qad suqiya bi-māʾi al-halāki li-uʿajjila laka bi-itlāfihi
sentences.l: And she said to him: Your command is obeyed; but I want, O-my-lord, that you give me a dagger that has been watered with the water of perdition, that I may hasten for you his destroying.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Your command shall be obeyed. But I would ask you, my lord, to give me a dagger that has been tempered in deadly poison, so that I may make quick work of his death for you.”
sentences.n: The print has فقانت, a misprint for فقالت, corrected here; and later in the sentence باتلاقه, a misprint for باتلافه (bi-itlāfihi, “his destruction”), also corrected here. The print sets yā mawlāya, “O my lord”, as one word, with alif maqṣūra for the final yāʾ. khinjar suqiya bi-māʾ al-halāk, “a dagger watered with the water of perdition”: a blade quenched in poison.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا سَاسَانُ مَرْحَبًا بِكِ ثُمَّ أَحْضَرَ لَهَا خِنْجَرًا يَكَادُأَنْ يَسْبِقَ الْقَضَاءَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Sāsānu marḥaban biki thumma aḥḍara lahā khinjaran yakādu an yasbiqa al-qaḍāʾa
sentences.l: And Sāsān said to her: Welcome to-you. Then he brought her a dagger that almost outstrips the decree.
sentences.i: Sāsān said to her, “Gladly,” and he brought her a dagger that all but outran fate itself.
sentences.n: marḥaban biki, literally “welcome to you”, here simply “by all means, gladly”. The print runs yakādu an, “almost”, together as one word; it is kept so. yasbiqu al-qaḍāʾ, “outstrips the decree”: kills faster than destiny can arrive.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةُ قَدْ سَمِعَتِ الْحِكَايَاتِ وَالْأَشْعَارَ وَتَحْفَظُ النَّوَادِرَ وَالْأَخْبَارَ فَأَخَذَتِ الْخِنْجَرَ وَخَرَجَتْ مِنَ الدَّارِ مُفَكِّرَةً فِيمَا يَكُونُ بِهِ الدَّمَارُ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat hādhihi al-jāriyatu qad samiʿati al-ḥikāyāti wa-al-ashʿāra wa-taḥfaẓu al-nawādira wa-al-akhbāra fa-akhadhati al-khinjara wa-kharajat mina al-dāri mufakkiratan fīmā yakūnu bihi al-damāru
sentences.l: And this slave-girl had heard the tales and the poems, and kept-by-heart the rare-anecdotes and the reports; and she took the dagger and went-out from the house, pondering on what the destruction would be by.
sentences.i: Now this slave woman had heard many tales and poems and knew by heart curious anecdotes and histories. She took the dagger and left the house, turning over in her mind how his ruin might be brought about.
sentences.n: Sajʿ in -ār runs through the sentence: ashʿār, akhbār, dār, damār. nawādir, plural of nādira, “rare, witty anecdotes”. fī-mā yakūnu bihi al-damār, literally “on that by which the destruction would be”.

sentences.t: وَأَتَتْ إِلَى كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَهُوَ قَاعِدٌ يَنْتَظِرُ وَعْدَ السَّيِّدَةِ قَضَى فَكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-atat ilā Kāna Mā Kāna wa-huwa qāʿidun yantaẓiru waʿda al-sayyidati Qaḍā Fakāna
sentences.l: And she came to Kān Mā Kān while he was sitting, awaiting the promise of the lady Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.i: She came to Kān Mā Kān as he sat waiting for the lady Qaḍā Fakān to keep her promise.
sentences.n: The print has اى, a misprint for الى, corrected here. waʿd, “promise”, here the tryst Qaḍā Fakān had promised him.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ قَدْ تَذَكَّرَ بِنْتَ عَمِّهِ قَضَى فَكَانَ فَالْتَهَبَتْ مِنْ حُبِّهَا فِي قَلْبِهِ النِّيرَانُ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna fī tilka al-laylati qad tadhakkara binta ʿammihi Qaḍā Fakāna fa-iltahabat min ḥubbihā fī qalbihi al-nīrānu
sentences.l: And he had on that night remembered the daughter of his paternal-uncle, Qaḍā Fakān, and there blazed from love-of-her in his heart the fires.
sentences.i: That night he had been thinking of his cousin Qaḍā Fakān, and the fires of love for her blazed up in his heart.
sentences.n: bint ʿammihi, “his paternal uncle's daughter”, his cousin, the match Arab custom favoured. The subject al-nīrān, “the fires”, is held back to the end of the sentence for rhyme and emphasis.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ كَذَلِكَ وَإِذَا بِالْجَارِيَةِ بَاكُونَ دَاخِلَةً عَلَيْهِ وَهِيَ تَقُولُ آنَ أَوَانُ الْوِصَالِ وَمَضَتْ أَيَّامُ الِانْفِصَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-al-jāriyati Bākūna dākhilatan ʿalayhi wa-hiya taqūlu āna awānu al-wiṣāli wa-maḍat ayyāmu al-infiṣāli
sentences.l: And while he was thus, and behold, the slave-girl Bākūn coming-in upon him, and she saying: The time of union has come, and the days of separation have passed.
sentences.i: While he was in this state, in came the slave woman Bākūn, saying, “The hour of union is here, and the days of parting are over.”
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- only marks who appears, and dākhilatan, “coming in”, describes her as she does. āna awānu al-wiṣāl, “the time of union has come”, rhymes with ayyām al-infiṣāl, “the days of separation”: a lovers' formula in sajʿ. The print has the madda in āna.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ ذَلِكَ قَالَ لَهَا كَيْفَ حَالُ قَضَى فَكَانَ فَقَالَتْ لَهُ بَاكُونُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّهَا مُشْتَغِلَةٌ بِحُبِّكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu dhālika qāla lahā kayfa ḥālu Qaḍā Fakāna fa-qālat lahu Bākūnu iʿlam annahā mushtaghilatun bi-ḥubbika
sentences.l: And when I heard that, he said to her: How is the state of Qaḍā Fakān? And Bākūn said to him: Know that she is occupied with love-of-you.
sentences.i: When he heard this, he asked her, “How is Qaḍā Fakān?” Bākūn answered, “Know that she is wholly taken up with love for you.”
sentences.n: The print has سمعت, samiʿtu, “I heard”, though it is Kān Mā Kān who hears and answers. It may be a misprint for سمع, “he heard”, or the narrator slipping into the first person, as happens elsewhere in this tale (Night 141); it is kept as printed. mushtaghila bi-, “busy with, absorbed in”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قَامَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ إِلَيْهَا وَخَلَعَ أَثْوَابَهُ عَلَيْهَا وَوَعَدَهَا بِكُلِّ جَمِيلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāma Kāna Mā Kāna ilayhā wa-khalaʿa athwābahu ʿalayhā wa-waʿadahā bi-kulli jamīlin
sentences.l: And at that Kān Mā Kān rose to her and took-off his garments upon her and promised her every fair-thing.
sentences.i: At this Kān Mā Kān rose and went to her, bestowed his own garments on her, and promised her every kindness.
sentences.n: khalaʿa thiyābahu / athwābahu ʿalā, literally “to strip off one's clothes onto someone”, is the gesture of reward: he gives her the clothes off his back.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي أَنَامُ عِنْدَكَ اللَّيْلَةَ وَأُحَدِّثُكَ بِمَا سَمِعْتُ مِنَ الْكَلَامِ وَأُسَلِّيكَ بِحَدِيثِ كُلِّ مُتَيَّمٍ أَمْرَضَهُ الْغَرَامُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu iʿlam annī anāmu ʿindaka al-laylata wa-uḥaddithuka bi-mā samiʿtu mina al-kalāmi wa-usallīka bi-ḥadīthi kulli mutayyamin amraḍahu al-gharāmu
sentences.l: And she said to him: Know that I shall sleep with-you tonight, and tell you of what I have heard of talk, and divert you with the story of every love-enslaved-one whom passion has made-sick.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Know that I will spend the night with you, and tell you the talk I have heard, and while away your hours with tales of every slave of love whom passion has laid low.”
sentences.n: anāmu ʿindaka, “I shall sleep at your place”: she will keep him company through the night, no more. mutayyam, “enslaved by love, love-crazed”. kalām / gharām make a closing rhyme.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ حَدِّثِينِي بِحَدِيثٍ يَفْرَحُ بِهِ قَلْبِي وَيَزُولُ بِهِ كَرْبِي فَقَالَتْ لَهُ بَاكُونُ حُبًّا وَكَرَامَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā Kāna Mā Kāna ḥaddithīnī bi-ḥadīthin yafraḥu bihi qalbī wa-yazūlu bihi karbī fa-qālat lahu Bākūnu ḥubban wa-karāmatan
sentences.l: And Kān Mā Kān said to her: Tell-me a story my heart rejoices by and my distress passes-away by. And Bākūn said to him: Lovingly and honourably.
sentences.i: Kān Mā Kān said to her, “Tell me a story to gladden my heart and lift my grief.” Bākūn answered, “With all my heart and gladly.”
sentences.n: ḥubban wa-karāmatan, literally “out of love and honour”, the stock reply of willing consent: “with pleasure”. qalbī / karbī rhyme.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَلَسَتْ إِلَى جَانِبِهِ وَذَلِكَ الْخِنْجَرُ مِنْ دَاخِلِ أَثْوَابِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma jalasat ilā jānibihi wa-dhālika al-khinjaru min dākhili athwābihā
sentences.l: Then she sat at his side, and that dagger was from inside her garments.
sentences.i: Then she sat down beside him, the dagger hidden beneath her clothes.
sentences.n: A circumstantial clause with no verb: wa-dhālika al-khinjaru min dākhili athwābihā, “that dagger (being) inside her clothes”. min dākhil, “inside”, is colloquial in flavour.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ أَعْذَبَ مَا سَمِعَتْ أُذُنِي أَنَّ رَجُلًا كَانَ يَعْشَقُ الْمِلَاحَ وَصَرَفَ عَلَيْهِنَّ مَالَهُ حَتَّى افْتَقَرَ وَصَارَ لَا يَمْلِكُ شَيْأً
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu iʿlam anna aʿdhaba mā samiʿat udhunī anna rajulan kāna yaʿshaqu al-milāḥa wa-ṣarafa ʿalayhinna mālahu ḥattā iftaqara wa-ṣāra lā yamliku shayʾan
sentences.l: And she said to him: Know that the sweetest of what my ear has heard is that a man used-to love the beauties, and spent on them his wealth until he became-poor and came-to own nothing.
sentences.i: She said to him, “Know that the sweetest tale my ears have ever heard is this. There was once a man who was enamoured of pretty women, and he spent his wealth on them until he was ruined and owned nothing at all.
sentences.n: al-milāḥ, plural of malīḥa, “the pretty ones”. ṣāra, “to become”, with a following imperfect, “came to be someone who owns nothing”. shayʾan: the print writes it with the hamza on an alif seat, شيأ.

sentences.t: فَضَاقَتْ عَلَيْهِ الدُّنْيَا فَصَارَ يَمْشِي فِى الْأَسْوَاقِ وَيُفَتِّشُ عَلَى شَيْءٍ يَقْتَاتُ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍāqat ʿalayhi al-dunyā fa-ṣāra yamshī fī al-aswāqi wa-yufattishu ʿalā shayʾin yaqtātu bihi
sentences.l: And the world grew-narrow upon him, and he took-to walking in the markets and searching for a thing he might feed by.
sentences.i: The world closed in on him, and he took to wandering the markets, looking for something to live on.
sentences.n: ṣāra yamshī, “he began to walk”: ṣāra with the imperfect marks a new habit. fattasha ʿalā, “to search for”, is colloquial; Classical prefers fattasha ʿan. iqtāta bi-, “to feed oneself on, subsist on”.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ مَاشٍ وَإِذَا بِقِطْعَةِ مِسْمَارٍ شَكَّتْهُ فِى إِصْبَعِهِ فَسَالَ دَمُهُ فَقَعَدَ وَمَسَحَ الدَّمَ وَعَصَبَ إِصْبَعَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa māshin wa-idhā bi-qiṭʿati mismārin shakkathu fī iṣbaʿihi fa-sāla damuhu fa-qaʿada wa-masaḥa al-dama wa-ʿaṣaba iṣbaʿahu
sentences.l: And while he was walking, and behold, a piece of a nail pricked him in his finger, and his blood flowed; and he sat and wiped the blood and bound his finger.
sentences.i: As he was walking along, a bit of a nail suddenly pierced his finger and drew blood. He sat down, wiped away the blood and bound up his finger.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-, “and behold”: the bi- simply marks the thing that turns up, here the stray nail. shakka, “to prick, pierce”; the print marks its doubled kāf.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ وَهُوَ يَصْرُخُ حَتَّى جَازَ عَلَى الْحَمَّامِ وَدَخَلَهَا ثُمَّ قَلَعَ ثِيَابَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma wa-huwa yaṣrukhu ḥattā jāza ʿalā al-ḥammāmi wa-dakhalahā thumma qalaʿa thiyābahu
sentences.l: Then he rose, crying-out, until he passed by the bath, and entered it; then he pulled-off his clothes.
sentences.i: Then he got up, crying out, and went on until he came by the bathhouse. He went in and took off his clothes.
sentences.n: jāza ʿalā, “to pass by”, is Middle Arabic usage (Classical jāza means “to pass through, cross”). al-ḥammām is masculine, but the text refers to it with the feminine pronoun, dakhalahā, “entered it”, as often in the Nights. qalaʿa thiyābahu, “pulled off his clothes”, is colloquial for Classical nazaʿa or khalaʿa.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارَ دَاخِلَ الْحَمَّامِ وَجَدَهَا نَظِيفَةً فَجَلَسَ عَلَى الْفَسْقِيَّةِ وَمَا زَالَ يَنْزَحُ الْمَاءَ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ إِلَى أَنْ تَعِبَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣāra dākhila al-ḥammāmi wajadahā naẓīfatan fa-jalasa ʿalā al-fasqiyyati wa-mā zāla yanzaḥu al-māʾa ʿalā raʾsihi ilā an taʿiba
sentences.l: And when he was inside the bath he found it clean, and he sat at the fountain-basin and did not cease drawing the water onto his head until he tired.
sentences.i: Once inside, he found the bath clean, so he sat down by the basin and kept drawing water and pouring it over his head until he was weary.
sentences.n: Again the feminine pronoun for al-ḥammām: wajadahā, “he found it”. naẓīfa, “clean”; possibly, as sometimes in late usage, “clear, empty of people”, which would suit what follows, but this is a guess. fasqiyya, “fountain basin”, a post-classical word. nazaḥa, “to draw (water) out”: he scoops it up and pours it over himself.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she ceased the speech allowed her.
